cia-0000102954:
Incarceration of Prisoners is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102954, dated March 2, 1986. The sample text covers Soviet practice across 1955 to 1979. It explains what happened to a prisoner after an investigation ended and a court had passed sentence.

After sentencing, the prisoner was moved to a labor camp, except that grave crimes could bring up to five years in prison first. For theft and hooliganism, the investigation usually lasted about two months, though it could run longer with permission. Prisons were usually overcrowded, yet no new ones were planned, a choice one Estonian official tied to ideology.
cia-0000108154: The Significance of the New Indonesian Government is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000108154, dated August 5, 1953. The heading asks what a new government in Indonesia meant, in one word: significance. No leader or party is named in the title itself. The brief record is a government change item from the summer of 1953 in the files.
cia-0000115454: Insurgency and Instability in Central America -- National Intelligence Estimate is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000115454, dated August 5, 1981. The title marks a formal estimate on unrest across one region, Central America. Two linked words, insurgency and instability, fill the front of the heading. The brief record is a regional estimate item from the summer of 1981 as released.
cia-0000119754: An October 1956 status report on Hungary, given by the CIA Director at the White House to a bipartisan group of leaders. The heading breaks off before finishing that word, but the setting is clear: the agency chief briefing both parties as the crisis deepened. Briefing leaders of both parties together was crisis practice in Washington, meant to keep the response united while events abroad moved at revolutionary speed.
cia-0000132654:
The views of Latin American governments toward Cuba are surveyed in a CIA paper dated January 1, 1961. The American break with Havana was days away, and the region was picking sides fast. Mexico stood apart from the rest, as it often did on Cuba.

Most other governments leaned toward Washington, though with varied warmth. The paper sets out each stance as analysts read it at the new year. For readers, it is a map of the hemisphere at a turning point. The lines drawn that winter would hold, with few changes, through the invasion spring that followed.
cia-0000136254: Dated 6 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records the location of CADICK, delegation of authority, and Calligeris, the chain of command mapped. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136354: An objective look at the aircraft problem opens this June 1954 LINCOLN cable. SYNCARP planes in Guatemala City would stand out either way. The planes could pass close inspection. But they would raise hard questions. How many planes are there? Who flew them? Who bombed which target? Answers would need an elaborate story. All would have to stick to it under investigation. Blaming military prerogative raises its own risks. The cable weighs exposure against use.
cia-0000136854: Rifle configurations cause a problem in this January 1954 cable to the senior representative at LINCOLN. Overall length with folding stock and barrel extension removed is thirty-six inches. An immediate reply is needed on whether any named category is satisfactory so work can continue; the writer's opinion is that none is completely satisfactory, though they may have to suffice. Shortening the barrel would widen the dispersion pattern at fifty yards and above, and disassembly takes two to five minutes under stress.
cia-0000136954: Hold a conference with Jimenez, REELFOOT is urged in this May 1954 cable, and return for debriefing when negotiations complete. CALLIGERIS requested representation with Jimenez, and Estrada was sent to confer with him and survey the situation on the spot. At a cordial meeting, CALLIGERIS said he needed three planes and pilots, preferably P-51s, to counterbalance Guatemala's new arms shipment; failing that, 200,000 dollars. Estrada promised to pass the request to Jimenez and send an answer soonest.
un-ga-res-a-69-54:
Many voices, not one, must shape arms deals, argues Resolution A/69/54, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its theme is the push for joint, many-sided work in disarmament and against the spread of arms. The text recalls a 2001 vote that tied such work to the fight against terror, and a chain of votes since 2002 on the same theme.

The UN's core aim frames the call: to guard peace by joint steps that head off threats and halt attacks on the peace. Arms questions, in this view, are too big for any one state or bloc to settle alone. Deals struck by all, the Assembly holds, are the deals that last.
un-sc-res-54:
Palestine crossed a legal line in Security Council Resolution 54, passed on 15 July 1948. The stopgap state of Israel had agreed in the main to stretch the truce in the land. The states of the Arab League had turned down plea after plea, from the UN mediator and from the Council, to do the same. Fighting had flared up anew in the land as a result.

The Council rules that the state of Palestine is a threat to the peace, in the terms of Article 39 of the Charter. It orders all states and chiefs in the fight to halt all armed acts. Cease-fire orders must go out to their troops, at a time the mediator will fix. It was the first such ruling of the young Council's life.
un-sc-res-354: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 354, which the catalog dates to 1974. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-1154: This library holds Resolution 1154 as an official Council record, dated 1998 in its catalog. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1454: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 1454 is catalogued here under 1990. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1554: Resolution 1554 survives as part of the Council's official record, transcribed for this collection by English Wikisource. The Security Council acts for the whole UN membership on peace and security, and its resolutions are the proof of that work. Inside this text, recitals establish the grounds and numbered clauses carry the decision itself.
un-sc-res-1754: In 2007 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1754, preserved here through a transcription of the official record. Such texts are negotiated until fifteen governments can live with every clause, which gives the final wording its careful tone. The entry keeps the final wording, so readers meet the compromise exactly as it was struck.
un-sc-res-2254:
Resolution 2254 set out the Security Council's roadmap for ending Syria's civil war. Years of fighting had killed huge numbers of people and driven millions from the country. For once, the United States and Russia backed the same text.

The plan calls for talks between Syria's government and opposition, a ceasefire, a new constitution, and free elections under UN supervision within eighteen months. It also demands aid access to besieged towns. Readers get the full diplomatic blueprint that later peace talks kept returning to, even as the war went on. The vote itself was unanimous.
cia-0000132754:
Most Cuba papers in this record look at the island alone, but this CIA briefing of January 4, 1961 pairs Cuba with Central America. It was written the day after the United States cut diplomatic ties with Havana. Analysts were already asking where Cuban influence might spread next.

That wider lens is the paper's point: Castro's revolution treated as a regional force, not a local event. Washington feared friendly governments or movements taking root in nearby countries. Preserved through the CIA Reading Room, the briefing shows the post-break alarm extending across the map of Central America.
cia-0000135754: A Spanish document dated 2 February 1961, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force. February 1961 was a month of final training before the brigade embarked for Cuba. The catalog record names no subject for this item. Preserved in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated piece of the brigade's own archive from the operation's last weeks of preparation.
cia-0000136554: Dated 3 October 1960, this Spanish-language document comes from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was in training that fall, growing under CIA direction toward the force that would land in Cuba. The catalog record gives no subject for the item. It is held in the original Spanish, a primary source from the brigade's buildup period, released decades later with the rest of its archive.
cia-0000136754: An estimated date of 1 January 1961 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, with the estimate marked in the catalog title. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, then in winter training. The record gives the document no subject. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the turn-of-the-year records in the brigade's archive, its timing approximate by the catalog's own account.
plos-pone-0000054:
Mathijs Baens, Heidi Noels, Vicky Broeckx, and co-authors exposed a flaw in a beloved lab tool in a 2006 paper. EGFP, a glowing green protein from jellyfish, is attached to other proteins so scientists can watch them move inside living cells. Labs worldwide trusted it as a passive tag that changes nothing.

The team found the dark side of that title: EGFP shows defective polyubiquitination, meaning the cell's tagging system for disposing of proteins handles it abnormally. A marker that bends the very process under study can mislead experiments on protein breakdown, a field central to cancer and brain disease. The paper is a caution that tools are part of the experiment.
un-sc-res-754:
Security Council Resolution 754, adopted on May 18, 1992, recommended Slovenia for membership in the United Nations. Some catalog notes give this vote to Croatia; in fact Croatia's bid was handled in the companion text adopted the same day, and this one names Slovenia. The Alpine republic had broken from Yugoslavia in June 1991 and held its freedom through a short war.

The Assembly seated Slovenia on May 22. Admission mattered beyond form: Yugoslavia's seat was in dispute, and each successor republic needed its own place in the world body. The short resolution is one step in the legal unmaking of a federation, taken while wars in Croatia and Bosnia were still raging.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d54: On October 23, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt once more, and the message became Document 54 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow Conference was in its middle days, and London was weighing what the talks would mean for the summit ahead. The record for this note gives the date and the names. Its contents are a matter for the printed text in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d154: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt dated November 21, 1943 stands as Document 154 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It shares its date with two companions, written as the parties settled into Cairo on the conference's eve. The catalog record gives no topic for this note and assigns none should be made for it. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the other papers of that crowded day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d254:
A meeting between Patrick Hurley and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek at Cairo on 23 November 1943 is covered by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. Flash-WAM distills a large multimodal world model into a smaller one, with modality-aware distillation that respects what each sense contributes. The goal is compact world models cheap enough to run inside real robots and agents.
arxiv-2606-05554: Economists assume people dislike risk, but does risk aversion actually change anything when risks shift over time? This irrelevance theorem shows that under time-varying risk, risk aversion can wash out — preferences that look important prove mathematically irrelevant. The result trims a beloved assumption down to where it truly matters.
arxiv-2606-05654: Content moderators judge posts written in code-mixed language — Hindi-English, Spanglish — but the same content in different surface forms gets different verdicts. This paired study shows surface form changes moderation decisions, exposing workflow instability. Inconsistent moderation is unfair moderation, and the paper quantifies exactly how shaky it is.
arxiv-2606-05754: Fiber optic cables can hear — distributed acoustic sensing turns them into thousands of microphones. This paper advances Sagnac-assisted enhanced phi-OTDR for that task, with a standardized benchmark and engineering evaluation framework. Standard tests let the industry compare sensing systems honestly instead of cherry-picking results.
arxiv-2606-06054: Personal AI agents remember your life — but retrieving memories by similarity alone surfaces plausible-sounding falsehoods. This paper moves beyond similarity to trustworthy memory search: retrieval that weighs evidence and provenance. Trustworthy memory is what separates a helpful assistant from a confident fabulist.
arxiv-2606-06154: Personalizing a foundation model on each user's device — federated adaptation — is expensive when done naively. This paper amortizes the cost with hypernetwork-driven LoRA: one network that generates personalized adapters cheaply. Amortized personalization makes private on-device AI practical for everyone.
arxiv-2606-06254: Pruning a code model to run cheaper risks dulling its defenses — especially against adversarial code mutations that sneak past. SecRL-Prune uses structured reinforcement learning to prune CodeLLMs while preserving that adversarial robustness. The method keeps models lean without making them gullible.
arxiv-2606-06554: Terahertz spectroscopy fingerprints polymers — but the spectra are subtle. This multi-scale feature attention network classifies polymers from those fingerprints, attending across scales. The method turns faint THz wiggles into reliable material IDs. Non-destructive testing gets a powerful new eye.
arxiv-2606-06754: Grading analytic essays usually needs trained models or tired humans. MADRAG scores them training-free: multi-agent debate with retrieval-augmented generation, where agents argue about the essay's merits. Debate plus evidence makes for fairer automated grading. The method grades essays without any training.
arxiv-2606-07254: Tracking non-Abelian quantum states over long horizons needs falsifiers — tests that catch wrong models. This held-out transition-pair falsifier does that job. The falsifier keeps long-horizon tracking honest. Wrong quantum models must be caught early. Principled falsification keeps long-horizon tracking honest.
tob-10554:
James Legge rendered Lao Tzu's eighty-one chapters again here under the fuller title The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and Its Characteristics. Legge, the Scottish missionary who became Oxford's first professor of Chinese, translated with a scholar's precision and copious notes. His version first made Chinese philosophy legible to many English readers.

The paradoxes remain intact, starting with the warning that the Tao that can be named is not the eternal Tao. Chapters on ruling without interference, the strength of weakness, and the uses of emptiness follow. Readers meet a Victorian landmark of translation, where careful notes surround verses that resist every attempt to pin them down.
tob-13554:
Extracts from al-Ghazali's Ihya, his Revival of the Religious Sciences, present some religious and moral teachings in digestible portions. Intention, gratitude, patience, and the diseases of the heart are among the subjects drawn from that vast manual. Al-Ghazali wrote the Ihya after his spiritual crisis, to rebuild religious life from the inside.

Shorter and more directly useful than his autobiography, these selections show the theologian as moral physician, diagnosing pride, envy, and heedlessness and prescribing remedies. The Ihya became Islam's classic manual of the inner life. Readers pressed for time can meet its central teaching here, then turn to the Confessions for the author's own story.
tob-4054:
Volume one of a four-volume edition of H. P. Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine carries the subtitle Cosmogenesis, Theosophy's creation story in full. Blavatsky presents stanzas from a claimed archaic book, the Book of Dzyan, surrounded by her vast commentary. The universe unfolds through cycles, rounds, and planes across unimaginable spans of time.

Hindu time-cycles blend with Victorian geology and evolutionary language as spirit descends toward matter. The commentary argues with contemporary science while borrowing its scale. Readers beginning the four-volume set should expect density and digression; the opening volume lays the cosmology on which the later volumes build their accounts of humanity, symbolism, and hidden history.
tob-4254:
A French study of Haitian Vodou spirits appeared in 1918 under the title Les Daimons du Culte Voudo, credited to the pen name Her-Ra-Ma-el. European readers of its day knew Vodou mostly through rumor and fright. The study instead catalogs the lwa, the spirits of the cult, one by one.

Rites, offerings, songs, and the families of spirits receive orderly treatment. Rada and Petro nations, healing and work spirits, the dead and the waters: the pantheon takes shape for a French audience. Verified from the 1919 edition, the book stands as an early European attempt to describe Haitian religion as its worshippers practice it.
afr-200-2-ufo-reporting-1954:
The Air Force gave its UFO hunt a rule book on August 12, 1954. Regulation 200-2 names the things UFOBs, sets the reporting chain for the whole service, and clamps the press line on hard cases. Chief of Staff Nathan Twining signed the order himself.

Each sighting of weight was to move up the chain in set form, with care and speed. Only a small desk in Washington could speak in public on the cases that stayed unsolved. The rule was Blue Book's spine for its whole life. It turned saucer reports into office routine across the whole force.
ennemoser-history-of-magic-vol-1-1854:
Joseph Ennemoser gave magic a grave past in The History of Magic, Vol. I, in English dress from 1854. William Howitt turned the German text to English. Ennemoser was a healer who held that trance and dreams hint at deep laws of the mind. He traces rites from old tribes to the age of the church.

Dreams, spells, and wild cures get a fair, calm look. He treats the theme as fit for true study. The pair of tomes is the age's great past of magic. This first half lays the broad base. Howitt, who turned the text, was a poet and tale smith too. His smooth prose helped the dense German work find a wide English crowd.
ennemoser-history-of-magic-vol-2-1854:
Joseph Ennemoser brings his long past of magic to a close in The History of Magic, Vol. II, in English from 1854. William Howitt's turn of the German text fills this tome as in the first. The tale runs on through witch hunts, seers, and the trance cures of Ennemoser's own day and land.

He asks what part is fraud, what part is law of mind. His calm, grave tone sets the work past mere tales of spooks. Read with the first tome, it is the age's chief past of magic. Its reach spans two fat tomes. Ennemoser came from the Tyrol hills and healed the sick by trance. His own cures feed the last parts of this long, grave survey.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen works through the kings in Vol. 2 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1854. The first tome laid out sources and script. Here the tale runs king by king, age by age, as Bunsen fits Egypt's long line into the frame of the world's past as his age knew it.

Lists, dates, and clashes with the Good Book fill the tome. His sums are now seen as too grand in span. Yet his reach taught the field to think big. The work is a vast, brave try.
brewster-more-worlds-one-1854:
David Brewster was a Scots man of science famed for his work on light. His More Worlds than One came out in 1854. The book is a direct reply to Whewell's tract of the year past. Its full title calls it the creed of the thinker and the hope of the Christian.

Brewster holds that a wise God would not leave vast worlds bare of life. He works through the planets and stars with the best facts of the day. Faith and star science walk side by side in his case. The book kept the claim of many lived-in worlds in fine health.
theologia-germanica-1854:
Theologia Germanica is a small book of soul lore from 1300s Germany. No name sits on the work; a priest of Frankfurt may have wrote it. Susanna Winkworth gave it English dress in 1854. Martin Luther had praised the book three hundred years past.

The text bids the soul let go of self will and rest in God. It sets the life of Christ as the path each soul must walk. Calm, plain words hide a deep and hard call to yield all. The wee book swayed Luther, the first church rebels, and mystics since.
thoreau-walden-1854:
Henry David Thoreau published Walden in 1854, his experiment in deliberate living at Walden Pond. The book is the founding text of environmental thought and simple-living philosophy in the American tradition today. Thoreau lived two years in a cabin he built on Emerson's land by the pond.

He tills beans, watches ants war, and sounds the pond's depth through winter ice in Concord. Economy preaches cutting wants, while Brute Neighbors and Winter Animals crowd the pages with keen natural seeing in detail. The seasons turn one full round, spring's thaw standing for the soul's rebirth in his famous close here. Simplify, simplify is the book's household motto, and its challenge still nettles comfortable readers in every age. Few American books have been reread so often for so many different reasons.
nerval-daughters-of-fire-1854:
Gérard de Nerval published Daughters of Fire in 1854, his linked stories, here in English translation for readers. The set holds Sylvie, Émilie, and Octavie, the dreamlike heart of French Romanticism in its late flower. Nerval, who walked a lobster on a blue ribbon in Paris, wrote these tales between spells of madness.

Sylvie, the crown of the set, shuttles between a village girl, a dancer, and a lost actress in Valois. Memory and present blur until the narrator cannot tell which love, or which year, he truly inhabits at all. Octavie and Émilie mix travel, theatre, and occult longing in Nerval's limpid, haunted prose of dream and waking. He hanged himself in 1855, weeks after the book appeared, and France slowly learned what it had lost in him. Proust and the surrealists later claimed these tales as scripture.
philo-yonge-vol1-1854:
Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher of the first century who read the Torah through Greek philosophy. Yonge's 1854 first volume of his complete works in English appeared in Bohn's Classical Library. It made Philo's full range open to Victorian readers for the first time.

Philo treats the stories of Genesis as allegories of the soul while holding fast to Jewish law and worship. His idea of the Logos, the divine word that orders the world, bridges Greek thought and later Christian theology. This volume holds his accounts of creation and the lives of the patriarchs.
edwards-freedom-of-will-1754:
Edwards's Inquiry into the Freedom of the Will, published in 1754, is the American Calvinist's great work of philosophy. He wrote it against Arminian writers who taught that the will must be free from all motive to be moral. The book defends determinism joined to moral agency.

Edwards argues that the will always chooses as the strongest motive inclines it, and that this costs us no true liberty. A person is free, in his account, when nothing stops him from doing what he most wants. The argument's tight logic still anchors debate on freedom, sin, and responsibility.
philo-yonge-vol2-1854:
Volume two of Yonge's Works of Philo Judaeus, published in 1854, holds Philo's allegorical commentaries on Genesis. Here Philo reads the creation story and the lives of the patriarchs as maps of the soul. The great treatises on the creation and on the virtues stand in this volume.

Abraham's journey becomes the soul's schooling, Sarah and Hagar become wisdom and its handmaid, and each command hides an inner sense. Yonge's plain Victorian English keeps Philo's dense Greek argument readable for students without the language. The volume shows Philo's fusion of Torah and Platonism at its most inventive.
philo-yonge-vol3-1854:
Volume three of Yonge's Philo, published in 1854, gathers the historical and apologetic works. Philo steps out of allegory here to defend his people before Rome and record their recent past. The Life of Moses and the Embassy to Gaius anchor the volume.

The Embassy tells how Philo led a Jewish delegation to the emperor Caligula after riots against the Jews of Alexandria. His account is an eyewitness record of Jewish life under Roman power at a moment of crisis. Historians prize this volume beside the allegories, since it preserves facts found in few other sources.
philo-yonge-vol4-1854:
Volume four of Yonge's Philo, published in 1854, completes the first English Philo with the Questions and Answers on Genesis and Exodus. Philo poses a question on a verse, then answers it on two levels, the literal and the allegorical. The form shows his classroom method at work.

Why did God plant a tree in Eden, why did Cain build a city, and what do the plagues of Egypt mean? Each answer turns law and story into teaching on the soul's growth and God's care. With this volume, English readers gained the whole surviving Philo in their own tongue.
feuerbach-essence-christianity-eliot-185:
Ludwig Feuerbach's Essence of Christianity appeared in English in 1854, translated by Marian Evans, who wrote as George Eliot. Feuerbach, a German philosopher, argued that God is a picture of human nature itself. The translation was Eliot's only work published under her real name.

Feuerbach held that qualities praised in God, such as love, wisdom, and justice, are human qualities projected upward. Religion, then, is humanity worshipping its own best image without knowing it. The argument shook German and British thought and fed later critiques of religion. Eliot's clear English carried the work into Victorian debates about faith, doubt, and what worship really means.
nott-gliddon-types-mankind-1854:
Josiah Clark Nott and George Robins Gliddon published Types of Mankind in 1854 in Philadelphia. Nott was an Alabama physician and Gliddon a popular lecturer on Egypt. Their large, illustrated treatise argued for polygenism, the claim that human races were created separately and unequally.

Chapters on skulls, ancient monuments, and natural history built a case that served the defense of slavery in America. The book was a bestseller and a scientific scandal at once, praised by slaveholders and attacked by clergy and later scientists. Modern scholars cite it as a foundational text in the history of scientific racism. It is kept and studied as evidence of how science was bent to serve bondage.
racine-phedre-french-1854:
Jean Racine wrote Phèdre in 1677, at the height of his career as France's leading playwright. The text here is the French original, in the Didot edition of 1854. Phèdre, wife of King Theseus, burns with a forbidden love for her stepson Hippolytus and cannot master it.

Phèdre's confession sets off a chain of lies, rage, and deaths. Theseus curses his son, Hippolytus dies, and Phèdre takes poison after clearing his name. Racine tells the tragedy in strict, shining verse, with few characters and great pressure. French readers rank Phèdre as the summit of their classical theater, a study of passion and shame.
keller-green-henry-1854:
Gottfried Keller, the Swiss writer, published Green Henry in German in 1854 and 1855. The text here comes from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, since no English translation is in the public domain. Heinrich Lee, nicknamed for his green coat, tells the story of his own youth and failed hopes.

Heinrich dreams of painting, drifts to Munich, and learns how thin his talent runs. Love, money trouble, and pride delay his return to his patient mother in Zurich. Keller drew the tale from his own life, softened by humor and hindsight. The novel ranks beside Wilhelm Meister among German artist novels. Its rich village and city scenes made it the great Swiss novel of growth.
bentivoglio-wars-of-flanders-1654:
Guido Bentivoglio, a cardinal who had served as papal nuncio at Brussels, wrote Della guerra di Fiandra in 1632. Henry Carey's English translation of 1654 gives it as The Compleat History of the Warrs of Flanders. The war in question is the Dutch Revolt, the Eighty Years' War of the Netherlands against Spain.

Bentivoglio watched that war from the Spanish side of the lines, with a diplomat's access to councils and commanders. His history tells the Counter-Reformation case with grace, fairness, and rare inside knowledge. He praises brave foes and blames folly on his own side. The work stands as the great Catholic history of the revolt, and a model of the historian's craft.
boole-laws-of-thought-1854:
Seven years after his first pamphlet, George Boole issued An Investigation of the Laws of Thought in 1854. The longer book gives the mathematical theories of logic and of probabilities. Boole widens his calculus from classes to whole statements that can be true or false. Reasoning and chance both come under his symbols.

He works out how to test arguments and how to weigh uncertain evidence. The system lets a reader compute with thought itself, in a strict sense. Later logicians refined his tools, but the leap was his. The book made logic a branch of mathematics. Its effects reached far past philosophy. Modern computing descends from it.
dods-spirit-manifestations-1854:
Dods answered the spirit rapping craze in Spirit Manifestations Examined and Explained, from 1854. Judge Edmonds, a noted believer, had defended the rappings as true spirit speech. Dods, the electrical psychologist, refuses that reading outright. The wonders, he argues, flow from minds and bodies under electrical laws.

He examines famous cases and mediums with his rival system in hand. The book records the passage from mesmerism to spiritualism in America. It speaks from the mesmerist side of that divide. Dods had built his name before the Fox sisters' knocks were heard. His defense of an older wonder against a newer one fascinates. Historians prize the primary view it gives.
zoist-vol-12-1854:
April 1854 to January 1855 fills the twelfth volume of The Zoist. Elliotson's long campaign for mesmerism nears its end in print. Reports still come in: cures under trance, operations without pain, and clairvoyant cases. Cerebral physiology holds its place beside the mesmeric record.

Britain is at war in the Crimea as these pages appear. The journal's world of provincial practice goes on regardless. Thirteen volumes, from 1843 to 1856, would complete the set. Volume twelve is the last full year but one. Its value lies in the unbroken chain of cases. Together the volumes let readers judge the movement from inside.
borlase-antiquities-cornwall-1754:
Cornwall's oldest stones drew William Borlase to write a county history unlike most others of its time. His Antiquities, Historical and Monumental, of the County of Cornwall came out in 1754. Borlase, a clergyman and keen observer of nature, spent years visiting sites across the far west of England.

Stone circles, cromlechs, and carved stones fill his pages, each one noted, drawn, and placed in its setting. Borlase linked many of these remains to the Druids, as writers of his age often did. Later students of old monuments still start with his record, since some sites have since changed or vanished.
king-american-eclectic-dispensatory-1854:
John King compiled The American Eclectic Dispensatory in 1854, a huge guide to the plant remedies of his school. King taught in Cincinnati, a center of eclectic medicine, which chose the best cures from every system. His book tells doctors what each drug is, how to prepare it, and when to use it.

Roots, barks, and herbs fill the entries, many of them native American plants little known in Europe. King gives doses, cautions, and the forms a medicine might take, from teas to extracts. For historians, the volume is the dispensatory of American botanical practice, a full shelf of plant lore in one binding.
pratt-voice-of-warning-1854:
Parley P. Pratt wrote A Voice of Warning in 1837, and the eighth edition of 1854 shows how long it kept selling. Pratt, an apostle and tireless missionary of the young Mormon church, aimed his tract at every reader he could reach. Prophecy, the Book of Mormon, and the coming kingdom of God fill its urgent pages.

No Mormon tract of the nineteenth century was reprinted more often or carried farther. Missionaries bore it across America and Britain, and converts often met the faith first in Pratt's clear voice. The book's warnings of judgment and calls to gather shaped how outsiders pictured the new movement for decades.
murchison-siluria-1854:
Roderick Murchison, a British geologist, named the Silurian system after an ancient Welsh tribe. His Siluria, published in 1854, sums up years of fieldwork in Wales and beyond. It is the founding text for one great slice of earth's past.

Murchison maps the old rock layers and the fossils that mark them. He traces the same system through England, Europe, and America. The work fixed the order of the oldest fossil-bearing rocks and gave geology a firm time scale. Later disputes over its borders only showed how central the book was. Welsh hills and quarries supply many of his best proofs.
smith-dictionary-greek-roman-geography-v:
William Smith edited his Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography in the 1850s, with Volume One, from Abacaenum to Hytanis, in 1854. It is the great Victorian gazetteer of the ancient world. Smith's scholars worked from the classical authors and from travelers' reports.

Each place gets its history, its coins, its ruins, and the ancient authorities that name it. Cities, rivers, mountains, and islands of Greece and Rome fill the pages. Woodcuts of sites and plans help the reader picture lost towns. Classical students used it to map every campaign and voyage in their texts. A companion set on ancient life and customs shares the same editor and plan.

Volume Two of Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography, also 1854, completes the gazetteer, from Iabadius to Zytus. A general index closes the set. William Smith's team matched the biography dictionary in scale and care.

The entries trace the rest of the ancient map: Italy's towns, the provinces, and the edges of the known world. Histories of sieges, colonies, and trade routes gather under each name. Coins and remains ground the literary record in things a reader could still see. The two volumes together gave Victorian readers the fullest ancient atlas in words that English has produced.
plos-pone-0003454:
Bahareh Vali and co-authors studied liver damage in people with two viruses in this 2008 paper. Hepatitis C harms the liver faster when HIV is also present. The immune reasons for that speed-up were unclear. The team looked for HIV-specific T cells inside the liver.

They examined patients co-infected with hepatitis C and HIV-1. T cells aimed at HIV were indeed found gathered in liver tissue. Fighters meant for one virus may add harm in the other's organ. That misplaced buildup could help explain the faster liver disease. Co-infection care must treat both viruses as one joint problem, not two separate ones.
plos-pone-0003554:
Magali Saint-Geniez and co-authors studied a growth factor's role in vision in this 2008 paper. VEGF is famous for building blood vessels, healthy and diseased alike. Evidence hinted it also acts directly on non-vascular cells. Anti-VEGF drugs are now widely used in eye care.

The team showed endogenous VEGF is required for visual function. It supports survival of Müller cells and of photoreceptors, the light sensors. Blocking VEGF too hard could starve the retina it should save. The finding urges care in dosing eye treatments. The same drugs also treat some cancers and lung diseases at higher stakes.
plos-pone-0003654:
M. Ángeles Serrano and Paolo De Los Rios published this network study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Flow networks move things along directed paths from input points to output points. Their large-scale shape decides how well the whole system works. The team asked what makes such networks efficient.

They studied percolated landscapes, where paths appear once enough links are in place. Their analysis links the layout of these networks to how much they can carry and how they change over time. The results apply to systems as unlike as water in rock and goods on roads.
plos-pone-0003754:
Ulrich Kirk published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. How much we like an object depends in part on the setting around it. Neuroimaging work had often studied context and perception, but less so beauty. Kirk used fMRI to watch aesthetic judgment at work.

He examined how the brain handles the link between an object and its context during judgment. The same image could please more or less depending on its frame. The study shows taste is not just in the object; the brain builds it from object and context together.
plos-pone-0003854:
Karim Hnia, Cécile Notarnicola, Pascal de Santa Barbara, and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Gastrokine-1 is a protein known from the stomach lining, and its role in smooth muscle cells was a mystery. To study it, the team first needed the native protein in pure form.

They established a protocol to purify gastrokine-1 from freshly dissected chicken gizzard smooth muscle. Then they characterized its biochemical properties, some of them unexpected. The groundwork sets up future study of what this protein actually does in muscle tissue.
plos-pone-0003954:
Joep P. M. Derikx, Dick A. van Waardenburg, Geertje Thuijls, and co-authors studied gut barrier loss during surgery in 2008. A leaking gut barrier is tied to complications after operations. Most study of that loss came from belly surgery itself. The team asked whether major surgery elsewhere also breaks the barrier.

Their PLOS ONE article followed twenty children having spinal fusion surgery. Spine surgery does not open the abdomen at all. Signs of gut barrier loss still developed in these patients. The finding widens concern about gut leakage to many major operations. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004054:
Elaine J. Gavin, Bo Song, Yuan Wang, and co-authors weakened a DNA protein in colon cancer cells in 2008. Their group had found Orc6 levels highly elevated in colon tumors. Orc6 also rose after treatment with the drug 5-fluorouracil. Those links made Orc6 a candidate drug target.

Their PLOS ONE article lowered Orc6 in human colon cancer cells. The cells then grew more sensitive to 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin. Pairing a target blocker with standard drugs could improve response. The work points to a combination strategy worth further testing. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004154:
Lane Yoder published this theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brain's wiring is so vast and tangled that exact, fully specified networks have rarely been explored. As a result, how the pattern of synaptic connections shapes the way the brain handles information is poorly understood.

Building on a recently proposed model of the retina, Yoder designs explicit logic circuits, networks written out connection by connection. He tests whether such circuits can tell one neural state from another. The work offers a concrete way to link wiring diagrams to the computations a brain circuit performs.
plos-pone-0004254:
Makoto Honda and colleagues published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Narcolepsy is caused by the loss of most neurons that make hypocretin, also called orexin, the brain chemical that keeps us awake. The loss is believed to result from an autoimmune attack, but what actually kills the cells is unknown.

The team studied IGFBP3, a binding protein for growth factors, in relation to hypocretin. They report that IGFBP3 colocalizes with hypocretin and regulates it. A regulator sitting alongside the missing chemical gives researchers a new lead on the narcolepsy puzzle.
plos-pone-0004354:
Lina Rodahl and colleagues published this tumour genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Several regulators of endocytic trafficking, the system that sorts cargo inside cells, have lately been named tumour suppressors in Drosophila. These include components of the ESCRT machinery, which packages proteins for disposal. Breaking ESCRT subunits leads to enlarged cells and tissue overgrowth.

The team report that disrupting Vps4, an ESCRT partner, and JNK function in Drosophila causes tumour growth. Two systems that seem unrelated, waste sorting and stress signalling, collide in this route to cancer. The flies make the genetics fast and cheap to test.
plos-pone-0004454:
Waves moving through flowing material behave in ways that matter for blood clotting, model Elena Ermakova, Emmanuil Shnol, Mikhail Panteleev, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many living and chemical systems carry traveling waves of excitation. In real settings the medium itself moves, as blood flows or as fluids stream through reactors.

The team studied two-dimensional waves in a channel with a smooth, curved flow profile. They used the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, a classic math stand-in for excitable tissue. Their results show how flow bends, speeds, or breaks up the waves as they travel. That insight reaches beyond math: clots form in flowing blood, and wave behavior in a stream helps decide where a clot grows and when it stops.
plos-pone-0004554:
Software that mines the medical literature for protein partnerships is presented by Min He, Yi Wang, and Wei Li in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tool is called PPI Finder. Published biomedical papers are growing so fast that no one can read them all, so text mining tools are needed to manage the overload automatically. One common job is extracting protein-protein interactions from PubMed abstracts.

Existing tools mostly hunted interactions by matching patterns or names. The authors set out to build a mining tool for human protein interactions with a fuller approach. Protein partnership maps are basic infrastructure for biology: they show which proteins work together. Automating their extraction from papers keeps those maps growing at the speed of publication.
plos-pone-0004654:
Eight villages in a secluded corner of Sardinia are far more different genetically than expected, report Giorgio Pistis, Ignazio Piras, Nicola Pirastu, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Isolated populations are prized for gene studies because their uniformity can make disease genes easier to find. But population isolates should not be assumed homogeneous, even when communities look alike.

To design association studies well, researchers must understand how history and isolation molded each community. Using genome-wide high-density SNP analysis, the team found high differentiation among the eight villages. Neighbors separated by hills and old marriage customs carry distinct genetic profiles. Gene hunters who treat them as one pool risk false leads; those who respect the structure gain a sharper tool.
plos-pone-0004754:
Tobias Wiedemann and colleagues showed that early immune response to stomach bacteria sets up later pre cancer change in gerbils, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Infection with Helicobacter pylori that can inject a toxin linked protein raises risk for severe stomach disease. The injection system and its cargo are key to that added risk in humans.

The team tracked infection over time in Mongolian gerbils, a good model for stomach disease. Early immune events predicted later changes that can lead toward cancer. The link argues for early treatment to cut long term risk. It also maps steps where intervention might help.
florence-worcester-chronicle-forester-18:
Florence of Worcester kept his chronicle in the twelfth century, and Thomas Forester's 1854 English version carries it to modern readers. The tale runs from creation to 1141. Norman conquest and the anarchy of King Stephen's reign form its grim late chapters.

A monk who lived through civil war tells of kings, battles, and portents. Castles rise, towns burn, and chroniclers count the cost in famines. The work stands as a base source for medieval English history. Forester's version, in a popular series, made the chronicle a household book for Victorians who wanted their past in the words of those who saw it.
kircher-oedipus-aegyptiacus-vol3-1654:
Kircher sums up Egyptian wisdom in the third volume of Oedipus Aegyptiacus, in Latin from 1654. Real learning and fancied lore stand side by side in the vast close. The work forms the last great monument of Renaissance Hermeticism, splendid in dress and mistaken in many of its bold decipherments of the ancient signs.

No other book shows the old magical world view so fully arrayed. Kircher's Rome workshop drew reports from missions across the globe for it. Engravers, printers, and patrons all served his boundless design for years. Readers leave with awe at the scale of the attempt, if not belief in its answers.
noizet-memoire-somnambulisme-1854:
Francois-Joseph Noizet studies the magnetic sleep in his memoir on somnambulism, in French from 1854, though written back in 1820. The French general treats mesmerism with a soldier's order and a scholar's care. His early account ranks among the first scientific treatments of the strange sleep and its claimed wonders of sense.

He reports trials, failures, and puzzles without the showman's gloss. Publication waited decades while the subject ripened around his manuscript. Psychology might have grown faster had his road been taken sooner. The memoir stands as a road not taken in the field's history, sober proof that the magnetic sleep drew serious minds early.
treaty-of-kanagawa-1854:
Commodore Matthew Perry of the United States Navy signed the Treaty of Kanagawa with Japan in March 1854. Perry had arrived with warships the year before, pressing Japan to end more than two centuries of near-total seclusion from the West. The talks took place under the shadow of those guns, and Japan's rulers knew refusal could mean war.

The treaty opened two ports, Shimoda and Hakodate, to American ships needing supplies, and promised safety for shipwrecked sailors. An American consul would also live at Shimoda. Trade itself had to wait for a later treaty, but the door was open, and the shock pushed Japan toward rapid change.
cia-0000008054:
A grave site linked to an American pilot is the subject of a CIA report dated August 1974. The heading notes an acquisition date in late September, a trace of how the information reached the agency. By then, American combat in Vietnam had ended, but many airmen remained unaccounted for.

Reports like this one fed the long effort to account for missing servicemen, grave by grave and village by village. A single location could give a family its first firm answer. The file is brief and grim, yet it shows careful record keeping after the fighting stopped. Each detail was preserved for follow-up work.
cia-0000008654:
An American plane went down over Long Toan district in Vinh Binh province, a September 1971 report states. Vinh Binh sits in the Mekong Delta, South Vietnam's rice-growing south. Delta fighting relied heavily on aircraft supporting ground troops in flat, flooded country.

Each downing started a chain: rescue if possible, then records, then questions for the crew's families. Reports from the district level gave that chain its facts. By 1971 the war was winding down for American forces, but losses continued. The file marks one more aircraft and crew entering the long record of the Delta war.
cia-0000009254:
Luc Nam district, in Ha Bac province, is named in a January 1973 sighting of an American prisoner of war. Ha Bac lies northeast of Hanoi, in country many captured airmen passed through. The report arrived in the month the Paris accords were signed.

Prisoner sightings at that moment were checked against the lists of men Hanoi agreed to free. Anyone sighted but not listed became an open question for years. Analysts therefore handled January 1973 reports with special care. This file preserves one such sighting in full, a district-level claim from the war's final settlement.
cia-0000013854: North Vietnamese officials in Vinh put shot down American planes on show, and a CIA note dated June 2, 1967, reports the display. Photos and wreckage were set out for the public to see. Such shows aimed to prove that the north could beat American air power. They also told watching pilots what a crash could mean.
cia-0000015254: Argentina is the source of a short CIA file on unidentified flying objects, dated April 2, 1965. The file holds only page three of its source, per the title. Saucer reports from South America reached Washington through the clipping net. A lone page shows how thin some of those far off reports could be.
cia-0000015454: Unidentified flying objects came before the Intelligence Advisory Committee in a CIA record dated January 3, 1953. That committee brought senior intelligence leaders together to weigh matters jointly. Saucer reports had grown too loud by early 1953 to stay at a low level. The entry marks the moment the subject reached the top tables of American intelligence, if only as one item among many.
cia-0000022354: Thanks from the Abel family for the return of Rudolf Abel fill a letter kept in a CIA record dated in 1962. Abel came home to the Soviet Union in the February 1962 swap that freed Gary Powers. A family's gratitude, filed by an intelligence agency, is an odd and human relic. The letter closes the swap story on a note of relief.
cia-0000023754: President Frei and the highest levels of the armed forces are the concern of a CIA document dated in 1970. The title breaks off at the words remain, leaving their state unstated. Eduardo Frei was Chile's president until late 1970, when Allende was set to succeed him. A document joining the president and the top brass belongs to that tense change of power.
cia-0000025054: An American Air Force pilot was captured near Ban Toumlan, in Saravane Province, Laos, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. The title adds subsequent events, then breaks off in the catalog. Saravane was a southern province crossed by the Ho Chi Minh Trail. A capture there in 1973 came at the very end of the air war over the trail.
cia-0000036854:
An editorial looking back over enemy losses fills a CIA record dated January 3, 1968. It recalls the numbers from November 1966 through November 1967, a full year of war. Counts of enemy dead were among the most argued-over figures of the Vietnam War.

The editorial returns to those yearly numbers and the claims built on them. American strategy leaned on loss counts, so each figure carried political weight. The file preserves a piece of that argument as it appeared in print at the time. A year-end editorial was a natural place to defend the count, since critics attacked it often.
cia-0000037954:
A CIA Latin America review dated August 1, 1982 takes up Peru and its Sendero Luminoso movement. Sendero Luminoso, the Shining Path, had launched its armed campaign in Peru in 1980. The review weighs the group early in its long and violent war.

Inside, the focus is the movement itself: its aims, its methods, and its growth. Reviews of this kind warned officials about threats still small enough to overlook. The file captures a turning point for the movement. The Shining Path was passing from a local problem in the Andes into a national danger. Peru would fight that danger for more than a decade.
cia-0000038454:
Lieutenant Commander James E. Teague is the subject of a CIA record dated January 2, 1974. The file notes that Mr. and Mrs. Erlan M. Teague requested information on his MIA and POW status. Family requests drove much of the accounting work in those years.

Inside, the parents' request stands at the center of the record. For every missing man there was a family asking the government what it knew. The file shows the human engine behind the vast paperwork. Two parents and one missing son stand behind it. An official system was built to give them an answer, however long it took.
cia-0000039954:
A CIA country survey titled simply Cuba is dated July 4, 1965. By then Fidel Castro's revolution had ruled the island for six years. Cuba sat at the center of Cold War tension in the Americas.

Inside, the survey presents the island as American analysts saw it in mid-decade. Country surveys of this kind covered government, economy, and armed strength in one brief. The file gives readers a dated portrait of Cuba in 1965. It came three years after the missile crisis. The island was still watched more closely than almost any other small country on earth.
cia-0000049154: Lt. Col. Guillermo Alfredo Benavides Moreno is the named subject of a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Benavides commanded the military academy whose troops carried out the Jesuit murders the year before. His file, kept while his case moved, is one of the series' most consequential dossiers.
cia-0000049254:
El Salvador's judicial process is assessed in a CIA paper from 1989, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. Courts were the war's weakest institution: judges were threatened, witnesses vanished, and cases against soldiers almost never reached a verdict. The paper grades that system while the war still ran through it.

Inside, the process is followed as a case would meet it, from arrest through investigation to the rare courtroom ending. The grade mattered beyond El Salvador, since American aid arguments leaned on claims that justice there worked. The paper survives as one of the clearest measures of how far those claims stood from the truth on the ground.
cia-0000049354: A Salvadoran insurgent offensive is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049354, dated February 1, 1982, filed under Central America. The item carries a Truth Commission note and centers on insurgent action. It is a short declassified record whose heading states the event type plainly, one of the agency's early-war notices on fighting in El Salvador.
cia-0000072254: Iraq's chemical warfare program, described as more self-reliant and more deadly, is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000072254, dated August 1, 1990. The record notes the paper as sanitized. Readers find a short declassified assessment whose heading states the program's direction in stark terms, preserved as the agency summarized Iraq's chemical effort at that date.

plos-pone-0004854:
Lijing Xing and colleagues linked phosphate tagging of wheat lectin VER2 to vernalization induced signaling and motility, in PLOS ONE in 2009. O-GlcNAc modification of proteins mediates stress response and motility in animal cells. The plant lectin concanavalin A can raise nuclear modification levels, yet function of modification in wheat vernalization. The cold requirement for flowering, remained unclear before this cellular study.

VER2 phosphate tagging connects cold sensing to cell movement. Vernalization prepares winter wheat for spring flowering. Molecular steps could improve crop timing. Climate shifts make such knowledge valuable. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0005454:
Watcharee Chokejindachai and David Conway set out a plan for malaria gene hunting in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Some forms of the malaria parasite cause far worse illness than others. To find the gene changes behind that, workers need many markers spread across the parasite's large genome.

The authors argued that Thailand was a good place to start the search. They laid out a case-control method that compares parasites from severe and mild cases. A clear plan matters because a weak search wastes samples, while a sharp one can point to the genes that make malaria deadly.
plos-pone-0005554:
Celia Perales, Rubén Agudo, and Esteban Domingo studied virus killing by mutation overload in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Some drugs kill viruses by raising their mutation rate until they cannot copy faithfully. A risk is that the virus evolves resistance to the mutating drug, as it does to normal drugs.

The team used a virus strain already resistant to one such drug, ribavirin. They showed that a second, different mutating treatment could still wipe it out. The result supports pairing mutating drugs so that resistance to one does not save the virus.
plos-pone-0005654:
Kelly Haston, Joyce Tung, and Renee Reijo Pera studied a gene in mouse germ cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Germ cells follow a special path: they multiply, travel to the gonads, reset their gene marks, and finally become eggs or sperm. Little was known about some steps of that path.

The team studied a gene called Dazl in the earliest germ cells, both in animals and in dishes. They found that it keeps the cells able to take any path and runs their genetic and marking programs. Faults there could underlie some infertility.
plos-pone-0005754:
Daniel Wiswede and co-authors tested in 2009 whether the body's own emotion signals change how the brain handles its mistakes. The embodiment idea holds that feelings involve the face, posture, and gut, not just the brain. Smiling or slumping can nudge what a person feels.

The team measured the brain's error signal while manipulating these body cues. That signal, seen after a slip, shows how the brain monitors performance. If body state shifts it, then emotion reaches deeper into basic control than assumed. The results link feeling and self-monitoring in a way lab tasks rarely capture.
plos-pone-0005854:
Heather Maughan and Rosemary Redfield traced in 2009 how a bacterium's talent for eating stray DNA evolved. Haemophilus influenzae can take up DNA from its surroundings and splice matching pieces into its own genome. Most incoming DNA is destroyed; a lucky fragment can bring new traits.

The pair reconstructed how this competence arose and changed across the species' history. The ability is costly to keep, so its persistence implies real benefits. Their history helps settle why sex-like gene swapping exists in bacteria at all. It also informs how resistance genes may move through this respiratory pathogen.
plos-pone-0006454:
Kathy Cai and colleagues linked two gene switches to ovarian cancer types in PLOS ONE in 2009. The GATA family of transcription factors guides how cells take on their roles in embryos and organs. Two members, GATA4 and GATA6, are often lost in ovarian cancer. That loss was proposed to explain how these tumors change character.

Their title reports that loss of GATA4 and GATA6 marks the histological subtypes of ovarian cancer. The loss also comes before the change of normal surface cells into cancer. An early, type-specific marker could aid diagnosis. It also suggests the switches help keep ovarian cells in their normal state.
plos-pone-0006554:
Oluf Røe and co-authors profiled genes in a rare chest cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malignant pleural mesothelioma is considered an almost incurable tumor with increasing incidence worldwide. It usually develops in the parietal pleura, from mesothelial lining cells. The team compared genome-wide profiles of mesothelioma with parietal and visceral pleura tissue.

Their aim was an emerging gene portrait of the tumor. Knowing which genes define mesothelioma can improve diagnosis, which is often late. It may also reveal drug targets. Comparing tumor to both pleural layers prevents mistaking normal layer differences for cancer changes.
plos-pone-0009454:
Jameson Miller, Miles Parker, and Robert Bourret built a computer model of a bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. Escherichia coli swims toward food and away from harm. It steers with a chain of signals inside the cell. Groups of receivers on its surface sense chemicals and pass the news inward.

Their model treats each molecule as an agent that follows simple rules. Thousands of agents act at once, as in a real cell. The team could then watch the steering system work step by step. The model offers a test bed for ideas about one of the best known signal chains in biology.
plos-pone-0009554:
Shinichi Sunagawa, Cheryl Woodley, and Monica Medina sampled threatened corals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Corals host rich communities of microbes on and inside them. Deep sequencing of DNA from such samples had shown that microbial diversity was once underrated. The team read the DNA in samples from corals at risk. They looked for kinds of microbes not seen elsewhere.

The samples held a wealth of microbial life, much of it rare. A few kinds dominated, while many appeared only in traces. The authors argue that threatened corals shelter microbial habitats that science has barely explored. Saving reefs thus saves more than the corals themselves; it saves whole unseen worlds.
plos-pone-0009654:
Bruno Vellutini and Alvaro Migotto documented the early life of a sea biscuit in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sea biscuits are flattened sea urchins that burrow in sand. The species studied is Clypeaster subdepressus. Its development from egg to juvenile had not been fully recorded. The team raised the animals in the lab and followed each stage in detail.

Their account covers the embryo, the swimming larva, and the young juvenile after settling. Stage by stage drawings and timings give a full atlas of its growth. Such atlases let scientists compare how related urchins build their bodies. They also fill a plain gap in marine biology for this group.
plos-pone-0010454:
Elena Gómez-Díaz and Jacob González-Solís mapped a seabird food web in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used chemical tracers, and they included the birds' parasites. Food web studies often leave parasites out, though they are everywhere. Parasites feed in varied ways, making their place in the web tricky. Stable isotope analysis reads diet from tissue chemistry, offering a way in. The team applied it to a seabird colony and its parasites.

Isotopes placed each parasite at a feeding level relative to its host. Some parasites feed higher than expected, effectively preying on predators. Including parasites changes the web's shape and its energy accounting. That matters for predicting how webs respond to species loss. The study argues parasites deserve seats in food web science.
plos-pone-0010554:
James Stapleton and James Swartz built a cell-free screen to find better hydrogen-making enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzymes called [FeFe] hydrogenases make and split hydrogen gas. That talent could serve renewable fuel systems. Natural versions, though, are fragile and easily damaged, which has blocked engineering. Screening improved versions inside living cells is slow and awkward. Their plate-based screen works without cells at all.

In tiny wells, enzyme variants could be made and tested in parallel. Speed lets researchers try many designs and keep the best. Cell-free methods trade living complexity for control. If sturdier hydrogenases emerge, biohydrogen gets closer to practice. This study supplies the sieve for that search.
plos-pone-0010654:
Marcela Dávila López and colleagues used gene order to find linked genes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neighboring genes are usually shuffled apart over evolution. Pairs that stay neighbors across many species are probably kept together for a reason.

Scanning whole genomes, the team found gene pairs whose order survived across eukaryotes. Those pairs often worked in the same process and were switched on together. Order itself became a clue to function for poorly known genes. The approach turns genome maps, which labs already have, into a guide for experiments they have not yet run.
plos-pone-0010754:
Ryan Boyko and Andrew Marshall tested ape counting methods with computer simulations, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Great apes are shy and hard to count directly. Survey teams instead count the nests apes build each night and convert nest counts into animal numbers. The conversion rests on guesses about building and decay.

The simulations modeled an orangutan population building nests over time. Different survey methods were then graded against the known true count. Some common methods drifted far from the truth under plain conditions. Knowing which methods hold up matters, since survey numbers decide where scarce conservation money goes.
plos-pone-0010854:
Jie Dong, Guoqian Jiang, Yan Asmann and co-authors published this development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are tiny molecules that fine-tune how much protein a gene makes, and they help shape growing organs. How whole networks of them behave while a lung forms was poorly mapped, so the team tracked them across mouse development.

They profiled both microRNAs and gene messages at every recognized stage of lung growth, from early embryo to adult, and matched the results against protein data. More than a hundred microRNAs rose and fell in clear time patterns, forming distinct groups. Dong and colleagues chart how these small regulators may coordinate with the genes they target. The map gives lung researchers a framework for studying birth defects and lung tumors alike.
plos-pone-0010954:
Manuel Gonçalves, Josephine Janssen, Maarten Holkers and co-authors published this cell fusion methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells merging with each other underlies fertilization, muscle building, and bone maintenance, and also plays roles in disease. Measuring those fusion events quickly and sensitively, in many kinds of experiments, was an unmet need.

Their system is a genetic switch split across two cell populations, delivered by lentivirus carriers so it works in dividing and non-dividing cells alike. Only when two cells fuse does a recombinase enzyme complete the switch and turn on a reporter. Gonçalves and colleagues designed the two modules for flexible pairing. A clean on-off signal for fusion lets researchers screen for genes and drugs that promote or block cell merging.
plos-pone-0011154:
Kowarsch, Marr, Schmidl and colleagues mapped RNA targets in PLOS ONE in 2010. Small RNAs tied to disease act in many signaling paths, but their effects shift by tissue. The team carried out a tissue focused analysis of which genes these small RNAs target in human pathways.

Their maps show that control by these RNAs depends strongly on context. The same RNA can matter in one tissue and do little in another. That insight matters for precise medicine, since drugs aimed at these RNAs must hit the right tissue. It should help design treatments with fewer off target effects elsewhere in the body.
plos-pone-0011254:
Vitzthum, Scutaru, Musial-Bright and colleagues mapped tobacco smoke research in PLOS ONE in 2010. Secondhand smoke, called environmental tobacco smoke, has been studied worldwide for decades. Using counting methods for science itself, the team charted where that research concentrates and where it is thin.

Their equalized maps show the global shape of the field at a glance. Funders and policy makers can see which countries and topics dominate and which are neglected. Such a bird's eye view helps direct money to gaps that matter for nonsmokers' health. It is research about research, used to steer future work.
plos-pone-0011354:
Aric Gregson and co-authors looked in 2010 for immune cells that might protect transplanted lungs. After a lung transplant, many patients develop a scarring condition that slowly blocks the small airways and is the main limit on long-term survival. The team searched lung grafts for regulatory T cells, a type that calms immune attack.

Patients whose grafts held a specific set of these calming cells were protected against the scarring syndrome. The cells carried two markers that together singled them out from other T cells in the graft. Finding a protective cell type gives transplant teams a possible early sign of who is safe and who is at risk. It also suggests that boosting such cells could one day help grafts last longer.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1254: Staff of the State Department wrote this internal memorandum on 25 July 1945. It moved inside the department, from desk to desk, as the summit ran abroad. Papers of this kind did the department's daily thinking while its chiefs sat at Potsdam. They fixed facts, framed choices, and kept a record of what was weighed, and why it mattered.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1354:
From London, Ambassador John Winant sent another cable to the acting secretary of state on 20 July 1945. It followed his message of two days before in the volume's Tangier and Spain papers. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Winant's seat in London made him a relay for British thinking on questions far beyond Britain itself. Spain and Tangier both touched British interests in the Mediterranean, so London's views reached Washington through him. Readers can follow how one embassy's reporting fed several files at once. The cable also shows the pace of July 1945, when no post, however senior, sent just one message and rested.
frus-1945-50-intel-d54:
Secretary Byrnes wrote to both Secretary Patterson and Secretary Forrestal on 10 December 1945. One letter to the two heads of the military departments shows the endgame of the autumn contest approaching. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

By December the rival plans had been cut down to a shape the president could accept. The secretaries were settling the last points among themselves. Byrnes writing to War and Navy together kept the talks at the top and in step. Readers should set this letter near Smith's November papers to Truman. Between them, the design of the National Intelligence Authority, announced six weeks later, becomes visible in the record before it was named.
frus-1945-50-intel-d154:
Dated 7 June 1946, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers) to the National Intelligence Authority. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 154 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d254:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 15 December 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 254 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d354:
Dated 22 November 1948, this memorandum runs from the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong) to the Intelligence Survey Group. The State Department prints it as document 354 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1861-d54:
On 14 June 1861, Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London. The dispatch is document 54 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid June found Adams deep in the routine of notes and calls in London. The grand question of British recognition hung over each small task. His report shows the daily grind by which a great issue was held off, one meeting and one letter at a time. The daily grind in London was the price of keeping a great power neutral. Great issues are often held off by small tasks done well, day after day.
frus-1861-d154:
Writing on 23 September 1861, William H. Seward kept William Dayton to the quiet autumn watch. The letter is document 154 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late September found no great turn in the war, and Seward's letters accept the lull. His note to Paris keeps the watch in place without fresh alarm. Such routine pages are the true bulk of the 1861 file, and its quiet strength. Routine pages like this one are the true mass of the 1861 record. Details of trade filled the small print where the blockade's fate was set. Quiet strength was the autumn's true policy.
frus-1861-d254:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 23 September 1861, addressed to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. It was printed as Document 254 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d54:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 28 April 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 54 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d154:
On 30 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, printed as Document 154 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter closed out a month of heavy mail between Washington and London.

September 1862 had brought Antietam and the emancipation plan, two events that reset foreign thinking about the war. British leaders put off any move to back the South, at least for the moment. Mail like this dispatch shows the steady pressure Washington kept on London while that choice hung in the balance through the autumn. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d254:
William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report on 21 February 1862, printed as Document 254 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris throughout this period.

Reports from Paris had a special flavor: Dayton dealt with a court where the emperor's wishes counted for more than public debate. He reported conversations, hints, and shifts of mood that rarely reached print in France. A February report like this one helped Washington judge whether Napoleon III meant to meddle in the war or only to watch it. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d354:
Edouard Thouvenel, the French foreign minister in Paris, wrote to Henri Mercier, his minister in Washington, on 19 January 1862. The instruction is printed as Document 354 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, among the French papers.

Thouvenel's letters were Mercier's orders, fixing the line France would take in Washington for weeks at a time. Seeing them in the American printed record lets readers watch French policy being made, not just received. This January instruction came as France settled into its solo course in Mexico and weighed the American war. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862.
frus-1862-d454:
John Lothrop Motley in Vienna received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 September 1862. It is Document 454 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Seward wrote on the eve of Antietam, with Lee in Maryland and the fate of the autumn campaign undecided. Motley, in Vienna, had to hold the Union's line at a court that watched and waited. Instructions sent at such a moment stressed resolve above all. The dispatch belongs to the mid-September cluster in which Seward wrote to nearly every post in Europe. He was preparing his ministers for either result on the battlefield. He was also preparing them for the emancipation order he knew was coming.
frus-1862-d554:
On 6 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Belgium. The instruction is Document 554 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Sanford was among the most active of Seward's ministers, traveling, reporting, and watching Confederate agents wherever they surfaced in Europe. Orders to Brussels in May 1862 came as Union arms advanced and the government's case abroad improved. Belgium's own stake was trade and its king's wide influence. Seward used Sanford's energy gladly, feeding him the arguments and news the Brussels post needed. The dispatch is part of a correspondence marked by unusual warmth and frequency for so small a mission.
frus-1862-d654:
