Dated 21 October 1861, this letter went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Townsend Harris, the American minister in Japan. It stands as document 654 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Harris would soon leave the post he had held since the legation opened.

Seward wrote to guide the men who spoke for the United States abroad. A letter like this one set out views from Washington that Harris was to use in his talks with Japan's rulers. Read with the rest of the file, it helps show how a small mission kept its footing while its home government fought for its life.
frus-1863p1-d54:
On 21 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to a Mr. Spence. Memminger was the Confederate secretary of the treasury in Richmond. The letter is document 54 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, among the Confederate papers printed in that volume.

The treasury's web reached into Britain, where agents and friends of the South worked on loans and sales of cotton. A letter like this one fed that web. It is dated the same week as Memminger's sheets to Mason in London, and it shares their theme: money, the South's scarcest weapon. Printed by the Union, it lets readers trace that hunt for cash in the foe's own words.
frus-1863p1-d154:
The pair of 13 April 1863 for London opens with this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 154 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-April pairs from Washington split the brief as it stood after the raider's seizure: hold the gain, watch the yards, mind the tone. Seward fed Adams those points sheet by sheet. This letter opens the pair of 13 April. It is desk work of a high order, brief in form and heavy in what it guarded.
frus-1863p1-d254:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 30 July 1863. It appears as document 254 of the 1863 papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d354:
Writing in Washington on 8 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 354 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d454:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 9 April 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d554:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 6 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d654:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 4 November 1863. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
plos-pone-0000154:
Elene R. Valdivia, Yajun Wu, Lian-Chao Li, and colleagues published this plant biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies a group-1 grass pollen allergen, a protein that also drives many hay fever cases. In maize, the authors test how this allergen affects pollen competition, the race between pollen grains to fertilize a flower.

A protein best known for making people sneeze turns out to matter in plant reproduction too. The authors measure its influence on which pollen wins. The work links an allergen's biology to plant breeding and to the spread of genes through maize populations, including questions about gene flow from crops.
plos-pone-0000254:
Per Unneberg and Jean-Michel Claverie published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tries a tentative mapping of interactions between chromosomes that are triggered by transcription, the reading of genes. Their data come from chimeric EST and mRNA sequences, messages that appear to join pieces from different chromosomes.

Chromosomes were once pictured as separate territories that rarely touch. Evidence of transcription-driven contact between them challenges that picture. The authors sift public sequence data for signs of such contact. The paper is exploratory, mapping a phenomenon that later work with new methods would test.
plos-pone-0000354:
Andy M. Reynolds and Mark A. Frye published this insect behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fruit flies track odors in free flight, zigzagging toward a food smell through moving air. The authors show this free-flight odor tracking is consistent with an optimal intermittent, scale-free search. Such a search is a pattern of bursts and pauses with no single characteristic scale.

A scale-free search is the best strategy when targets are sparse and clues are patchy. Showing flies match that optimum links their flight control to search theory. The result interests both biologists and engineers building small flying robots that must find odor sources.
plos-pone-0000454:
Yoshan Moodley and Michael W. Bruford argued for joining two fields to save Africa's wildlife, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Molecular biogeography uses DNA to map where species and their populations came from and how they are related across landscapes. The authors laid out a framework for conserving pan-African biodiversity built on that evidence.

Africa's wildlife crosses borders that conservation plans often respect more than animals do. DNA maps can show which populations are unique, which are connected, and where protection matters most. The paper is a call to integrate genetics into conservation decisions across the whole continent, rather than reserve by reserve.
plos-pone-0000554:
John Stephen Yap, Chenguang Wang, and Rongling Wu built a computational method described in PLOS ONE in 2007. It maps genes that shape how organisms handle heat. Thermal performance curves chart how well an organism grows or moves across temperatures. Their approach performs functional mapping of quantitative trait loci, the genome regions that regulate those curves.

A curve, not a single number, is the trait: genes may shift its peak, width, or height. Mapping such dynamic traits needs math that treats the whole curve at once. With climates warming, knowing which genes set thermal limits has direct ecological and agricultural stakes.
plos-pone-0000654:
Nathalie van der Velde, Bruno H. Ch. Stricker, Jos R. T. C. Roelandt and colleagues asked whether heart ultrasound can predict falls in older people. European and American guidelines call for echocardiography in patients with syncope, meaning fainting. Half of older adults with syncope present with a fall. Yet no published data had addressed heart scan findings in older fallers.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study set out to determine whether echocardiographic abnormalities mark those at risk. Falls injure and kill many older adults, so any test that flags risk early has value. The study tests whether a scan already used for fainting can do double duty for fall prevention.
plos-pone-0000754:
Renata Freitas, GuangJun Zhang and Martin J. Cohn found an old pattern of gene activity in shark fins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The evolution of limbs from fins required new distal structures, the digits at the far end. In four-limbed animals, genes at one end of the HoxD cluster switch on in two distinct phases during limb development. The second phase builds the digit region.

Shark paired fins, the authors show, also display this biphasic Hoxd expression. That pushes the distal limb domain's origin far back, before fins became limbs. Sharks are not primitive leftovers here; their development preserves the ancient program that digits later inherited.
plos-pone-0000854:
Stephanie D. Shaw, Sutapa Chakrabarti, Gourisankar Ghosh and colleagues trimmed a splicing factor and found it still worked, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Serine/arginine-rich proteins, called SR proteins, are essential splicing factors. They carry one or two RNA-recognition motifs and a tail rich in arginine and serine, the RS domain. SR proteins bind splicing enhancers in the RNA and were thought to promote splicing from that position, using the RS domain.

Deleting the N-terminus of the SR protein SF2/ASF permitted splicing independent of the RS domain, their title reports. A part thought indispensable turns out dispensable after trimming. Results like this revise the mechanics textbooks give for splicing.
plos-pone-0000954:
Dietmar Dirnberger and Klaus Seuwen tested whether human frizzled receptors can talk to a yeast mating pathway, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Frizzled receptors span the cell membrane seven times, like the large GPCR family, but they are classed as atypical members. Yeast mating runs through a classic GPCR system, making yeast a handy test bed.

By placing human frizzled receptors into that system, the pair could watch for signaling in a clean setting. Yeast offers a blank background, free of the many partners found in human cells. Results from such swaps help sort which receptors truly couple to G proteins, a question with direct drug relevance.
plos-pone-0001054:
David Plachetzki, Bernard Degnan and Todd Oakley traced how new protein partnerships arose in animal eyes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Biologists increasingly understand the genetic bases of change in form. The origins of traits built on brand new protein interactions, though, remain largely undocumented.

Opsins are the light catching proteins of vision, and their partners decide what an eye can do with light. The team analyze opsin evolution across animals to catch new interactions as they arose. A documented origin is worth more than a plausible story. Their case gives eye evolution a rare before and after record.
plos-pone-0001154:
DNA barcoding uses a short stretch of DNA to identify a species, much as a barcode identifies a product. Chodon Sass and colleagues tested whether proposed barcodes work for cycads, an ancient group of plants, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Barcodes are most needed when a specimen lacks the features used for visual identification.

The authors evaluated the candidate marker sequences for telling cycad species apart. Reliable barcodes could become a forensic tool for conservation, since many cycads are endangered and traded illegally. Their tests show how well the proposed markers perform in this plant group.
plos-pone-0001254:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is the most common motor neuron disease, currently incurable, with treatment largely limited to supportive care. Katrina Gwinn and colleagues survey the genetics of the disease in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They also call for a new era of collaborative gene discovery. Family history raises the risk of ALS, and many inherited causes had already been found.

The authors argue that progress now depends on groups pooling samples and data, since each individual cause is rare. Their piece is a perspective on how ALS research should organize itself. It reflects a shift toward large consortia in human genetics.
plos-pone-0001354:
In mature neurons, the genes for MHC class I are repressed. These genes encode the immune system's identity-display molecules. Neurons are normally invisible to immune patrols in this respect. Julie Miralvès and colleagues studied a repressor behind that silence, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. MeCP2 is a protein that binds methylated DNA and represses genes; its own gene's mutations cause Rett syndrome.

The authors report that high levels of MeCP2 depress MHC class I expression in neuronal cells. The MHC genes are rich in the CpG sites MeCP2 reads. Their finding links a famous neurodevelopmental protein to immune invisibility in the brain.
plos-pone-0001454:
Tadashi Nomura and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on what makes the mammal cortex unique. The cortex has six neat layers of nerve cells, built in a set order as the embryo grows. No other class of backboned animal has a true match for it. The team asked which growth traits make this layered build possible.

They point to the pattern of nerve cell birth and to the level of a guide protein called Reelin. Both traits prove vital for a mammal type cortex to form. The work helps explain how a new brain design arose in evolution. It also frames why faults in these steps cause grave brain ills.
plos-pone-0001554:
Hoau-Yan Wang, Maya Frankfurt, and Lindsay Burns published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on opioid tolerance. Very low doses of opioid blockers can boost pain relief and cut tolerance. They do so by stopping a switch in how the opioid receptor links to its cell partners. Where the blocker binds to force that was not known.

The team show the blocker binds a protein called filamin A with high strength. That bind is the grip that stops the switch. A named grip gives drug teams a clear target. Drugs built on it could hold pain relief longer with less dose gain and less dependence.
plos-pone-0001654:
Marta Pires de Miranda and co-authors dissected a virus protein that hijacks B-cell signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gammaherpesviruses set up lifelong latent infections in B cells, the antibody-making cells of the immune system. To do so, they switch on pathways that normally sit below the B-cell receptor. One such viral tool is m2, a protein of murine gammaherpesvirus 68.

The team shows that m2 gathers several cell proteins at once, a multi-docking assembly. It bends the Fyn and Vav signaling pathway to the virus's ends. The full text gives the binding tests and the signals they recorded. Knowing how a virus imitates the cell's own switches helps explain how these infections persist for life. The question also bears on the human gammaherpesviruses.
plos-pone-0001754:
Emma L. Meczes, Kathryn L. Gilroy, Katherine L. West, and their co-authors studied a tail piece of a DNA-handling enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Type II DNA topoisomerases are essential enzymes that solve tangles arising as DNA is copied and read. They pass one double helix through a temporary break in another, powered by ATP.

The team measured the impact of the human enzyme's C-terminal domain, its tail region, on activity. The full text gives the enzyme assays with and without the tail and what changed. These enzymes are targets of major cancer drugs, so knowing which parts control activity can help design drugs and explain resistance.
plos-pone-0001854:
Lieven Thorrez, Katrijn Van Deun, Léon-Charles Tranchevent, and their co-authors warned against a common lab shortcut in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Housekeeping genes are needed in every tissue, since their expression is required for cell survival, integrity, or duplication. They are commonly used as reference genes to normalize gene expression data, on the assumption that they are expressed at constant levels.

Using ribosomal protein genes as the test case, the team shows that assumption can fail: reference genes vary more than users expect. The full text gives the expression data across tissues. Bad normalization quietly distorts thousands of published gene measurements, so this cautionary tale has unusual reach.
plos-pone-0001954:
Francois van Loggerenberg and co-authors described the work of building a high-risk HIV study group in South Africa, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The group, part of the CAPRISA 002 study of acute infection, follows people at high risk so that new infections can be caught early. Such groups are the base for vaccine and prevention trials.

Between August 2004 and May 2005, the team enrolled the cohort and recorded its health and social profile. They also report new infection rates and the hard parts of keeping such a group intact. Honest accounts of these hurdles help later trials plan for real life.
plos-pone-0002054:
Sanjeev Mahanta and co-authors found the smallest piece of a cancer-linked protein that drives growth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, MUC1, is made in abnormal form on many solid tumors. On healthy lining cells it clusters at the top face only; on cancer cells it spreads over the whole surface. A direct link from that change to cancer growth had been elusive.

The team whittled MUC1 down to a minimal fragment. As the title states, that fragment alone mediates the growth of cancer cells. A small active piece is a cleaner drug target than a huge protein.
plos-pone-0002154:
Melissa Bowlin and Martin Wikelski measured the true flight costs of migrating songbirds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Migrant birds, bats, and insects tend to have more pointed wings than species that stay put. Pointed wings and low wing loading were thought to save energy on long flights. Low wing loading means low body mass per wing area. The idea had never been tested directly.

Bowlin and Wikelski report that pointed wings, low wing loading, and calm air each cut the cost of migratory flight. Their tests turn a long-held guess about wing shape into measured fact. The results help explain why long-distance migrants look the way they do.
plos-pone-0002254:
Lina Guerra and co-authors used a bacterial toxin to find a key player in the response to DNA damage, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When adherent cells meet DNA-damaging agents, such as the bacterial cytolethal distending toxin or radiation, they switch on the small protein RhoA. RhoA builds stress fibers and delays cell death, but the signals between damage and RhoA were missing.

The team identifies Net1, a factor that activates RhoA, as a key effector in that response. Filling in the chain from DNA damage to cell survival helps explain how cells buy time to repair themselves. How cancer cells may abuse the same delay.
plos-pone-0002354:
Ziyin Li and co-authors found a new passenger complex that guides cell division in a parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Aurora B kinase is a key part of the chromosomal passenger complex, which steers chromosome segregation and the final split of one cell into two. In Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind sleeping sickness, an Aurora B relative was known but its partners were missing.

The team identifies a novel chromosomal passenger complex in the parasite. They also show it takes a unique position during cytokinesis, the final split. A division machine that differs from the human one is attractive for drugs that must kill the parasite, not the patient.
plos-pone-0002454:
In 2008, Desmond and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Chris Desmond, Ruth M. Bland, Gerard Boyce, and others. Its subject is scaling-Up Exclusive Breastfeeding Support Programmes: The Example of KwaZulu-Natal. Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for six months is the mainstay of global child health.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002554:
A research team led by Stoel reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Berend C. Stoel, Terry M. Borman, and others. Its subject is a Comparison of Wood Density between Classical Cremonese and Modern Violins. Classical violins created by Cremonese masters, such as Antonio Stradivari and Giuseppe Guarneri Del Gesu.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002654:
Jayabalan M. Joseph led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the actinome of dictyostelium discoideum in comparison to actins and Actin-Related proteins from other organisms. Authorship is credited in the record to Jayabalan M. Joseph and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Actin belongs to the most abundant proteins in eukaryotic cells which harbor usually many conventional actin isoforms as well as actin-related proteins (Arps). Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002754:
Chiara Pastori led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was arterially perfused Neurosphere-Derived cells distribute outside the ischemic core in a model of transient focal ischemia and reperfusion in vitro. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Chiara Pastori, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Treatment with neural stem cells represents a potential strategy to improve functional recovery of post-ischemic cerebral injury. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002854:
Thomas A. Terleph led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was response properties of the auditory telencephalon in songbirds change with recent experience and season. The catalog record names Thomas A. Terleph first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) is a telencephalic auditory area that is selectively activated by conspecific vocalizations in zebra finches and canaries. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002954:
Paul Makidon, Anna Bielinska, Shraddha Nigavekar and co-authors tested a new hepatitis B vaccine form in animals in 2008. Hepatitis B stays a major global health problem despite safe, effective vaccines. Current vaccines need cold storage and three shots, which restricts use where clinics are scarce.

Their candidate uses a nanoemulsion, a mix of tiny oil droplets, given through the nose as a mucosal vaccine. Pre-clinical evaluation means testing before human trials. Published in PLOS ONE, the work explores a form that could ease delivery in the developing world if later trials support it.
plos-pone-0003054:
Paul Medina, Ryan Worthen, Lawrence Forsberg and co-authors studied dendrite upkeep in neurons in 2008. Neurons need precise control of their inner skeleton: microtubule tracks carry cargo in axons and dendrites, while actin organizes synapses. Their unique shape makes neurons especially sensitive to faults in that system.

The actin-binding protein Capulet genetically interacts with the microtubule motor kinesin to maintain dendrite homeostasis, the title reports. Pairing an actin factor with a microtubule motor shows the two systems cooperate. Published in PLOS ONE, dendrite stability underpins learning circuits and their disorders. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003154:
Georgiy Bobashev, Robert J. Morris and D. Michael Goedecke examine airport networks in epidemic models in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Models of global spread for flu, SARS and tuberculosis often treat a sample of international airports as the network that carries disease. Yet there was no agreement on how that sample should be chosen.

The authors study sampling choices and the topology, or shape, of an international airport network. Readers see why the airports picked can change what a model predicts. The work matters for planners who rely on such models to judge how fast a new infection might travel around the world.
plos-pone-0003254:
Natasha Webb, Geoff Connolly, Judy Tellam and colleagues reassess a virus pathway claim in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Previous studies had indicated that Epstein-Barr virus can modulate the Wnt pathway in virus-infected cells, and that this effect is mediated by the viral oncogene latent membrane protein 1, or LMP1. The team reassessed the role of LMP1 in regulating expression of various pathway components.

The title reports that Epstein-Barr virus modulation of the Wnt pathway is not dependent on LMP1. Readers see a causal credit reassigned after a direct check. Such corrections keep virus cancer research from building on the wrong viral protein.
plos-pone-0003354:
Ingrid Masse, Laurent Molin, Laurent Mouchiroud and colleagues find a new lifespan factor in worms in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The PTEN tumour suppressor encodes a phosphatase, and its daf-18 orthologue in Caenorhabditis elegans negatively regulates the insulin and IGF-1 DAF-2 receptor pathway that influences lifespan in worms and other species. The team set out to identify new DAF-18 regulated pathways involved in lifespan.

The title reports a novel role for the SMG-1 kinase in lifespan and oxidative stress resistance in C. elegans. Readers get another gene in the ageing network beyond insulin signaling alone. Worm lifespan genes often nominate pathways later found in mammals.
plos-pone-0007454:
Adam Margolin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the math behind modern protein measurement. New machines now let biologists count thousands of proteins in a single test. That flood of data feeds a broad view of how cells work. Yet the tools for making sense of the data had lagged far behind the machines. The team set out to close that gap.

They built a new framework based on empirical Bayes methods. The approach borrows strength across many measurements at once, which steadies the results when data are noisy. Sounder math means the protein counts can support firmer claims about how cells behave. The framework is built for the large data sets such machines now produce as a matter of routine. It helps turn raw machine output into results biologists can trust.
plos-pone-0007554:
Michela Traglia and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was Val Borbera, a valley in the northwest Apennines of Italy whose people have lived apart for a long time. Such groups are prized for gene hunting. They share one stable setting, carry a narrower range of gene variants, and show long linked stretches of DNA. The team set out to describe this large group in full.

They measured how strongly traits run in the valley's families. The work shows why such a group gives gene hunters an edge. A well-mapped group like this becomes a natural lab for the study of common disease. The paper lays the base: who lives there, how they tie to each other, and what their genes can show. Later work in this valley stands on that base.
plos-pone-0007654:
Thomas Bettecken and Edward Trifonov published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the code that packages DNA into chromatin. It is widely accepted that DNA's own sequence strongly governs how it wraps. DNA spools around proteins called nucleosomes, and certain two-letter combinations favor particular positions on the spool. That packaging code is layered over the code for proteins. The team catalogued the repertoires of those positioning dinucleotides.

A catalogue of the signal pairs refines our reading of the chromatin code. Different genomic regions carry different mixes of the signals. Those mixes help explain why some DNA wraps tightly and other DNA stays open. Open and closed packaging decides which genes a cell can use. The study is an inventory paper, and inventories of codes are how codes get cracked.
plos-pone-0007754:
Taylor Chomiak and Bin Hu published a theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks what insulation thickness is best for nerve fibers in the rat brain. A fatty coat called myelin wraps many fibers and speeds their signals. The g-ratio compares the fiber's inner width to its full outer width.

That ratio serves as a standard index of healthy myelination. Myelin is complex to build and is often hit by injury and disease. The authors use theory to find the optimal g-ratio for rat central fibers. A firm target value helps researchers judge damage and repair in myelin diseases.
plos-pone-0007854:
Renata Goncalves and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how a blood meal reshapes a mosquito's flight muscles. The mosquito is Aedes aegypti, a carrier of dengue and yellow fever. Digesting blood releases products that can harm cells.

Flight muscle mitochondria, the cell's power plants, sit at the center of the story. After blood feeding, their function changes in a measurable way. Those changes are reversible once digestion ends. The muscle must keep the mosquito flying to find its next meal. The study shows how a blood feeder balances energy and damage.
plos-pone-0007954:
Francine Matthys and colleagues judged a standard retreatment plan for tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. The World Health Organization's Category II plan is the usual second try when TB comes back or a first course fails. Their patients lived where many TB strains no longer yield to first-line drugs.

Outcomes under the standard plan were poor in that setting. When strains resist the main drugs, a fixed recipe that assumes they still work will miss often. The authors' data press for drug testing up front and for plans matched to local resistance, rather than one recipe for all places.
plos-pone-0008054:
Yingjie Wu and colleagues bred a better gene-cutting mouse for PLOS ONE in 2009. Modern mouse genetics rests on tools that delete or swap genes in chosen tissues. One such tool, FLP, worked sluggishly in its older forms, wasting time and mice.

An improved form, FLPo, was placed in the most common lab mouse strain. The new line cuts its target DNA cleanly and with high success. A trusty, fast deleter line speeds nearly every mouse study that needs a gene removed, which is to say much of modern biomedicine.
plos-pone-0008154:
Derek Murphy and colleagues mapped where a childhood cancer's master gene grips the genome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuroblastoma arises from young nerve tissue and is a major cancer killer of children. Extra copies of the gene MYCN mark the worst cases.

Across the genome, the MYCN protein bound at spots marked by distinct DNA motifs, and often near zones where DNA was heavily methylated, a silencing tag. The combined map shows how an overgrown master gene rewires a cell. Each stronghold it holds is a place where treatment might pry it loose.
plos-pone-0008254:
Nicasio Mancini and colleagues studied hepatitis C antibodies in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Hepatitis C virus comes in several genotypes that differ in surface proteins. Some human antibodies can neutralize many types at once. They target spots on the E2 surface protein that stay conserved across genotypes. Such antibodies are central tools for understanding virus and host interplay.

Finding them in infected people would support vaccine and treatment design. Antibodies aimed at conserved spots are harder for the virus to escape. The team examined whether infection itself elicits these broad antibodies. Their answer informs strategies for prevention and therapy.
plos-pone-0008354:
Johannes Hirrlinger and colleagues presented a gene control tool in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. DNA recombination systems such as Cre/LoxP let researchers regulate genes in living animals. Precise targeting of one cell type at one time point has remained challenging. Spatial control often comes at the cost of timing control. The team split the Cre protein into fragments to solve this.

Their Split-CreERT2 system restores Cre activity only when fragments complement each other. A drug trigger adds control over timing. Together these switches allow finer experiments on gene function. The tool serves genetics studies that need exact timing.
plos-pone-0008454:
Severine Mazaud Guittot and co-authors study the GATA4 gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. GATA4 makes a factor that switches other genes on and off. It is needed for the growth and work of many organs. Yet how the GATA4 gene itself is controlled was little known. The team focus on the start region of the gene.

They find that the gene can use more than one first exon. An exon is a coding piece spliced into the final message. The same first pieces are used across species. That shared pattern hints they matter for control. The work clarifies how a key organ gene is switched on.
plos-pone-0008554:
Matthieu Chalopin and co-authors find a target for red wine compounds in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Diets rich in polyphenols are linked to lower cardiovascular risk. Polyphenols are plant compounds abundant in red wine and fruits. Their vascular protection is generally accepted. Yet the molecular targets for those effects remained unknown. The team study the endothelium, the inner lining of blood vessels.

They identify estrogen receptor alpha as a key target on the endothelium. Red wine polyphenols act through that receptor to protect vessels. The receptor is best known for mediating estrogen hormone effects. Its new role connects diet, hormones, and heart health in one pathway.
plos-pone-0008654:
Hai Li and co-authors analyze a chitinase domain in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Chitinases are enzymes found across archaea, bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals. They break down chitin, the second most abundant carbohydrate in nature after cellulose. Chitin forms insect shells and fungal cell walls. Many chitinases contain an insertion domain that helps bind chitin. The team perform sequence and structural analysis of that insertion domain.

They reveal two conserved motifs involved in chitin binding. Those motifs appear across distant species, marking them as essential. Knowing the binding motifs aids design of antifungal and insecticidal enzymes. It also clarifies how nature recycles a vast chitin pool.
plos-pone-0008754:
Paul ThiamJoo Tan, A. T. Heiny, Olivo Miotto, and colleagues sifted flu pieces for vaccine building blocks. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seasonal flu vaccines chase a virus that changes its coat yearly. Epitope-based vaccines would instead target pieces that T cells recognize. Such pieces must stay stable across many viral strains. They must also fit common human immune types.

The team checked H1N1 epitope candidates for conservation and variety. Strong candidates appear in most strains yet vary little. A vaccine built from them might work across seasons. Their shortlist guides the search for longer-lasting flu protection.
plos-pone-0008854:
Rebecca Baker, Claire Kent, Rachel Silbermann, and colleagues probed a disputed family of gene switches in mouse breast tumors. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The PEA3 family of Ets factors shows up at high levels in many breast tumors. Some reports cast them as tumor promoters. Others suggest they might restrain tumors instead. Mice whose mammary tumors are driven by Wnt1 gave a clean test.

Changing PEA3 factor activity in those tumors revealed their true contribution. Evidence from a defined model beats correlations from mixed human samples. The verdict helps decide whether drugs should block or boost these factors. Breast cancer biology gains a firmer fact.
plos-pone-0008954:
Jean-François Pombert and Patrick Keeling read the power-plant genome of a parasitic alga, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helicosporidium is an alga that lost its green colour and its ability to feed on sunlight. Instead it lives as an obligate parasite inside insects and other small animals. Its cysts burst open inside the host and release a thread-like cell.

The pair sequenced the DNA of its mitochondria, the cell's energy-making parts. That genome is stripped down compared with free-living algae. Comparing it shows what a parasite can throw away once a host feeds it. The genome adds a data point to the story of how parasites evolve.
plos-pone-0009054:
Ryota Matsuo and co-authors reported a slug brain healing itself after injury, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adult mammal brains recover poorly from damage, which makes stroke so hard to treat. The land slug Limax offers a different model for smell processing. Its higher olfactory centre handles the slug's sense of smell.

After that centre was injured, it recovered on its own. The team describes the regrowth as a novel mode of regeneration. Function returned along with structure over the following weeks. A simple animal that rebuilds a brain centre may teach principles mammals lack.
plos-pone-0009154:
Claire Shovlin and co-authors found a second source of a key clotting protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Factor VIII is the protein missing in haemophilia A. Too much of it, conversely, predicts repeat blood clots in veins. High levels also track with pulmonary hypertension driven by local clots.

The liver was thought to be plasma factor VIII's source. Endothelial cells, the vessel lining, also process the protein, the team showed. They even make alternatively spliced versions of its message. A vessel-wall source could explain clots forming exactly where they do.
plos-pone-0009254:
Georgina Thorborn and co-authors published this HIV immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In HIV infection, regulatory T cells, the immune system's brakes, decline in number. That loss was blamed for the uncontrolled immune activation that drives disease. But the story may be more subtle than cell counts alone.

The team studied people with HIV who had no symptoms yet. They measured not just how many regulatory cells remained, but how their targets respond. Effector T cells had grown more sensitive to suppression by the regulators. That extra sensitivity compensated for the reduced regulator numbers. Balance, it turns out, can be kept even with fewer brakes.
plos-pone-0009354:
Feng Wang and co-authors published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ behind tuberculosis, lives inside human cells and resists study. New tools are needed to speed drug and vaccine work against it. The team built one such tool.

They developed a way to insert unnatural amino acids into the germ's proteins. These are building blocks that nature never uses, placed at chosen spots by genetic tricks. A tagged protein can be lit up, tracked, or fished out of the cell. The method gives tuberculosis researchers a handle on proteins inside a stubborn pathogen.
plos-pone-0011454:
Nima Dehghani and co-authors used source modeling in 2010 to ask whether two common brain recordings see the same sleep events. Sleep spindles are brief bursts of activity during deep sleep that help lock in memories. They are recorded both by EEG on the scalp and by MEG, which senses the brain's magnetic fields, and the two traces do not match neatly.

Modeling where each signal comes from in the cortex, the team found the two methods pick up different generators of the same spindles. The tools are therefore not interchangeable windows on sleep but complementary ones, each favoring different sources. Sleep researchers who combine both gain a fuller picture than either gives alone. The paper is a caution against treating a familiar brain wave as one simple thing.
plos-pone-0011554:
Mark Anderson and Charles Ferree argued in 2010 for a change in what conservation saves first. As climate shifts, species will move, vanish, or arrive in new places, making any reserve picked for today's species a gamble. The authors proposed saving the stage instead: the varied rocks, soils, slopes, and landforms whose diversity generates and shelters living diversity in any climate.

Geology changes slowly, so a reserve network chosen for geophysical variety should keep offering many kinds of habitat whatever the climate does. Species can then sort themselves across a rich stage rather than being stranded on a poor one. The reframing is strategic, not poetic: it turns an unknowable bet on future species into a durable bet on future options. Land trusts and agencies can act on it now, with maps that already exist.
plos-pone-0011654:
Chandan Goswami and co-authors studied a sensory channel called TRPV4 in cultured cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. TRPV4 lets calcium and other ions into cells and responds to physical force. Both the channel and the cell's inner skeleton, the cytoskeleton, have been tied to how cells sense touch and pressure, and to heightened pain.

The team showed the channel and skeleton influence each other in both directions. TRPV4 interacts with the actin and microtubule networks, and those networks in turn tune the channel's behaviour. That two-way control helps explain how cells convert mechanical signals into chemical responses.
plos-pone-0011754:
Sandhya Das and co-authors tested both forms of an immune call signal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rapid movement of neutrophils from blood vessels to infection and injury sites is critical for resolving inflammation. The chemokine CXCL8 is central to recruiting them, and it occurs both singly and in paired form.

Working in living animals, the team showed both the single and paired forms are essential for neutrophil recruitment. Neither form alone could do the job fully. That two-key requirement reveals a finer control on calling in immune reinforcements than a single signal would allow.
plos-pone-0011854:
Far Chiang, Hannah Kuper, and Robert Lindfield led a rapid survey in 2010 of blindness that could have been avoided in the Occupied Palestinian Territories. No recent figures existed for how common blindness and poor vision were among people aged fifty and older there. Their survey was designed to produce answers quickly enough to guide real services.

Field teams examined older adults and recorded both the scale of vision loss and its causes. Many causes of blindness, such as cataract, can be treated or prevented when services reach people in time. A clear count of where the need sits helps eye care programs spend scarce staff and money where they will restore the most sight.
plos-pone-0011954:
Isabelle Laporte and co-workers studied in 2010 how the return of wolves changes the behavior of elk and cattle sharing the same range. Wolf predation and harassment of livestock are a central conflict in wolf conservation. Wild elk answer wolves with anti-predator behavior, but cattle, shaped by breeding, may not.

Comparing how elk and cattle respond clarifies where livestock losses come from and which husbandry steps actually help. Behavior, not just killing, is the channel: fear alone can move herds, change grazing, and raise costs. Evidence on that channel gives ranchers and conservationists something more useful than slogans on either side of the wolf debate.
plos-pone-0012054:
Phillip Cassey and co-workers compared in 2010 bird eggshell colors across museum collections to study why they vary so much. Eggshell diversity has inspired many adaptive explanations, from camouflage to signaling. Progress was blocked by three problems, starting with measuring color reliably in a way birds themselves would see.

Working with museum eggshells gave the team a comparative sample no single field season could gather. Standardized color measurement across species lets hypotheses about climate, nesting habits, and predators be tested fairly. Museum drawers, often dismissed as stamp collections, here serve as a century-deep data set on evolution's palette.
plos-pone-0012154:
Caroline Hall, Rachel Kassel, Robert Tacke, and co-authors studied how hepatitis C virus quiets the immune system, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Few viruses are better at staying for life once they infect a person, and this one often ends in lasting liver disease. A key part of its trick is weakening the T cells that should clear it, helped by regulatory T cells that calm immune attacks.

The team showed liver cells carrying the virus can push ordinary T cells to become regulatory ones, using a calming signal the infected cells release. That is a direct route by which the virus builds its own shelter. Naming it suggests ways a future therapy might lift the calm and let the immune system finish the job.
plos-pone-0012254:
Olga Rivero, Andreas Reif, Julio Sanjuán, and co-authors tested a brain development gene's link to schizophrenia in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, AHI1, is needed to build parts of the human brain, changed quickly during human evolution, and sat in a chromosome region that family studies had tied to schizophrenia. Those clues made it a natural suspect for a case-control test.

Comparing patients and healthy controls, they weighed whether the gene's variants raise the risk of the disease. Genes that guide brain building are strong suspects when thinking goes wrong, but suspicion is not evidence. Careful association studies, including ones that come back negative, are how psychiatry sorts real risk genes from near misses.
plos-pone-0012354:
Michael Behnke, John Wootton, Margaret Lehmann and co-workers mapped gene activity across the fast growth cycle of Toxoplasma gondii in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Toxoplasma is a widespread parasite that infects people and animals and can harm unborn babies and weak immune systems. In its fast form, called the tachyzoite, the parasite builds new copies of itself in a tightly timed cycle.

The team found that the cycle runs on two coordinated sets of genes that switch on in waves, one set handling the standard cell cycle and the other building parasite parts. That two-track program explains how the parasite times growth so precisely. It also exposes steps that drugs might block to stop infection.
plos-pone-0012454:
Danielle Ulanet and Douglas Hanahan studied a tumor guard's loss in a staged mouse cancer model, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The guard, p19 Arf, senses abnormal growth signals and usually calls in p53, the famous tumor suppressor. The authors asked what else happens when Arf is lost as tumors form step by step.

Losing Arf flipped the angiogenic switch early — tumors built blood vessels sooner — and sped tumor initiation through both p53-dependent and independent routes. Extra vessels feed faster growth, so the loss is doubly dangerous. The work helps explain why tumors lacking this guard behave so aggressively and resist single-pathway drugs.
plos-pone-0012554:
Daisuke Yamamoto, Kaori Shima, Kou Matsuo and colleagues tested a polyamine blocker in oral cancer cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Gene activity is set partly by methyl tags on DNA and on histone tails; cancers often misplace those tags. Blocking polyamine production — a growth chemistry — was known to affect methylation, and a protein called antizyme carries out part of that block.

Raising antizyme stripped methyl marks from genome DNA and from a key histone site in the oral cancer line. Removing silencing marks can wake protective genes that cancer shut off. The mechanism suggests antizyme pathways as a fresh route to epigenetic cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0012654:
Hong, Chung and Kim worked out a better way to compute how tightly small peptides grip SH3 domains. These domains pass signals inside cells by grabbing short peptide pieces on other proteins. Knowing the grip strength helps predict which proteins will pair up in a cell's signal web.

Their 2010 method combines many protein shapes and many peptide templates instead of relying on one of each. Real proteins flex, so averaging over shapes should match reality better. Sharper grip predictions help map cell signalling and design drugs that block bad pairings.
plos-pone-0012754:
Dawes, Kuzevski, Bettelheim and co-authors surveyed mobile drug-resistance packages in E coli from people and animals. Class 1 integrons are gene traps that collect resistance genes and pass them around between bacteria. Their 2010 study screened more than five hundred E coli samples of human and animal origin.

They charted a particular form in which a segment called IS26 has cut out part of the integron's conserved tail. Such cuts can reshape which resistance genes the trap keeps and spreads. Tracking these forms shows how resistance travels between farms, clinics and the wider environment.
plos-pone-0012854:
Stelzer, Schmidt, Wiedlroither and co-authors reported a small water animal that gave up sex and shrank. Asexual lines should enjoy a head start, since every individual can reproduce, yet they rarely last in nature. Their 2010 study follows a tiny metazoan lineage that took that path.

The lineage lost sexual reproduction and became dwarfed compared with its sexual relatives. Its fate tests theories about why sex persists despite its costs. Tiny animals with both kinds of relatives offer rare, clean comparisons for that old question.  Its relatives still reproduce both ways for comparison.
pmc-1395354:
Drummond, Ho, Phillips, and co-authors tackle how to date family trees of species with honest confidence. Tree building often assumed genes change at one steady rate, the strict clock model. The authors note that both that model and its opposite extreme clash with how evolution truly works.

Their relaxed approach lets change speed up or slow down along different branches. It also reports how sure each date estimate is, rather than hiding doubt. Better dating matters for tracing virus spread, species origins, and past shifts in climate and life, where timing is the core question.
pmc-3090754:
Tadel, Baillet, Mosher, and co-authors present Brainstorm, a user-friendly program for analysing MEG and EEG recordings. Brainstorm is a shared, open-source program for viewing and processing signals that record brain activity from outside or on the scalp. It stresses finding where in the cortex signals start.

The software integrates locating sources with brain images from magnetic resonance scans. That pairing lets researchers connect timing with location in brain activity. A friendly interface opened advanced brain signal analysis to labs without their own coders, growing its user base.  Clinical researchers use it to study disorders of brain timing.
pmc-3096954:
Prat, Parker, Karginova, and co-authors characterise the claudin-low subtype of breast cancer in depth. Gene expression studies had defined five tumour subtypes, each with distinct biology and outlook for patients. Claudin-low was the most recently identified of them and the least understood.

The team describes its traits at both visible and molecular levels. Understanding what sets this subtype apart helps explain its behaviour and treatment response. Their portrait gave oncologists a fuller reference for a hard-to-treat group and guided later work on targeted care.  Tumours of this subtype often lack the usual hormone markers guiding therapy choices.
pmc-3810854:
Nawrocki and Eddy present Infernal 1.1, a far faster version of their RNA homology search software. Infernal builds probabilistic profiles, called covariance models, of an RNA family's sequence and secondary structure. The input is a structurally annotated alignment of known family members.

The software then uses those models to search sequence databases for new members of the family. Version 1.1 runs about a hundred times faster than before, the authors report. Speed made structure-aware RNA search practical across whole genomes, supporting the Rfam database and RNA gene discovery.  Faster searches also cut the energy cost of annotating huge sequence archives substantially.
pmc-5069754:
Walters, Hyde, Berg-Lyons, and their colleagues improved marker gene primers in 2015 for microbial community surveys. Such surveys read a marker gene, often the 16S rRNA gene in bacteria, to census microbes in a sample. A wealth of findings had connected microbes to human and environmental ecology.

The team updated primers for the bacterial 16S gene regions V4 and V4-5 and for fungal marker regions. As knowledge and technique improve, primer tools can be modified to raise accuracy. Better primers capture more of the true community and bias results less. Shared, improved primers let microbiome studies across labs be compared fairly.
pmc-5687754:
Florian Rohart, Benoit Gautier, Amrit Singh, and colleagues introduced the mixOmics software package in 2017. Modern labs produce huge data sets from genes, proteins, and small molecules in the same samples. Making sense of several such data sets at once is hard without the right tools.

mixOmics runs in the R language and helps users pick the most useful features from each data set. It can also combine data sets so shared patterns stand out. Clear plots guide users through each step. For biologists facing multi-part data, the package offers a tested way to find signals that one data set alone would miss.
pmc-5762154:
Aviv Regev, Sarah Teichmann, Eric Lander, and a large international team laid out the Human Cell Atlas plan in 2017. New single-cell methods can profile thousands of cells one by one. The authors argue the time is right to name every cell type in the human body.

The plan calls for shared standards, open data, and maps that combine gene activity with cell position in tissues. Early pilot work would cover key organs before scaling to the whole body. A finished atlas would give medicine a reference much like the human genome. Doctors could compare sick tissue against a healthy standard cell by cell.
pmc-5802054:
Alexander Wolf, Philipp Angerer, and Fabian Theis introduced Scanpy in 2018. Scanpy is a Python toolkit for single-cell gene expression data, which can cover millions of cells. Analysts need cleaning, grouping, and plotting steps that still run fast at that size.

The toolkit covers preprocessing, clustering, trajectory building, and tests for genes that differ between groups. It can also simulate gene networks for method testing. Its design borrows the data handling style of larger machine learning tools. Scanpy became one of the main ways single-cell data are explored, and many later tools build on it.
pmc-6291454:
The GBD 2016 Dementia Collaborators published this global dementia analysis in 2019. More people are living with dementia each year, which strains families, communities, and health systems. A sound response starts with an accurate count of the burden.

The study reports cases, deaths, and disability from Alzheimer disease and other dementias across most countries. Numbers rose mainly because populations grew older and larger. Rates at a given age changed little in many regions. The authors argue that prevention of risk factors like smoking and high blood pressure is the main lever available while cures remain out of reach.
pmc-6591954:
Ryan Wick, Louise Judd, and Kathryn Holt compared nanopore basecalling tools in 2019. Basecalling turns the raw electrical signal from a nanopore sequencer into DNA letters. Every later result depends on getting those letters right.

The team ran several neural network callers on the same bacterial data sets. They measured accuracy, speed, and how errors cluster in hard regions. Newer callers clearly beat older ones, but none was perfect everywhere. Their benchmarks help labs pick a caller and set honest expectations for assembly and variant work. The authors share their test data so future callers can be judged on the same ground.
plos-pone-0358354:
Huiyue Pan, Leilei Zhai, Shupeng Zhao, Ziyi Guo, and Ping Yao published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies ulcerative colitis, a chronic inflammation of the colon, made worse by a high-fat diet. The authors focus on fatty acid oxidation, the process cells use to burn fats for energy, and on injury to mitochondria, the cell's power stations.

The mechanism they name runs through the AMPK/PPARα pathway, a signaling route that controls energy use in cells. When that pathway falters, fat burning drops and mitochondria suffer, which the authors present as a key route by which rich diets aggravate colitis. Researchers hunting drug targets for bowel inflammation are the main readers.
plos-pone-0359954:
Nandakumar Ravichandran, Etimbuk Umana, Tomas Breslin, Aoife Cotter, and Walter Cullen wrote this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. Zhuozhi Gong and six colleagues check whether hair loss drugs carry a hidden link to male infertility, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Finasteride, dutasteride, and minoxidil are widely used against pattern baldness, and scattered reports have raised fertility worries. The team combined drug safety databases with gene data from testicular tissue to look for both warning signals and a plausible biological route.

Safety reports from American and European systems, covering roughly two decades, showed reporting signals for all three drugs, strongest for finasteride. In tissue from infertile men, one gene, HIF1A, stood out as more active, including in sperm producing and hormone making cells, and its activity tracked with immune and wound healing pathways. The authors present HIF1A as a candidate worth laboratory follow up, not settled proof of harm.
plos-pone-0358754:
Guibo Nie and four co-authors study a Xi'an tourist district that sells history without old buildings, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Datang Everbright City is a themed precinct built to evoke the Tang dynasty through scenery and performance, with no genuine relics on site. The authors asked how such staged surroundings can still stir visitors' cultural identity, and whether that feeling turns into loyalty to the place.

Surveying close to three hundred tourists, they traced how the district's physical and social atmosphere feeds a sense of belonging. Cultural identity carried the effect onward: it fully explained loyalty for several parts of the visitor experience. The findings matter for China's many built from scratch heritage districts, where designers cannot rely on authentic remains and must make symbolism do the work instead.
plos-pone-0345354:
Csaba Varga charts where highly pathogenic bird flu struck wild waterfowl and poultry across the United States from 2022 into 2025, in a single author PLOS ONE study published in 2026. The H5N1 strain that reached North America in early 2022 spread unevenly, and understanding its clustering could sharpen farm defenses. Varga analyzed public detection records at county level and scanned for places and times with more cases than chance would predict.

Wild birds logged more than seventeen thousand detections across nearly fifteen hundred counties. Four species, mallards, Canada geese, green winged teal, and snow geese, supplied about forty percent of them. Poultry outbreaks hit turkey farms hardest, then egg layers, broilers, and ducks. Several spillover waves moved from east to west, with wild bird detections sometimes preceding nearby farm outbreaks. The timing links give poultry regions a warning signal worth watching.
plos-pone-0354754:
Mustafa Çam leads a team of eight studying how storage temperature affects chukar partridge eggs before incubation, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Game bird breeders hold eggs for a week or two before setting them, and standard poultry advice recommends a narrow cool band. The team stored eggs at four temperatures, from near refrigeration to warm room level, for seven or fourteen days, then examined development and hatched the rest.

Most egg and hatching traits barely differed across the whole temperature range. Eggs kept at the middle cool setting produced slightly lighter chicks and took longer to hatch. Warmer storage nudged embryos toward later developmental stages before incubation, without clearly harming outcomes. The authors conclude that partridge eggs tolerate a far wider storage range than industry guidance assumes, a practical finding for small breeders without precise cold rooms, within the storage times tested.

Min Kyu Yang, Seong Jung Ha, and Ho-Seok Sa sort out a confusing eye condition in PLOS ONE in 2026: inflammation that swells only the muscle pair lifting the eye and eyelid. They reviewed fifty-eight patients with this isolated pattern and asked which diseases caused it and how the causes could be told apart on examination and scans, since treatment differs sharply by cause.

Thyroid eye disease accounted for about two thirds of cases and an unexplained muscle inflammation, idiopathic orbital myositis, for most of the rest; only two patients had the IgG4 related form. Tendon involvement on imaging strongly favored the myositis group, while limits on looking downward clustered in thyroid disease. Myositis patients whose lid drooped were diagnosed faster and responded better to steroids. The comparison gives eye specialists a practical checklist for a rare presentation.
plos-pone-0358654:
Konstantinos G Baroutis leads a team of eight exposing a laboratory trap hidden in room light, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Verteporfin, a light activated drug, is widely used in dishes as if it were a plain blocker of a growth protein pair, YAP and TEAD. The team shows that much of its apparent work is photochemistry instead. The compound cross links proteins when samples sit under normal lighting after the cells are broken open.

The effect appeared within an hour in cell free extracts, hitting several proteins at once. Two protective chemicals blunted it, pointing to radical and oxygen based light reactions. YAP itself was highly vulnerable to cross linking, while its partner protein resisted. On a protein blot, that pattern masquerades as selective drug action. The authors warn that part of the record using this compound may need re reading, this time with the lights in mind.
plos-pone-0357054:
Luca Alessandri traced ancient settlement change in Latium vetus, the old region around Rome, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. From the Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age, small settlements grew toward towns. Alessandri applied machine learning methods that can explain their own reasoning to that long shift.

The models highlight which factors best explain where people settled and how sites grew or shrank. Because the methods are explainable, archaeologists can judge the reasoning, not just accept a score. Understanding how early communities clustered helps explain the roots of Rome itself. The study also shows how transparent AI can serve history without turning it into a black box.
plos-pone-0358454:
Zoe Dellaert and Hollie M Putnam studied gene activity across a reef-building coral, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. A coral colony is not uniform: tips, sides, and base live in different light and flow, and do different jobs. The pair used methods that keep location information while reading which genes are active.

Dellaert and Putnam's map shows how the coral Pocillopora acuta divides labor across its own body. That spatial view helps explain how corals grow, feed, and respond to stress as a colony rather than as single polyps. Reefs are in steep decline, and colony-level insight may guide breeding of tougher corals. Basic maps like this underpin every later attempt to help reefs survive warming seas.
plos-pone-0358254:
Yonghui Zhang and Fangtao Li modeled how rock breaks under pressure and water, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Wet rock fails differently from dry rock, a fact tunnel and dam builders ignore at their peril. Their statistical damage model includes pore water pressure and the multifractal patterns found in real rock structure.

Zhang and Li's model helps engineers predict rock failure where water and stress combine, such as deep tunnels and reservoir slopes. Better prediction means supports designed for real conditions, not dry-lab ones. Fractal detail matters because rock is not uniform; its cracks follow patterns the model tries to honor. Safer underground works, from mines to metros, rest on models like this being right.
plos-pone-0357754:
Dewi Wulandari led a team of seven authors mapping hepatitis B mutations in Indonesia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The virus mutates to escape control, notably in two control regions, the precore and the basal core promoter. The team studied patients who lack a certain viral antigen, called HBeAg-negative, yet carry high viral loads.

Wulandari's mutation patterns give doctors information for choosing treatments likely to work. Mutations in these regions affect how the virus copies itself and how disease progresses. Indonesia carries a heavy hepatitis B burden, so local mutation data beat imported assumptions. Knowing which variants circulate helps labs pick the right tests and helps clinics anticipate which patients need closer watching for liver damage.
plos-pone-0354154:
Ahmed Ali A Shohan and co-authors measure three decades of city growth in five Saudi Arabian cities, from the early nineteen nineties to the early twenty twenties, using satellite images. Fast growth in an arid kingdom strains water, land, and services. The team classified land cover across time with vegetation and water indices and checked their maps carefully, then modeled how land shape steered growth.

One holy city grew most in raw area, the capital grew fastest in proportional terms, and another holy city barely expanded because steep land hemmed it in. Growth patterns differed too: compact and centered in the holy cities, sprawling in the capital and coastal cities. Shohan and colleagues give planners a city-by-city record for steering the next wave of building.
plos-pone-0354954:
Anjelica Martinez and colleagues put a widely used cultural values questionnaire under the microscope for Mexican American college students. The scale was built for teenagers and their caregivers, yet researchers keep using it with college students to study grades and well-being. Using existing data from several hundred undergraduates at Hispanic-serving campuses, the team tested whether the scale's structure, covering family duty, respect, religion, gender roles, and mainstream success values, still fits.

It did not. Formal checks showed clear misfit for Mexican American students, and attempts to stretch the scale to other Latinx students also failed, with the scale behaving differently across groups. Martinez and colleagues warn that results built on this mismatch may mislead, and they call for values measures built or revalidated with college students themselves.
plos-pone-0354454:
Fatemeh Ahmadnia and co-authors steeped Russian knapweed, itself an aggressive invader, in water and tested the extract on the seeds of three weeds, two crops, and rye. Their 2026 laboratory study measured germination and seedling growth across rising extract strengths, hunting for a dose window where weeds suffer but crops shrug, the basic recipe for a plant-based herbicide.

The window exists. Germination fell in a straight line with dose for everything, but weeds were stopped dead at far lower strengths than wheat or rye needed. Chemical profiling fingered several candidate compounds, including phenolics and a fragrant sesquiterpene. The authors stress these are dish experiments; soil, microbes, and weather may rewrite the story in a real field.
plos-pone-0345554:
Megan Dreher and colleagues separated two ways music is supposed to help runners: rhythm and motivation. They replaced music with its ingredients. Their 2026 study had fifteen adults run on a treadmill in three conditions. One was silence. One used a flashing visual metronome matched to their stride. One added a non-rhythmic motivational speech to the metronome. Sensors tracked trunk movement and balance, and runners rated their effort.

Both stimulus conditions trimmed perceived effort slightly, shy of statistical significance. The combined condition measurably steadied the trunk. It reduced sway acceleration in every direction compared with the metronome alone. The design offers researchers a clean way to test which part of music does the work. Early evidence credits motivational content with real biomechanical calm.
plos-pone-0355554:
Helen Edith Müller and seven colleagues give the first detailed anatomical account of dogs' whisker follicles in this 2026 study, entering a live animal welfare debate. Trimming whiskers for show grooming is common, and some claim dogs' whiskers are reduced and unimportant, especially in poodles. The team examined facial skin from forty-four dogs of varied breeds, ages, and sizes, counting and measuring the follicle-sinus complexes and probing their nerve supply with stains and electron microscopy.

Each dog carried roughly sixty of these complexes, with the muzzle whiskers longest, and size scaled with body weight. The structures held a rich sensory architecture, several kinds of touch receptors and free nerve endings, with nerve tissue making up a substantial share of each complex. No breed, poodles included, showed reduced equipment. The authors say the anatomy refutes the claim that canine whiskers lack function.
plos-pone-0356254:
Mazin Mansory interviewed Saudi teachers and school staff about moral injury and burnout during the country's Vision 2030 education reforms. Moral injury means the distress people feel when their work forces them to act against their own values. His 2026 study drew on long interviews with educators across Saudi Arabia, analysed in depth.

Six themes ran through the accounts, including rigid curricula, heavy testing pressure, and a felt lack of care from institutions. Many teachers said set mandates clashed with Islamic teaching values of care and fairness. Newer teachers described shaky professional identity, while veterans described teaching two ways at once. Mansory argues reforms land better when they respect teachers' ethical commitments.
plos-pone-0355354:
Sângia Feucht Freire and colleagues surveyed the heads of intensive care units across Brazil about safe breathing support for sore lungs. Gentler ventilator settings can spare hurt lungs. Their 2026 survey covered units in every region and scored what chiefs knew, felt, and did in daily care.

Most units had a wide range of gear on hand. Most said stocks grew after the COVID-19 pandemic. Clear gaps still split one region from the next. Scores for knowledge ran high on the whole. Units with more gear scored a bit higher, but the link was weak. Freire and colleagues say gear alone does not set good care, and poor regions need a fairer share.

Their 2026 study compared six ranking loss functions and five ways of describing drugs across two large screening datasets.

List-based losses led on both early and overall ranking quality. Mixing molecular fingerprints with basic chemical descriptors improved results further. The team added attention maps and an explanation tool that flagged genes and drug fragments behind each ranking. The explanations separated two breast cancer subtypes and highlighted known active parts of real drugs. Sarmeili and colleagues present the work as a step toward ranking tools doctors can inspect.
plos-pone-0355854:
Emmanuel Kwame Darkwa and co-authors measured how many people with epilepsy in two Ghanaian districts receive no proper treatment. Epilepsy is highly treatable, yet a wide treatment gap persists in poorer countries. Their 2026 population study screened communities inside a long-running health surveillance area across most of a year.

Epilepsy affected just under nine people per thousand. Seven in ten confirmed cases formed the treatment gap; only three in ten used standard seizure medicine. The commonest reason among untreated people was never having been diagnosed at all. Beliefs played a role too: over a third of respondents blamed witchcraft or supernatural causes. Darkwa and colleagues call for diagnosis drives paired with belief-sensitive education.
plos-pone-0353754:
Martin Weiß and colleagues track in 2026 how personality and the moment together shape whether people want social contact in daily life. Over two weeks, participants reported many thousands of real interactions through phone prompts, noting their own motives, how they saw their partner's motives, and how much they wanted the interaction. Stable traits for seeking or avoiding contact were measured as well.

A combined view using traits, momentary states, and partner views predicted preferences best. Seeking related traits and states raised the wish to interact, while avoidance states lowered it. Effects faded quickly between interactions. People with poor social functioning wanted less contact overall, with similar underlying patterns.
plos-pone-0355054:

Vesicles are eyed as antigen carriers for cancer vaccines, but how dendritic cells take them in was unclear. Only one receptor in the family strongly boosted vesicle uptake, helped by both bridging proteins. A small inner stretch of that receptor proved vital for showing vesicle antigens onward. Tumour bearing mice had more such dendritic cells, hinting at a vaccine target.
