plos-pone-0350854:
Asma ElAdel, Imen Filali, and Mourad Zaied published this 2026 study of artificial intelligence screening for diabetic retinopathy, serious eye damage from diabetes that blinds when caught late. Eye specialists remain the gold standard but are slow and scarce. Their model uses a compact vision transformer, an attention-based design good at linking distant parts of a retinal image.

The system was built to grade disease severity and flag likely cases quickly for human review. ElAdel pitches it for pre-screening and telemedicine, especially where ophthalmologists are few and diabetes is rising.
plos-pone-0353554:
Zhang and Hedayati Marzbali, in a 2026 study, ask what makes residents of old Chinese villages satisfied with tourism in their home places. Reviving traditional villages through tourism is a favored path to rural renewal, but residents' feelings can make or break it. The team surveyed people in three traditional villages in Yongzhou.

Two ideas guided the work: whether tourism met what residents expected, and how attached residents felt to their place. Higher expectations were linked to lower satisfaction, a letdown effect. Feeling that tourism brought real value carried the good effects of place pride and attachment into satisfaction. Age mattered: older residents were more satisfied, and several links between feelings and satisfaction differed by generation. The authors advise planners to keep promises modest, share value visibly, and design tourism with each generation in mind, so villages gain without residents feeling used.
plos-pone-0349654:
Han and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a vision model that can tell whose sheep is whose on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Overgrazing is wearing down the grassland, and knowing which flock grazes where would help balance herds with grass and settle disputes between herders. Sheep carry natural color patterns on their backs, and the team trained a segmentation model to read them.

Their model upgrades a strong existing design with three additions. A module reads the scene at several scales. Another keeps meaning consistent. A third rebuilds fine detail when enlarging the output. On a purpose-built data set of sheep in varied light and backgrounds, it beat its base model on every score. It also held up on a public benchmark and small test sets. The authors offer the tool for precision grazing management on fragile high grassland.
plos-pone-0353654:
Raeon Jang and seven colleagues ran a small randomised trial of laser acupuncture delivered inside the knee joint's acupuncture points, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Forty-five people with knee osteoarthritis were split among two laser wavelengths and a sham treatment that mimicked the procedure. Sessions ran twice a week for six weeks, and pain, stiffness, and daily function were tracked afterwards.

Both laser groups improved more than the sham group on pain at rest and in motion, and on standard joint scores, at several follow-up points. No treatment-related side effects appeared. Because the trial was a pilot, the authors call the pain relief a promising signal that larger trials must confirm.
plos-pone-0354254:
Yangming Zhang, Baohui Tian, and Hufeng Guo improve an artificial intelligence detector for cracks in bridge concrete, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Cracks are thin, faint, and easily confused with stains and rough texture, yet they are the earliest visible warning of structural decline. Their modified detector analyses images in the frequency domain as well as the ordinary spatial view, and adds a module dedicated to sharpening edges.

On two public crack datasets the improved detector beat its base model on the standard detection scores, by several percentage points on the stricter measures. Sharper automated eyes could let road agencies survey thousands of bridges from camera footage instead of sending inspectors onto scaffolding.
plos-pone-0353354:
Gang Chen, Qinjuan Zhong, and Ning Tang test whether tiny parcels shed by a medicinal herb can fight stomach cancer, in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. The herb is danshen, long used in Chinese medicine. From it the team purified exosome-like nanoparticles — microscopic bubbles carrying small RNA molecules — and fed them to human stomach cancer cells growing in dishes.

The cancer cells swallowed the parcels and slowed down: they survived less well, formed fewer colonies, and migrated less. Sequencing catalogued the RNA cargo, which appears to drive the effect. Plant-derived parcels are attractive because they are cheap and naturally tolerated, but the authors stress this is dish-level evidence, far from a treatment.
plos-pone-0353954:
Akihito Nakanishi and eight colleagues test a new way to probe hearing damage. The damage comes from a chemotherapy drug. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug, cisplatin, saves lives. But it often costs patients their high-frequency hearing. The team delivered ultrasound through the skull bone. They measured the brain's electrical response. Then they compared shifts in two ranges. One was the bone-conducted ultrasound range. The other was the ordinary hearing range.

Ordinary thresholds worsened clearly after the drug. The ultrasound responses shifted much less. That mismatch carries a warning. The ultrasound route taps a different part of the hearing machinery. It cannot simply stand in for standard tests. Anyone hoping to use it as a quick damage gauge should take note.
plos-pone-0352654:
Guan and colleagues designed a soft robot gripper for holding odd-shaped objects in a 2026 study. Soft grippers bend gently, but they can be too floppy to hold firm. Their design pairs a rubber-like material that bends when voltage is applied with a printed star-pattern support that adds stiffness without blocking sideways bend.

Computer models tested how stretching the rubber and squeezing the support changed the bend. A built version with two rubber layers was then checked in trials against the models. Tuning those two settings gave stronger, more controlled bending. The design points toward gentle robot hands that can still hold their shape under load.
plos-pone-0351254:
Semin Kazazoglu and four colleagues developed this 2026 PLOS One questionnaire measuring how dehumanized academics feel by their own universities. Managerial, metric-driven governance has raised complaints that scholars are treated as numbers rather than people. Working with two samples of Turkish academics totaling nearly six hundred, the team built and tested a scale for this perception.

The final thirty-four-item scale splits into two dimensions: feeling devalued and feeling treated as a mere instrument. Statistical checks showed the scale is highly consistent and mostly succeeds at measuring something distinct from neighboring concepts. The authors offer it to researchers and university leaders as a diagnostic tool for spotting where institutional practices make staff feel less than human.
plos-pone-0353154:
Liyun Su, Linke Hou, and Jiaodi Liu present this 2026 PLOS One engineering paper on a flexible version of the Stewart platform, the six-legged device that moves flight simulators and precision machines. Their design adds piezoelectric elements to correct tiny motion losses in the telescopic legs. The hard problems are calculating leg lengths for a desired pose and, harder still, working backward from leg lengths to pose.

For the backward problem they trained a neural network enhanced with a stronger fitting algorithm, using exact formulas to generate its training data. In simulations the network predicted platform pose with errors under half a percent across the whole workspace. The authors say the approach beats both the classic iterative method and standard neural networks, supporting ultra-precise positioning in robotics and measurement.
plos-pone-0350554:
Simon de Gans and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One observational study of how medical teams work together for patients with several chronic conditions at once. The researchers filmed and recorded two kinds of treatment meetings: interprofessional meetings, where specialists pursue one shared patient-centered goal, and multidisciplinary meetings, where each specialist mainly argues their own field's case.

The interprofessional meetings sat people around a table with a designated chair and a relaxed, learning-friendly tone, while multidisciplinary meetings used a theatre layout with more passive listeners and disease-centered talk. Clinicians who attended both formats joined in far more actively in the interprofessional ones. The authors distill their observations into nine practical keys for better collaboration, aimed at hospital teams drowning in complex patients.
plos-pone-0352254:
Hayato Ishii and six colleagues mine breast cancer data for prognostic signals in this 2026 study. Their focus is the genes that build junctions between cells. Those junctions hold epithelial tissue together, and their failure has long been tied to cancer spread. The team analysed one hundred seventy-nine junction genes across breast cancer subtypes. Two large datasets supplied the discovery material. An independent Scandinavian cohort provided validation.

A combined junction signature predicted survival within subtypes. High scores meant poorer outcomes nearly everywhere. The effect bit hardest in Luminal B and basal-like tumours, the aggressive kinds. High scores also forecast recurrence inside the first five years. Such tumours switched on matrix and scaffolding pathways, as if loosening their moorings. Single-cell data showed which cells carry the signature genes. A junction-based score could help oncologists spot, early, the patients whose cancers are likeliest to return.
plos-pone-0343954:
Meng Wang and four colleagues build a network that names the style of a painting. Their 2026 study tackles a slippery computer vision problem. Style cues scatter across a canvas, tangled with subject matter and background. The proposed network reads the whole composition and local brushwork together. Four modules share the labour: encoding style features, generating attention maps, learning by contrast, and checking attention counterfactually. That last module asks what the prediction would lose without each highlighted region.

Counterfactual checks suppress flashy but irrelevant regions. Contrastive training pulls fine-grained styles further apart in the model's internal space. Tests ran on public art datasets, including the large WikiArt collection. Interpretability is the selling point alongside accuracy. Curators and heritage managers need systems that show their working. A classifier that points to the brushstrokes behind its verdict is far more useful for digital archives than one that merely announces a label.
plos-pone-0351754:
Fadi Al Zoubi and six colleagues adapt an evidence-based practice questionnaire for Hong Kong clinicians. Their 2026 study imports a tool built for recent Canadian therapy graduates. Evidence-based practice means blending research, expertise, and patient values. Measuring it fairly requires wording that survives translation and culture. First came translation into the local language and back again, scrutiny by an expert panel, and probing interviews with thirty-six providers. Then two hundred forty-eight clinicians completed the final version.

The tool's structure survived the journey. Its two models cover six ideas, from actual use of evidence to knowledge, confidence, attitudes, and resources. Statistical modelling checked that items behaved consistently and treated groups fairly. One model needed only language adjustments. Hong Kong's health system employs thousands trained across many traditions. A validated measure lets educators see whether evidence habits are spreading, rather than assuming imported questionnaires mean the same thing abroad.
plos-pone-0352154:
Carly Lightstone and five colleagues interview patients in the raw days after losing a leg. Their 2026 qualitative study sits in a vascular surgery service. The patients had peripheral arterial disease and chose planned, primary amputations. Interviews ran five to ten days after surgery. The premise is that adjustment begins long before the operation. A patient's emotional state approaching amputation shapes recovery, rehabilitation, and quality of life afterwards. Understanding that inner process is the study's aim.

Conversations were analysed thematically for recurring patterns. The authors frame psychological support as part of surgical care, not an afterthought bolted on later. Surgeons deciding with patients about amputation hold more than a technical choice. Fear, grief, identity, and hope all sit in the consultation room. By documenting patients' own accounts so soon after surgery, the study gives care teams language and timing for support that patients will actually recognise as help.
plos-pone-0352454:
Qianyao Yuan and colleagues compared scans and tissue features of a rare lung cancer that mixes two cell types in one tumor. Adenosquamous carcinoma grows both gland-like and flat squamous cancer cells, behaves aggressively, and is hard to name before surgery because its scans resemble either parent type. The team reviewed twenty-seven such cases against forty each of the two pure types.

Against squamous cancers, the mixed tumors sat more often toward the lung's edge and showed more pleural pulling, spiky borders, and spread to lymph nodes. Measures built from these traits separated the groups usefully. For surgeons and radiologists, the work lists concrete scan clues worth weighting when a lung mass could be this mixed, harder-to-treat cancer rather than a commoner one.
plos-pone-0351154:
Lucas David, Nicolas Pellerin, and Michaël Dambrun adapted a questionnaire on selflessness and self-centeredness so it can measure a single day rather than a person's general character. A trait version already existed, splitting selflessness into four parts and self-centeredness into three. Three studies, with hundreds and then over a thousand respondents, checked whether the daily version keeps that shape.

The daily scale did reproduce the seven-part structure, and its scores lined up with mental health, relationships, and care for the environment in ways theory predicts. Days on which people felt more selfless differed measurably from self-centered days. A day-level tool lets researchers ask how these states rise and fall with events, sleep, or practice, and whether nudging a single day can nudge a life.
plos-pone-0343754:
Checking newborns for hidden disease is expanding, and gene-based screening could soon test for hundreds of conditions at birth. Camille Level and colleagues surveyed about sixteen hundred forty French parents on whether such expansion feels acceptable, in this 2026 PLOS One study run through maternity wards and an online panel.

Parents weighed an expanded test panel against a genomic version, rating feelings, expected benefit, and fairness. A trade-off exercise probed what they would accept in exchange for more information. The team used an established acceptability framework to separate enthusiasm from ethical unease. Their findings aim to guide French policy so growth in screening keeps public trust.
plos-pone-0337254:
Cesilia Charles and colleagues surveyed health workers at Katavi Regional Referral Hospital in Tanzania in mid 2025. They wanted to know how well staff follow basic steps that stop infections from spreading in the hospital. Close to two hundred doctors, nurses, and lab staff took part, using questionnaires and checklists during visits to wards.

Average compliance sat below seventy percent, and fewer than four in ten workers reached the high level. Doctors scored lower than nurses. Workers did better when they felt motivated, had regular supportive supervision, and worked where an active infection committee existed. Soap and water were still missing in many latrines, which helps explain the gap.
plos-pone-0351554:
Scott W Gill and colleagues studied health understanding among people held in prisons in New South Wales, Australia. They used answers from a standard health literacy survey given to more than four hundred people. Grouping methods sorted people with like strengths and struggles. Interviews with ten people inside added daily detail about getting care.

Grouping found fourteen distinct profiles for the whole sample, and nine for people who identified as Aboriginal. Staff and advocates then helped shape twenty three short portraits, each standing for one profile. The portraits show that average scores hide wide differences. Care and health teaching can fit real needs better when they start from these varied profiles instead of one score for everyone.
plos-pone-0351054:
Xiaoyuan Jin and colleagues built a light vision model that spots faults on power line insulators even in fog. Fog blurs small cracks and dirt marks, and drone photos add busy backgrounds. Their model cleans fog noise, lifts faint fault marks, and blends detail at several scales while staying small enough for field gear.

On a fog data set the team built, accuracy reached a solid mark with under three million settings to tune. Scores held up on two public fog sets and on a clear weather road scene set as well. Light weight matters here: a model that runs on a drone can flag faults during flight instead of after landing, cutting inspection time for power crews.
plos-pone-0349554:
Arshad M Khanani and colleagues ran a multi site trial of a cooling device that numbs the eye before injections into the eye. Many patients need repeated eye injections and dread the pain. Eighty patients who had long used numbing drops or gel tried set cold doses, from minus ten to minus fifteen degrees for ten to twenty seconds.

Pain fell most with the shortest cold dose, ten seconds at the colder setting, with average scores staying low across visits. A longer dose at the same cold hurt more on average. Mild surface marks appeared in one group but not the other. Cold numbing can ease eye injection pain, the trial finds, when dose is kept brief.
plos-pone-0348354:
ZhiPeng Wu proposed a new weather forecasting method in 2026 that blends graph networks with a diffusion model. Standard computer models of the atmosphere are costly and strain against its chaotic behaviour, while many learning methods miss how conditions vary from place to place.

The method maps weather onto graphs at several scales to catch local and wide patterns, then lets a diffusion model trace how conditions evolve over time in a compressed form. On real data sets it beat leading rivals in accuracy and speed, doing especially well for temperature, air pressure height, and wind. Sharper cheap forecasts aid farms and disaster planning.
plos-pone-0350454:
Liping Wu and colleagues assessed the reliability of a key valve system in coal gasification plants in 2026, using a blend of two artificial intelligence methods. The lock bucket valve works under harsh conditions, and its failure can halt a plant.

A learning network first tuned the starting numbers of a dynamic risk model that tracks how failure chances shift over time. The tuned model then judged the system forward and backward. Without upkeep, predicted reliability after three hundred hours was very low, and maintenance lifted it greatly. The optimised model gave more cautious estimates than the untuned one, a warning against rosy assumptions.
plos-pone-0349854:
Alexandra Poeschla and co-authors tracked a fungal infection marker in Ugandan outpatients with advanced HIV from 2017 to 2022 in work published in 2026. Cryptococcal disease kills many such patients, and a blood antigen test can catch it before symptoms, as national screening expanded.

More than four hundred adults tested positive. Their immune counts were very low, and the median marker level sat at a mid range tied to risk. Over the years the share already on HIV treatment at screening fell, while marker levels drifted up without a clear trend. The data show screening reaching people later, a gap programs must close.
plos-pone-0349954:
Xiao-Ying Huang and Xiang Zheng studied a combined inflammation score in critically ill patients with high blood fats in 2026, using a large intensive care database. The score folds four blood cell counts into one number meant to capture immune strain.

More than twelve thousand first time intensive care patients were followed for deaths at one, three, and six months, plus kidney injury and delirium. Higher scores meant higher death risk at every horizon, with risk climbing sharply past a clear threshold. The top quarter fared worst. A score from a routine blood count could help flag fragile patients on day one.
plos-pone-0341754:
Raksha M Narasimhan, Crystal S Taswell, and co-authors looked back at women treated for early breast cancer that had spread to a few nearby lymph nodes. After mastectomy, doctors still debate whether radiation to the chest wall helps these patients live longer or stay cancer free. Their 2026 review covered women treated at one center over more than two decades.

Only fifty-seven patients fit the study, and about two in five received radiation. Radiation was not linked to better survival or fewer recurrences, even in the aggressive triple-negative type. Hormone therapy did help, while having more involved nodes predicted worse outcomes. The authors say treatment choices should rest on each patient's tumor traits and overall therapy, though the small group limits firm answers.
plos-pone-0348054:
Sahar Abed and Abdolrazagh Hashemi Shahraki led a hunt for a virus that kills drug-proof bacteria. The target germ causes pneumonia and resists last-resort drugs. The team found the virus in hospital wastewater. They named it Halo KS-7. Gene reading, done with help from AI tools, mapped its makeup. Tests ran in dishes and in mouse wounds.

The virus hit the target germ hard. It worked best at body heat and in salty settings. It broke bacteria open after a short wait of about twenty minutes. Mouse wound tests tracked healing and tissue health. The team calls the virus a strong hope for treating a germ that badly needs new foes.
plos-pone-0349754:
Kétlin Fagundes Teixeira, Ana Carolina Cadore-Rodrigues, and co-authors tested how surface preparation affects the fatigue strength of zirconia ceramic used for dental crowns. Crowns fail by cracking after years of chewing, and how the ceramic is treated before cementing may decide its lifespan. Their 2026 lab study prepared ceramic discs with five treatments, from sandblasting with different grits to glazing, then cemented them with thick or runny resin cements and flexed them to failure.

Surface treatment mattered greatly, while cement thickness did not. Glazing produced the strongest discs, with smooth, even surfaces. Coarse sandblasting performed worst and left the deepest defects, while fine sandblasting and glaze-plus-acid landed in between. The authors conclude that gentle glazing beats aggressive roughening for long-lasting zirconia restorations.
plos-pone-0317254:
Erin Ingalls and colleagues interviewed seventeen recreational runners who had ended a daily running streak of at least one hundred days. Run streaking, running at least a mile every single day, is praised for building strong habits. The researchers wanted the other side of the story: what breaking such a streak feels like and whether it can backfire.

Some runners admitted they had run through injuries and treated the streak as a burden before it ended. Afterward, many felt sadness, anger, or disappointment, and some described a grieving process, though relief appeared too. The pain was sharpest for runners most attached to their streak, a warning for habit programs built on never missing a day.
plos-pone-0349354:
Kimia Taki and colleagues optimized a venturi tube reactor that pasteurizes milk without heat, using collapsing bubbles to kill germs. A venturi tube narrows a pipe so fast-moving liquid forms cavitation bubbles; their violent collapse destroys bacteria while the milk stays cool. The team used fluid dynamics simulations and a statistical design method to tune the tube's throat size, length, and angles.

The tuned design maximized turbulence in the cavitation zone while keeping energy losses and pressure drop low. In experiments the reactor cut E. coli counts by nearly three orders of magnitude, while milk fat, protein, and lactose stayed essentially unchanged. Heat-free pasteurization that keeps fresh flavor and nutrition intact is a long-sought goal for small dairies.
plos-pone-0329054:
Jair Alonso Góngora-Bendezú and colleagues checked the lungs of four hundred Peruvian workers who had recovered from COVID-19 and who regularly work at high altitude despite living at sea level. All had confirmed past infection, and each took a careful breathing test in twenty twenty-four. The team looked for lasting damage and for which workers were hit hardest.

More than seven in ten workers showed abnormal breathing patterns, most often a mixed pattern that stiffens and narrows the airways at once. Risk climbed with obesity, other illnesses, years of breathing workplace fumes, years of altitude exposure, and having had severe COVID-19. The authors urge steady lung monitoring for this workforce, with closest attention to those carrying several of these risks at once.
plos-pone-0344454:
Zahra Cheraghali and Mohsen Rostamy-Malkhalifeh tackle a management problem: in organisations run from a centre, which handful of branches or units lifts the whole system's performance most? Standard efficiency scoring rates each unit on its own, ignoring how much a unit matters to the group. Some newer fixes can produce impossible or runaway answers unless constants are guessed in advance.

Their new model picks a set of outstanding units of a chosen size in one optimisation, needs no preset constants, and is guaranteed to return a feasible, bounded answer. Two real-world datasets were used to show the method works in practice. The authors frame it as a decision-support tool for headquarters teams deciding where praise, investment, or replication efforts will pay off most.
plos-pone-0349254:
Ryota Yamamoto and co-authors tested whether brain responses to flashing patterns can measure the eye's focusing power objectively, useful for patients who cannot report what they see. Twenty-one students viewed checkerboard patterns and the same boards rotated into diamonds while the team blurred their vision with lenses in steps and recorded the brain's electrical reply. The replies were compared with each student's own measured focusing range.

The brain signal's height shrank as blur grew, even when its timing held steady. Diamond patterns predicted focusing power more accurately and tracked the students' own measurements more tightly than upright boards. The authors trace this quirk to how vision favours horizontal and vertical lines over slanted ones. They propose the diamond test as the better candidate for an objective focusing exam.
plos-pone-0339554:
Mojisola Fasokun and co-workers link loneliness with self-reported thinking decline among adults in the United States. Their 2026 study uses national survey data collected over eight years. Close to eighty-six thousand adults answered questions on how often they feel lonely. They also said whether their memory or thinking has slipped.

The chance of reporting thinking decline rose step by step with loneliness. Adults who always felt lonely reported decline nearly half the time, against about one in ten among those never lonely. The gap ran wider for women at the loneliest level. Age and background changed the picture little. Treating loneliness as a health risk, the authors argue, belongs in brain-health planning.
plos-pone-0348954:
Aya Sugiyama and co-workers follow how long COVID-19 symptoms lasted across pandemic waves in Hiroshima, Japan, comparing adults and children. Their 2026 study extends an earlier group to nearly twenty-seven hundred people infected between twenty twenty and twenty twenty-four, asking about thirteen symptoms and how long each hung on.

Adults fared worst in the Delta period, when close to half still had symptoms at six months. Later variant periods left fewer adults affected, and children's rates ran far lower throughout. Symptoms lasting past two years rarely cleared after that, though children's remaining symptoms did not disrupt daily life. Younger age sped recovery most. The long tail of illness shrank with newer variants but never vanished.
plos-pone-0347854:
Takafumi Ishii, Takashi Kojima, Yusuke Yasuda, and Kazushi Fujimoto present a way to compute entropy, the measure of disorder, for small local regions inside rubber-like materials. Rubber's springiness comes from entropy in its tangled molecular network, but local entropy changes had resisted calculation. Their method counts the states available to atoms from how they jiggle in molecular dynamics simulations.

Tested on simulated polymer networks, the computed entropy agreed qualitatively with thermodynamic expectations and with values from established integration techniques. The method works for the whole system and for local patches around cross-links. The authors offer it as a tool for understanding why elastomers stretch and snap back.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
By mid-1968, Cyprus renewals had become a New York routine. On 18 June, the Council adopted Resolution 254 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the peace force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past March of that year.

The text restates the long chain of earlier Cyprus decisions. It urges the parties to seize what it calls a hopeful climate for a deal. It then extends the posting to 15 December 1968. One hope is spelled out at the end. Enough progress by then might let the force shrink or go home. That hope came back, unmet, for years.

Slovenia's smooth exit from Yugoslavia contrasts with the war around it in 1992. On 18 May, the Council adopted Resolution 754 without a vote. The Republic of Slovenia had claimed freedom the June before. It had survived a ten-day war at that time. Wide recognition came in January 1992. It was the first Yugoslav republic to firm up its statehood.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Slovenia. It was seated days later, with Croatia and Bosnia beside it. The calm of its entry stood out sharply. Bosnia was sliding into chaos at that same moment. Slovenia's path marked Yugoslavia's least violent break.

The Central African Republic became independent from France on 13 August 1960. Ten days later its UN application was already before the Council. Resolution 154 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The vote happened at the busy 891st meeting. That same session handled applications from Congo and Upper Volta as well.

Members recommended admitting the Central African Republic. The General Assembly followed within weeks. The landlocked state joined during the famous Year of Africa. Seventeen African nations gained independence in 1960. A UN seat offered the new republic recognition and contacts. It also tied the country to the decolonization debates then reshaping the Assembly's agenda and voting balance.

Cataloguers sometimes shelve Resolution 1354 under Western Sahara. The text itself is about Cyprus. It was adopted unanimously on 15 June 2001. The Secretary-General's report of 30 May 2001 had reviewed the UN operation there. It pressed both sides to deal seriously with missing persons. Cyprus's government agreed the peacekeepers should stay.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 December 2001. A report was due by 1 December. The recurring Strovilia dispute appears again. Turkish Cypriot limits on the force, imposed in June 2000, had to be rescinded. The earlier military position there must be restored. These six-month renewals, repeated for decades, quietly froze the island's green line in place.

Resolution 1654, adopted on 31 January 2006, restarts the expert team policing Congo's arms embargo. The Council said it was determined to watch compliance closely and enforce penalties against violators. Eastern Congo remained crowded with militias despite the formal end of the war, and the embargo was leaking.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council asked the Secretary-General to re-establish the Group of Experts within thirty days, this time running until 31 July 2006. The group had to keep applying the mandate set in earlier resolutions, brief the sanctions committee by 10 April, and file a written report before 10 July. All parties and states were again told to grant its members safety and immediate, unhindered access.

South Africa's raids into Angola are condemned in Resolution 454. It passed on 2 November 1979. Twelve members backed it, and three did not vote either way. Angola had sent a formal plea and a note from its ruling party, the MPLA. Two past texts had condemned South Africa's attacks on Angola. They had told it to respect Angola's freedom and its borders.

The new strikes are called planned and steady. They hit Angola's air space and its soil. Their timing, the Council said, aimed to block peace deals in the south of Africa, above all the 1978 Namibia plan. The text mourns the lives lost and the homes and goods wrecked by the raids.

Resolution 1954, adopted on 14 December 2010, lets Yugoslavia tribunal judges stay past their terms to finish their trials. The tribunal's own completion reports admitted it could not finish all work in 2010, the target set years before. Its president also warned that experienced staff were leaving, threatening the remaining cases.

The Council extended the terms of the judges concerned, so trials and appeals already under way would not collapse for want of a bench. It urged the tribunal to complete its work as fast as possible. The extensions were practical housekeeping with real stakes: war crimes trials for the Balkan wars of the 1990s depended on continuity among the judges hearing them.

The Rwanda tribunal's final stretch is managed by Resolution 2054, adopted on 29 June 2012. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda had to finish work by 31 December 2014 and hand over to the Residual Mechanism, whose Rwanda branch would open on 1 July 2012. One judge was moving to the Appeals Chamber and five ad litem judges were leaving. Staff losses and homes for acquitted persons remained problems.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets three trial judges whose terms expire on 30 June 2012 stay until 31 December 2012 to finish the trial they had begun. It extends the tribunal President's term to 31 December 2014 so the court's work can be completed, with a review in June 2013. The tribunal must report its plan for shifting functions to the Mechanism. States are urged to help arrest and surrender all remaining fugitives and to accept relocated acquitted persons.

Liberia's last sanctions are renewed again by Resolution 1854, adopted on 19 December 2008. Timber and diamond measures had already ended, and Liberia was applying Kimberley Process controls and taking part in revenue-transparency initiatives. The Panel of Experts still found too little progress toward the conditions for lifting the arms and travel measures, and none on the asset freeze.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and travel ban for 12 months, with the standing exemptions for vetted Liberian security forces. Notice to the Sanctions Committee is required on delivery. The asset freeze under Resolution 1532 (2004) remains, and the Committee must update the public reasons for each listing. The Panel of Experts is extended to 20 December 2009. It must report midway by 1 June 2009. Its work is to check compliance, judge the forestry law and Kimberley controls, and help keep the listing reasons current.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/54 (2014) backs multilateralism in disarmament and non-proliferation. The Assembly is troubled by the erosion of multilateral approaches. It is troubled by states turning to unilateral action on security concerns. It reaffirms multilateralism as the core principle for working out arms rules and for settling compliance concerns. It urges all interested states to take part in multilateral talks openly, with no one shut out. It asks parties to weapons-of-mass-destruction treaties to settle compliance disputes through those treaties' own procedures, rather than through unverified accusations.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1154, adopted in 1998 under Chapter VII, deals with Iraq's compliance with the disarmament obligations set by resolution 687 (1991) after the 1991 Gulf War cease-fire. The Council says its earlier resolutions form the governing standard of Iraqi compliance and that it is determined to secure immediate and full compliance, without conditions or restrictions.

The Council endorses the memorandum of understanding signed on 23 February 1998. It was signed between Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister and the Secretary-General. The deal was meant to reopen inspections. The Council asks for procedures for presidential sites to be finished quickly, with the heads of UNSCOM and the IAEA. It stresses that Iraq must give both bodies immediate, unconditional and unrestricted access. It warns that any violation would have the severest consequences for Iraq.

Changes to the Goods Review List used in Iraq's oil-for-food programme are adopted on 30 December 2002. The programme had just been extended for 180 days from 5 December. The list decides which imports Iraq may buy freely and which need review because they could serve military ends.

Changes to the list and to the procedures for applying it are adopted. A full review of both is ordered after 90 days and again before the 180-day period ends, with regular reviews after that. The sanctions committee is told to study the list as part of its regular work and suggest additions or deletions.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 29 July 2004, and the Abkhazia deadlock is taken up once more. Geneva meetings of the Group of Friends had kept some momentum in the talks. But the lack of progress toward a settlement is again called unacceptable, and the 2001 helicopter attackers remain unidentified.

Both sides are urged to negotiate in earnest, with a warning that a lasting deal will require concessions from each. They are pressed to work through the Geneva task forces on economic cooperation, refugee return, and political and security questions, and through the Sochi working groups. Law enforcement and safety in the Gali district are to improve so displaced people can return.

Direct talks between Morocco and the POLISARIO Front on Western Sahara are called for on 30 April 2007. Both sides had just sent the Secretary-General rival proposals, Morocco's in April backed as serious and credible efforts. The long impasse over the territory's future was, for the first time in years, met with a negotiating push.

The parties are called on to enter negotiations without preconditions and in good faith. The goal stays a just, lasting, and mutually acceptable political solution providing for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. The Secretary-General is asked to host the talks under his auspices, with member states lending help, and to report on their progress by 30 June 2007. MINURSO's mandate is renewed alongside the call.

Syria's civil war had brought years of suffering by the end of 2015, with no end in sight. On 18 December 2015 the Council adopted Resolution 2254. It set out a road map for ending the war through politics rather than fighting. The plan built on the Geneva Communiqué of 2012. It also built on talks held in Vienna by an international support group.

The Council backed formal talks between Syria's government and the opposition. The talks were to start in early January 2016, under United Nations guidance. Within six months, the process had to set up a credible and inclusive form of government. A timetable for writing a new constitution was part of that step. Free elections under United Nations supervision were to follow within eighteen months. A nationwide cease-fire was to move forward alongside the talks.

Cyprus broke into war in July 1974, after a coup and a Turkish military intervention on the island. Resolution 354 was adopted unanimously on 23 July 1974, three days after an earlier cease-fire call. The short text reaffirms Resolution 353 of 20 July in full. It demands that all parties to the fighting obey that call at once. All firing in the area had to stop immediately. All states were asked to show the utmost restraint and to take no action that might make the situation worse.

The truce in Palestine broke down in July 1948, and the Council hardened its line. Israel had accepted a longer truce in principle. The states of the Arab League had rejected repeated appeals from the United Nations mediator and from the Council itself. Resolution 54 was adopted on 15 July 1948.

The Council determined that the situation in Palestine was a threat to the peace, under Article 39 of the Charter. The governments and authorities involved were ordered to stop military action. They had to issue cease-fire orders by a time set by the mediator. Refusal would count as a breach of the peace. For Jerusalem, an immediate and unconditional cease-fire was ordered within twenty-four hours. The mediator had to supervise the truce, examine alleged breaches, and keep working toward the demilitarization of the city.
un-sc-res-254:
Conditions in Cyprus looked more hopeful in 1968, and the Council wanted the parties to use the moment well. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 11 June, said the peacekeeping force was still needed to maintain peace. Cyprus's government had agreed the force must stay. Resolution 254 was adopted unanimously on 18 June 1968.

The Council reaffirmed its string of Cyprus resolutions, back to Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to make the most of the favorable climate on the island. They had to keep working together toward the Council's goals, with determination. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 December 1968. The Council hoped that progress by then would allow a withdrawal, or at least a large cut in the force.
un-sc-res-1354:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed in June 2001 with a familiar complaint attached. On 15 June 2001 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 December 2001. The Secretary-General's report had again raised the missing persons issue. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay. The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions, led by 1251 of 1999. Aid work on disease control among peacekeepers also drew a welcome.

Turkish Cypriot leaders and Turkish forces had to lift limits placed on UNFICYP in June 2000. They also had to restore the military position at Strovilia. That small village post had become a symbol of the force's blocked movement. The Secretary-General owed a report by 1 December.
un-sc-res-1654:
The Congo arms embargo's expert watchers were re-established on 31 January 2006. The Security Council restated its resolve to track compliance with the embargo set by resolution 1493 (2003) and widened by resolution 1596 (2005). It meant to enforce travel and money measures against those who broke the embargo. The Congo's situation still threatened international peace and security, the Council held.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council asked the Secretary-General to re-establish the Group of Experts within thirty days. The new group's term would run to 31 July 2006. It would carry on the mandate set by resolutions 1533, 1596, and 1649 (2005). The group owed the sanctions committee an update by 10 April 2006 and a written report before 10 July. All parties and states had to cooperate fully with the group. Its members were to get safety, free access to people, documents, and sites, and no delays.
un-sc-res-454:
South African attacks on Angola were condemned by the Security Council on 2 November 1979. Angola's representative had brought the complaint, with a party communiqué sent on 31 October. Resolutions 387 (1976) and 447 (1979) had already condemned Pretoria's aggression and demanded respect for Angola's borders. The Council called the latest violations planned, persistent, and sustained.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's aggression against Angola. South Africa had to stop all acts of aggression and provocation at once. It had to respect Angola's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity in full. It also had to stop using Namibia, a territory it held illegally, as a base for attacks on Angola and other front-line states. Member states were asked to give Angola and its neighbors urgent help to strengthen their defense. The Council said the raids aimed to wreck talks on settlements in Namibia and Zimbabwe.
un-sc-res-1854:
Liberia brought the Council to Resolution 1854, adopted on 19 December 2008. Liberia had made steady progress since 2006 in rebuilding the state. Its timber rules were in force, and it had joined the Kimberley Process for diamonds. Yet the Council found too little progress toward the terms for lifting sanctions.

Acting under Chapter VII, the text renews the arms and travel measures for twelve more months. The asset freeze from 2004 stays in force, with yearly review promised. The Panel of Experts gains a new term until 20 December 2009. The panel must check the timber and diamond sectors, judge how the freeze works, and report by June and December 2009.
europmc-pmc10087054:
Mattsson-Carlgren and a large team test whether blood markers can predict memory decline before Alzheimer's disease symptoms appear, in a 2023 study. Alzheimer's builds up in the brain for years in a silent phase. How long that phase lasts varies a lot between people, which makes trial design and early care hard.

The team followed people with amyloid buildup but no symptoms, using blood tests over time. They asked which markers forecast later decline in thinking. Their results help sharpen the choice of patients for early treatment trials and future screening.
europmc-pmc10115554:
Thieblemont and a large trial team report dose expansion results for epcoritamab in large B-cell lymphoma that returned or resisted past care, in a 2023 study. Epcoritamab is an antibody given under the skin that grabs both T cells and cancerous B cells. By linking them, it directs T cells to kill the cancer cells.

Earlier dose-finding work had shown strong anti-tumor activity. This phase of the trial tested a set dose in more patients. The paper reports response rates and side effects in detail. Those results informed the drug's later approval path.
europmc-pmc10412454:
Gulen and colleagues showed in 2023 that a DNA alarm path drives inflammation in old age. Low-grade swelling is a hallmark of ageing and fuels decline. The path pairs two proteins, cGAS and STING, which sense loose DNA inside cells. Loose DNA can leak from worn cell power units.

When the team blocked STING, old human cells and tissues calmed down. In old mice, blocks cut swelling in many organs and in the brain, and tissue function rose. In the brain, the path woke microglia, the local immune cells, into states that harm nerve cells. Memory also fell when the path was forced on. The work marks the path as a drug target for ageing.
europmc-pmc1064854:
Leone and co-authors cut a gene in mice in 2005 to learn how the body manages energy. The gene makes PGC-1alpha, a helper that switches on genes for cell power units. Those units, mitochondria, burn fuel to make energy. Mice born without the helper lived, yet deep checks found faults in many systems.

Growth of the heart and slow muscle lagged after birth. Leone reports fewer, weaker power units in slow muscle, with less stamina as a result. Body fat rose with age, most of all in females. The mice could not hold body heat in the cold. After a short fast, fat clogged their livers. Brain tissue showed small hollow lesions as well.
europmc-pmc10772854:
Collins and co-authors opened a three-part series in 2024 on how to judge clinical prediction models. Such a model gives a person's risk of a disease or a future event. It weighs traits such as age, symptoms, and blood pressure. Doctors lean on these numbers for daily choices, so their accuracy is vital.

Most new models never reach real care, Collins notes. Small samples, overfitting, and patchy reports block the path. The core flaw is weak or missing tests of how a model fares in its target group. The piece lays out inner and outer validation, the checks done inside and outside the build data. It also urges tests of fairness across groups of patients.
europmc-pmc10920854:
Zhou and co-authors review a form of cell death driven by iron that may help fight cancer in this 2024 paper. Ferroptosis is a death path where iron sparks a build-up of harmful fats in cell membranes. It differs from the tidy cell death path called apoptosis. The body uses it to suppress tumours on its own.

Some cancer cells that shrug off standard therapy are highly prone to this death, the review notes. That makes it attractive for hard-to-treat cancers. Yet firing it can also blunt the immune attack on tumours, a real risk. The authors map its control paths and its talks with the tissue around tumours. They survey its use with immune therapy, radiation, and drug therapy. Markers to guide patient choice are discussed.
europmc-pmc11701654:
CZI Cell Science Program presents a single-cell data platform called CZ CELLxGENE Discover in this 2024 paper. Labs have now analysed single cells by the hundreds of millions, using high-throughput transcriptomic methods, which read gene activity cell by cell. The pooled knowledge could unlock insights into health and disease. Yet the sheer number of datasets and their varied formats block meta-analysis.

The platform hosts a growing, community-contributed corpus: over 93 million unique cells in all, the authors report. The data are curated, standardised, and tagged with consistent cell-level metadata. The collection is the largest of its kind, they state. It is available through a free online portal for exploration and modelling. The authors link the platform to new machine learning directions, including large language models applied to cell data.
europmc-pmc1269454:
Thomason and colleagues tracked delirium in non-ventilated ICU patients in 2005. Delirium is common in ventilated patients and predicts worse outcomes. Data for patients not on ventilators were scarce. The cohort held 261 medical ICU patients at a university hospital.

Nurses screened for delirium at least twice daily. Nearly half, 125 patients, had at least one delirium episode. Patients with delirium were older on average. Statistical models treated delirium as a time-based factor. Thomason tests whether delirium itself predicts longer hospital stay. The design separates delirium effects from illness severity. The study ran from February 2002 to January 2003. Nurses did the checks two or more times each day on the ward.
europmc-pmc1277854:
Shafer, Meyer, and Crofton reviewed pyrethroid insecticides and the developing brain in 2005. Pyrethroids hold 25 percent of the world insecticide market. Adult nerve effects are well characterized. Effects on developing brains were far less charted.

Newborn rats proved at least ten times more sensitive than adults. That gap held for two tested pyrethroids. Most others lack age-specific toxicity data entirely. The review covers 22 developmental studies in depth. Motor activity and a brain receptor density changed most often. Shafer flags sodium channel development as the key backdrop. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2005.
europmc-pmc1291354:
Ferwerda and co-authors tested two immune sensor systems against tuberculosis bacteria in 2005. Sensing the bacteria starts both rapid and learned immune responses. Toll-like receptors were the known sensors. A second sensor, NOD2, was their focus.

Cells with either receptor type responded to the bacteria. Mice lacking one receptor made over 50 percent fewer signaling molecules. Cells from people with a NOD2 mutation showed an 80 percent defective response. Both systems proved necessary, not backups for each other. Ferwerda establishes NOD2 as a core tuberculosis sensor. People with the NOD2 mutation showed the clearest defect.
europmc-pmc1395354:
Drummond, Ho, Phillips, and Rambaut introduced relaxed methods for dating family trees in 2006. Strict molecular clocks assume steady evolution rates. Unrooted models assume nothing about rates at all. Both extremes are biologically unrealistic, the authors argue.

Relaxed clocks let rates vary across branches in measured ways. The method estimates trees and divergence times under rate uncertainty. It also measures how clocklike a dataset actually is. Three large datasets showed no significant rate self-link in rates among branches. That undercuts models assuming rates are inherited smoothly. Datasets were placed on a clock fit scale for comparison. Yeast and bacteria sets were both in the test.
europmc-pmc1533854:
Scholars track citations to find landmark papers and gauge their own reach. Bakkalbasi and co-authors compared three citation tools in 2006: the long-standing Web of Science, plus newcomers Scopus and Google Scholar. They sampled articles from cancer and physics journals, from 1993 and 2003.

Counts differed by tool, field, and year. Web of Science led for 1993 cancer papers, at 45.3 citations on average. Scopus led for 2003 cancer papers, at 8.9. Web of Science led both physics years. Bakkalbasi shows that coverage gaps make counts depend on the tool chosen, so no single source tells the whole story.
europmc-pmc1550954:
Most surgical deaths in the UK strike a small high-risk group. Pearse and co-authors measured that group in 2006, using records from 94 hospitals over five years. They classed procedures with death rates of five percent or more as high risk.

Of 4.1 million operations, the high-risk group held just 12.5 percent of cases. Yet it accounted for 84 percent of all deaths, with a death rate of 12.3 percent. These patients stayed a median of 16 days in hospital. Pearse argues that spotting and resourcing this small group could save the most lives.
europmc-pmc1564154:
Comparing microbe communities across many sites needs tools that respect ancestry. Lozupone, Hamady, and Knight launched UniFrac in 2006, a free web tool for that task. It uses the family tree of microbes to judge how alike two communities are.

UniFrac can cluster many environments at once and test which ones truly differ. Applied to river, estuary, and ocean samples, it revealed patterns the first analysis had missed. Lozupone expects tree-based comparison to redraw the picture of microbe life in both nature and medicine. The tool needs only a web browser.
europmc-pmc1570054:
Extreme heat and cold kill, but not everyone faces equal risk. Medina-Ramón and co-authors scanned 7.8 million deaths in 50 US cities from 1989 to 2000. They flagged days beyond the 99th percentile of heat or the coldest one percent.

Older people, diabetics, black residents, and those dying outside hospitals were more prone to heat deaths. Cardiac arrest deaths spiked most on extreme cold days, rising about 14 percent in relative terms. Heart disease deaths in general rose more in cold than in heat. Medina-Ramón argues protection programs should target the groups and causes most at risk.
europmc-pmc1638054:
Arsenic in well water poisons millions in South Asia. Chowdhury and co-authors mapped the crisis in 2000 across Bangladesh and West Bengal, India. Forty-two districts in Bangladesh and nine in West Bengal held groundwater above the world limit of 50 micrograms per liter.

The team analyzed over 69,000 water samples. In Bangladesh, 59 percent topped the limit; in West Bengal, 34 percent. Hair, nail, and urine tests showed most sampled people carried arsenic above safe levels. About a quarter of examined Bangladeshis had arsenic skin lesions. After a decade of study, Chowdhury warns the seen harm is only the tip of the iceberg.
europmc-pmc1713254:
Transfer RNAs, the adapters that build proteins, are not spread evenly across the body. Dittmar, Goodenbour, and Pan measured them in 2006 with a new microarray holding 63 probes for nuclear and mitochondrial tRNAs. Levels varied widely among eight human tissues.

Brain expressed more nuclear tRNAs than all but one tissue, and more mitochondrial tRNAs than any other. Individual tRNA species showed tissue-specific patterns. tRNAs serving chemically similar amino acids rose and fell together. In some tissues, tRNA supply matched the codon usage of highly expressed local genes. Dittmar argues tRNA variety helps tune protein production by tissue.
europmc-pmc1885954: Analysis of nucleolar protein dynamics reveals the nuclear degradation of ribosomal proteins. — a 2005 science paper on nucleolar protein decay. It reveals the nuclear degradation. The paper is the decay study: the findings on ribosomal ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1914054: Comparison of miRNA expression patterns using total RNA extracted from matched samples of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) cells and snap frozen cells. — a 2005 science paper on miRNA from fixed cells. It compares the miRNA patterns. The paper is the miRNA study: the findings on FFPE cells, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2000354: miRNA profiling of naïve, effector and memory CD8 T cells. — a 2005 science paper on miRNA in CD8 T cells. It profiles the naïve cells. The paper is the CD8 study: the findings on miRNA, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2271054: Stimulation of chitin synthesis rescues Candida albicans from echinocandins. — a 2005 science paper on chitin-saving Candida. It finds the chitin rescue. The paper is the rescue study: the findings on Candida, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2346554: The impact of recombination on nucleotide substitutions in the human genome. — a 2008 science paper on recombination and substitutions. It measures the recombination impact. The paper is the impact study: the findings on genome ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2363254: P53 germline mutations in childhood cancers and cancer risk for carrier individuals. — a 2008 science paper on p53 germline mutations. It studies the childhood mutations. The paper is the mutation study: the findings on cancer, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2427054: Multisensory interplay reveals crossmodal influences on 'sensory-specific' brain regions, neura — a 2008 science paper on sense-mixing in the brain. It shows the sense-mixing for labs. The paper is the sense-mix study: the notes on brain ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2515854: LOSITAN: a workbench to detect molecular adaptation based on a Fst-outlier method. — a 2008 science paper on the LOSITAN tool. It detects the molecular adaptation. The paper is the LOSITAN guide: the findings on the tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2582454: c-Myc is required for maintenance of glioma cancer stem cells. — a 2008 science paper on c-Myc in glioma stem cells. It proves the c-Myc requirement. The paper is the c-Myc study: the findings on glioma ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2631154: Using sequence similarity networks for visualization of relationships across diverse protein su — a 2008 science paper on sequence similarity networks. It visualizes the protein relationships. The paper is the network study: the findings on protein ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2653554: Stepwise development of MAIT cells in mouse and human. — a 2008 science paper on MAIT-cell development. It tracks the stepwise development. The paper is the development study: the findings on MAIT ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2675854: Analysis of gene expression data using BRB-ArrayTools. — a 2008 science paper on BRB-ArrayTools. It analyzes the gene expression. The paper is the BRB guide: the findings on gene ills, filed here in full session today twice over now daily.
europmc-pmc2685454: Turning meiosis into mitosis. — a 2008 science paper on turning meiosis into mitosis. It turns the meiosis into mitosis. The paper is the turning study: the findings on meiosis ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
rondelet-de-piscibus-marinis-1554:
Guillaume Rondelet, a French doctor and teacher at Montpellier, published his Books on Marine Fishes in 1554. The Latin work is a founding text of ichthyology, the science of fishes. Rondelet drew and described Mediterranean species from his own dissections and harbor-side study.

Real fishes fill most of his pages, carefully distinguished kind by kind. Yet the sea-monk and other marine monsters stand among them, reported in good faith. Science and marvel share his learned page without quarrel. Rondelet taught a generation of naturalists, Gesner among them. His fish book marks the moment when close looking began to sort the sea's true tenants from its legends.
plos-pone-0004954:
In type 2 diabetes, pancreatic beta cells fail and die. These cells make the body's insulin. Fatty acids are part of what harms them. Glucose makes that fat-driven harm worse, for unknown reasons. Etti Bachar and co-authors investigated the pairing in PLOS ONE in 2009.

They used the fatty acid palmitate on beta cells. Glucose amplified the stress it caused in the endoplasmic reticulum. That structure is the cell's protein-folding workshop. The effect ran through a signaling complex called mTORC1. The chain links high sugar, fat and a named pathway. It gives diabetes research a clearer target for protecting beta cells.
plos-pone-0005054:
Myelodysplastic syndromes are bone-marrow disorders. They can turn into leukemia. Telling low-grade from high-grade cases shapes treatment. Xiaorong Yang and colleagues built a tool for that task in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used SNP arrays, which read DNA variation across the genome. Copy number aberrations were their signal.

A new algorithm, called CMA, finds the aberration patterns. Pattern selection then boosts power and discrimination. The method separates low-grade from high-grade syndromes. Genetic fingerprints become a diagnostic aid. The tool sharpens care for marrow disorders. It is a step toward precision medicine. Better grading means patients get treatment matched to their risk.
plos-pone-0005154:
Chickpeas tolerate drought better than many crops. A protein called CaZF helps them. Deepti Jain, Nilanjan Roy and Debasis Chattopadhyay studied it in yeast. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. CaZF comes from a drought-tolerant chickpea variety. It also gives salt tolerance to tobacco plants. Salt-sensitive yeast mutants were their test bed.

CaZF rescued the yeast through two known stress pathways. It also worked parallel to them, on its own route. The pathways are the HOG pathway and the calcineurin pathway. A plant switch plugs into yeast machinery and adds its own. The finding reveals a portable stress-tolerance tool. Moving such genes could harden crops against salt and drought.
plos-pone-0005254:
Malaria vaccines are urgently needed, and one candidate is built on a parasite surface protein called AMA-1. Spring and colleagues ran an early-phase trial of that vaccine, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Volunteers got the protein mixed with one of two booster systems.

The trial checked safety, the strength of the immune response, and signs of protection. Comparing the AS01B and AS02A boosters head to head shows which partner works better with AMA-1. Early trials like this one decide which vaccine recipes deserve large field tests. Malaria kills most in young children, so each step that moves a safe vaccine dose closer to field trials in Africa counts for a great deal.
plos-pone-0005354:
Wnt5a is a signaling protein best known for guiding development before birth. Its pattern in adult human skin had not been fully studied. Romanowska and colleagues mapped that pattern in PLOS ONE in 2009, along with two of its receptors.

Wnt5a showed layer-specific expression in adult skin, sitting in set layers rather than throughout. It was also upregulated in psoriasis, the scaly autoimmune skin disease, and it synergized with type 1 interferon. A development signal returning in diseased skin is a clue to what drives psoriasis. Psoriasis is not just a skin rash. it links to joint pain and heart risk, so a skin signal that teams up with an immune signal may flag the cases most in need of strong care.
plos-pone-0005954:
Food can act almost like a drug when the dose is right. Ismayil Ahmet, Edward Spangler, Barbara Shukitt-Hale and colleagues tested blueberries in a 2009 PLOS ONE study with rats. They asked whether a diet rich in blueberries could guard the heart when blood flow is cut and then restored, an injury called ischemic damage.

Harmful oxygen byproducts play a big part in that injury, and simple lab-made antioxidants have given mixed results at best. A whole food offers a broader mix of guards. The title states the outcome: the berry-fed rats' hearts were protected. The work supports the idea that diet can brace the heart before injury strikes.
plos-pone-0006054:
Losing one copy of a gene can matter as much as losing both. Isabel Rubio-Aliaga, Gerhard Przemeck, Helmut Fuchs and colleagues proved that for the gene Dll1 in adult mice in 2009. Dll1 belongs to the Notch pathway, an ancient signaling route that patterns embryos and renews tissues. Their PLOS ONE paper maps the full set of effects in grown animals.

The half-dose mice showed a complex mix of changes across metabolism and immunity. A single missing copy thus ripples far beyond the embryo where Notch first acts. The catalog of effects helps predict what milder Notch flaws might do in people, and it warns that adult health can rest on gene doses set before birth.
plos-pone-0006154:
The Parkinson's drug L-dopa fills in for missing dopamine, but its help may stop at movement. Thomas Jubault, Laura Monetta, Antonio Strafella and colleagues tested that boundary with brain scans in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses fMRI during a set-shifting task, after overnight withdrawal, to see which brain networks L-dopa restores in Parkinson's disease.

L-dopa restored activity in the motor cortico-striatal loop but did not modify the cognitive network, the title reports. A drug that fixes motion and leaves thought loops untouched matches what patients describe. The split guides honest counseling and pushes the search for separate treatments for Parkinson's thinking troubles.
plos-pone-0006254:
Known protein shapes lag far behind known protein sequences, by more than two hundred to one. Michael Lee and colleagues built PSPP, a structure prediction pipeline for computer clusters, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Predicted shapes fill part of that gap and guide drug and vaccine design.

The pipeline spreads prediction work across clustered machines to gain speed. Faster shape prediction means more proteins can be modelled for study. Each model is a hypothesis about how a protein works. The tool helps labs with modest resources attempt predictions that once needed specialist centres.
plos-pone-0006654:
George Hinkal, Neha Parikh, and Lawrence Donehower timed tumor suppressor loss in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inactivating mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene occur often in progression of human cancers. The p53 protein inhibits outgrowth of nascent cancer cells through anti-proliferative mechanisms. The team used timed somatic deletion of p53 in mice.

Their title reports the timing reveals age-associated differences in tumor progression. Losing p53 young versus old does not give the same cancers. Age context shapes what a mutation does. That insight matters for interpreting cancer risk across the lifespan.
plos-pone-0006754:
Lora L. Shadwick and colleagues rebuilt the family tree of certain slime molds in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protosteloid slime molds make tiny fruiting bodies of stalk and spores. They were classically grouped with other slime molds as Eumycetozoa. The larger supergroup in question is Amoebozoa. Whether the classical grouping holds was unsettled.

The team sequenced a ribosomal RNA gene across many species. That gene, called SSU rDNA, is a standard family-tree marker. Their phylogeny tested whether Eumycetozoa equals one true branch. The answer reshapes how slime mold groups are named and related. Clear trees help every later study of how these organisms evolved.
plos-pone-0006854:
Karen L. Wozniak and her team probed how mice beat a grave fungus in PLOS ONE in 2009. The fungus is Cryptococcus neoformans. It strikes men and women whose immune shield is weak. It can cause dire lung illness and brain illness. Past work gave mice a tame strain of the fungus. That strain made interferon gamma, and the mice were safe when the wild fungus came.

In that lung model, the team asked what does the guarding. Which parts of the immune force truly keep mice safe? The reply could guide vaccine design for the frail. Those with weak shields need guarding most, yet vaccines work worst in them. The mouse work shows what a win looks like.
plos-pone-0006954:
Andrew Haddow, Carl Jones, and Agricola Odoi examined disease risk reporting in PLOS ONE in 2009. Focal arboviral infections strike only a subset of a population. These mosquito and tick borne infections pose overlooked problems for risk assessment. Reported risk can shift a lot with the group chosen as the population at risk.

The authors measured how much risk estimates vary under different choices. They also looked at how those choices affect the search for spatial patterns. Their point is practical. A risk figure can mislead if the at-risk population is drawn carelessly, and control programs may aim at the wrong places.
plos-pone-0007054:
Christopher Hale, Sean Sun, and Denis Wirtz settled a cell mechanics question in PLOS ONE in 2009. Einstein first linked random thermal forces to how small particles move in fluid. Later work on actin networks hinted that living cells add non-thermal forces. The role of actomyosin, the cell's contractile machinery, was disputed.

The team measured cell stiffness using microrheology, tracking tiny probes inside cells. They resolved how much actomyosin contraction drives the readings. The answer matters for reading cell health from mechanical tests. Tumor and stem cells are often judged partly by how soft or stiff they feel.
plos-pone-0007154:
Alexandra-Chloé Villani, Mathieu Lemire, Edouard Louis, and colleagues tested a fever gene in bowel disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The MEFV gene causes familial Mediterranean fever when faulty. It builds pyrin, a regulator of the inflammasome, the platform that activates inflammatory signals. Pyrin interacts with the product of another inflammation gene, NLRP3.

The team asked whether MEFV variants change risk of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Both are chronic inflammatory bowel diseases. Shared inflammatory machinery makes the question sensible. A confirmed link would tie periodic fever biology to common bowel disease in a useful way.
plos-pone-0007254:
Anna M. Mileo, Claudia Abbruzzese, Stefano Mattarocci, and colleagues studied a cancer virus protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human papillomavirus type 16 is a classic high-risk virus. Such viruses cause nearly all cervical cancers, and their E6 and E7 genes are usually active in those tumors.

The authors examine the E7 oncoprotein and its partner GST P1, a detoxifying enzyme. They report that E7 interacts with GST P1 and enhances its role in cell survival. That interaction may help infected cells live longer, giving the virus time to push them toward cancer.
plos-pone-0007354:
Nga T. Lao, Alan P. Maloney, John F. Atkins, and colleagues built reporter systems to study a translation quirk in plants in 2009. Translation usually stops at the first stop codon in a message. Many viruses, and some cell messages, contain stop codons that some ribosomes read through instead, adding another amino acid.

That readthrough can produce extended proteins with new functions. The authors present versatile dual reporter gene systems for plants. The systems measure how often readthrough occurs. Their PLOS ONE tools help researchers study a process viruses exploit and cells sometimes use deliberately.
