arxiv-2606-16554: A pure mathematics paper on discrete Laplacians — the graph version of the operator governing heat flow and vibrations — in the m-sectorial setting, with complex-valued weights. The author connects these operators to recurrence: whether random walks on such graphs keep returning. It targets specialists in spectral graph theory.
19949-autographs-for-freedom-volume-2-of:
Autographs for Freedom was an abolitionist gift book sold to fund the cause. Volume two of two is dated 1854. Its editor praises the contributors' ripe judgment and earnest purpose. Their generous sympathies win her warm thanks here. She hopes to meet many of them in future numbers. Julia Griffiths edited the volumes in Rochester, New York. Frederick Douglass's circle stood behind the enterprise.

Gift books gathered famous names between pretty covers. Here the names wrote against slavery itself. Essays, poems, and letters fill the autograph pages. Sales supported Douglass's newspaper and antislavery work. The volume is a who's who of the movement in 1854. Its literary quality served a fundraising purpose.
arxiv-2601-06854:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Luigi Romano and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers semilinear single-track vehicle models with distributed tyre friction dynamics. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The work introduces a new family of single-track vehicle models that incorporate a distributed representation of transient tyre dynamics. Whilst simultaneously accounting for nonlinear effects induced by friction.

The core of the proposed framework is represented by the distributed Friction with Bristle Dynamics (FrBD) model. Which unifies and extends classical formulations such as Dahl and LuGre by describing. The rolling contact process as a spatially distributed system governed by semilinear partial differential equations (PDEs). Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-06954:
Research by Holger Boche and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with arithmetic complexity of solutions of the dirichlet problem. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The classical Dirichlet problem on the unit disk can be solved by different numerical approaches. The two most common and popular approaches are the integration of the associated Poisson integral and, by applying Dirichlet’s principle.

Solving a particular minimization problem. For practical use, these procedures need to be implemented on concrete computing platforms. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-08154: M. Anzorena and a large team report a Forbush decrease seen on May 10, 2024. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses the ALPAQUITA air-shower array to record the event. A Forbush decrease is a sharp drop in cosmic rays after solar activity disturbs Earth's space environment. The array covers a wide rigidity range, from 70 to 1000 gigavolts. Observations across that range show how the drop varies with particle energy. Such records help space weather researchers link solar events to effects measured on the ground.
arxiv-2601-08654: Yihan Hong and co-authors present Rulers, a framework for robust language model evaluation with locked rubrics. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation promises scalable rubric-based grading. Aligning frozen, black-box judges with human standards stays hard due to generation randomness. The authors reframe judge alignment as a criteria transfer problem. They isolate three failure modes: rubric instability from prompt sensitivity, unverifiable reasoning, and scale misalignment with human grading. Evidence-anchored scoring aims to fix all three for more trustworthy automatic grades.
arxiv-2601-06754:
Dixi Yang and six co-authors find how swimming germs stick fast to a wall in a 2026 paper. Swarms of germs stick in a flash from thin, weak broths of them. Flows push germs to hug walls but can not hold them there in a stable way.

Charge forces at walls push germs off more than they pull them in. Yet the germs stick fast, which those forces can not explain on their own. The team joins lab tests with large runs on a fast machine. Two germs are used in the tests: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Both sit in a two-part mix of water-based gels for the lab work. They find that wet-linked phase split acts as a trap based on energy. The split of the mix at the wall traps the germs there, they report.
arxiv-2601-07454:
Yuxuan Hu and colleagues introduce WaveMan, a sensing system for humanoid robots, in this 2026 preprint. Their goal is room-scale human interaction perception inside homes. Two demands shape the work: robots must cope with users standing anywhere, and they must respect user privacy. Cameras can fail the second demand, so the team turns to radio sensing instead.

WaveMan uses millimeter-wave signals, which can sense people without recording images. Earlier mmWave systems, the authors note, generalize poorly to new distances or viewpoints. A system trained in one spot may misread a person in another. WaveMan is built to handle that spatial variation across a whole room. The paper matters for home robotics, where privacy and reliability must come together.
arxiv-2601-07954:
Haoan Jin and colleagues align language models with Chinese medical ethics using human-centered methods. Language models now serve many healthcare tasks. Aligning them with medical ethics, especially in complex real cases, remains underexplored. Their 2026 preprint presents MedES, a dynamic, scenario-centric benchmark. It is built from 260 authoritative Chinese medical, ethical, and legal sources. The scenarios reflect challenges in clinical decision-making.

Ethics in medicine involves consent, confidentiality, and duties that vary by situation. A benchmark drawn from real authoritative sources tests those nuances better than generic questions. Chinese sources matter because norms and law differ across countries. Human-centric construction keeps clinicians and ethicists in the loop. The paper serves medical AI scholars and health policy readers. It argues alignment must be tested where care actually happens.
arxiv-2601-07854:
Jing Wang and coauthors look for immune patterns that point to recovery from Long COVID. The after effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection can last for months. What drives full relief of symptoms is still not well defined. The team studied 97,564 checks over time from 13,511 people in the study. Vaccine records were linked to those checks. Their 2026 preprint splits mere passage of time from change tied to vaccines.

Recovery trajectories vary widely between patients. A density measure of immune traits may show why some get well faster. Large longitudinal data let the authors watch trajectories rather than single snapshots. To split plain gains with time from vaccine linked gains matters when staff advise patients. The study speaks to clinicians and scholars managing Long COVID care. It searches for measurable signs that recovery is on track. The scale is large, and that scale is what lets faint trends show up at all.
arxiv-2601-09554:
Rayan Chouity, Charbel Hannoun, Jihad Fahs, and Ibrahim Abou-Faycal ask when the best estimate of a stable random variable is a simple linear one. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies jointly stable random variables under two dependence models. Stable laws are the heavy-tailed distributions that arise from generalized limit theorems.

One model takes a linear mix of two independent stable variables; the other is a sub-Gaussian symmetric stable vector. In both cases, the authors show the conditional mean estimator is linear. They also find the linear estimators that minimize dispersion. Simple optimal rules matter in signal processing, where stable noise models fit real interference.
arxiv-2601-09854:
Ben Lang explores puzzles that arise when a multi-level atom talks to light in a waveguide. His 2026 arXiv paper studies the optical dipole interaction between a multi-level quantum system and a single-mode waveguide of any local polarization. Several of the findings look paradoxical at first sight.

One case gives two non-orthogonal quantum states. Each sends photon flux in the opposite direction from the other. The paper works through such cases and resolves them. Waveguides are the wiring of photonic quantum devices, so exact results matter. Resolved paradoxes sharpen the theory that device designers rely on.
arxiv-2601-09954:
Nahid Alam and a large team name a blind spot in vision and language models. These models pair a photo with text. They have grown fast in skill. But they still fail at where things sit in a scene. Left, right, near, and far trip them up.

The team blames how the models are built. Most use an image coder trained to match text to a whole photo. The photo is cut into tiles and laid flat in a line. That flat line drops the two way shape of the scene. The paper tests this flaw and maps where it bites most.
arxiv-2601-10054:
Nick Truong, Pritam Karmokar, and William Beksi built a test set for motion seen from under water. Under water shots are hard to read. Light fades by hue, dust clouds the view, and light is dim in patches. True motion is near out of reach to mark by hand.

Event based cams offer a way past these ills. They mark change with fine time steps and a wide light range. The set is named UEOF. It gives marked motion data for such cams under water. Labs can use it to test and train their tools on the same base.
arxiv-2601-10254:
Irina Abdullaeva and co authors test if AI has a raw feel for shape. Most shape tests let a model work it out by steps. That tests algebra more than sight. A model may pass yet lack a true sense of space. The team made a new test set named NoReGeo.

The set asks for direct shape calls. Can a model tell if lines cross, if a point sits in a shape, or if forms match? No step work should be needed. The set thus tests if shape sense is built in. It gives a clean check that past sets did not.
arxiv-2601-10654:
A short note in operator algebra takes up the Connes embedding problem, a long-running question about von Neumann algebras. The note shows that a certain completely bounded map exists. The map runs from a C*-algebra with the lifting property into a QWEP von Neumann algebra. The key point is what the map cannot be.

The map is not strongly similar to a *-homomorphism, the nicest kind of map between such algebras. That gap between bounded maps and star-shaped maps carries the result. Notes of this kind sort out which algebra maps can be cleaned up and which cannot.
arxiv-2601-10954:
Nikko John Leo S. Lobos solves the Dunkl-Schrödinger equation exactly for the Deng-Fan potential. The Deng-Fan potential models how atoms bind in a molecule. The Dunkl version of the equation adds reflection terms that appear in some quantum models. Exact solutions are rare and prized, since they anchor numeric methods.

Lobos uses the Pekeris approximation to handle the centrifugal singularity, the blow-up at the center. He then applies the parametric Nikiforov-Uvarov method. The result is closed-form expressions for the energy spectrum and the radial wavefunctions, written with Jacobi polynomials. Spectroscopists and theorists gain formulas they can evaluate directly for this molecular model.
arxiv-2601-11054:
Zhejian Zhang and co-authors search for galaxy cluster-scale strong lenses in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. Strong lensing by a whole cluster bends light from distant galaxies into arcs. Such systems are rare. They are prized tools for probing dark matter and dark energy, and they magnify the distant universe beyond normal reach.

Large imaging surveys now offer the raw material to expand the lens sample. The authors mine the DESI Legacy data for cluster-scale candidates. Each new lens is a natural telescope and a weighing scale for dark matter at once. A bigger sample sharpens both uses. The work feeds follow-up campaigns that turn candidates into confirmed, modeled systems.
arxiv-2601-11754:
Andrew Mummery studies gas disks that swirl into black holes while also blowing gas out. He works with the thin disk rules in Newtonian gravity. The maths track how the disk mass spreads and drains with time.

He finds Green's function forms for the case with outflows. In set limits, the forms are plain and exact. They look much like the classic forms with no outflows, due to Lynden-Bell and Pringle. Yet the fine points and what a scope would see are quite unlike. The forms help link disk maths to real light from such systems.
arxiv-2601-11854:
Yifei Zhang, Hooshang Nayyeri, Rinat Khaziev, and their co-authors build a test bed for chat agents that do tasks. New agents use large models plus many tools and APIs. They can hold long talks, juggle mixed goals, and act ahead of time on their own.

Old test sets do not check these new skills in a set way. Their frame, called ATOD in the work, fills that gap. It tests how agents plan, track context, and use tools over a long task. Such tests help buyers pick agents with proof, not claims.
arxiv-2601-12254:
Kazuki Yamauchi, Masato Murata, and Shogo Seki filter speech data cleaned by generative tools, using confidence scores. Generative speech enhancement can make clean speech from noisy clips. That could turn noisy text-to-speech sets into high-grade ones.

But such tools can hallucinate, dropping sounds or changing the speaker. Old quality gauges often miss those flaws. Their confidence-based filter aims to catch them. Clean sets with fewer hidden flaws train better speech tools.  The filter aims to keep clean clips pure at scale.  Such reviews help new teams skip paths that failed in the past.
arxiv-2601-11354:
Weiyi Wang, Xinchi Chen, Jingjing Gong, Xuanjing Huang, and Xipeng Qiu build a space benchmark. Their 2026 preprint is named AstroReason-Bench, on agentic planning. Space missions pose planning tasks of many unlike kinds. Past tools solved each kind with its own algorithm.

The bench tests one unified agent across that spread. A central agent picks tools from a kit to plan each task. That shift, from split tools to one agent, is the core move. Fudan University and the OpenMOSS team back the work. The bench can show where a general agent still fails. It can also show where one agent now beats narrow tools.
arxiv-2601-11454:
Yashpal Singh, Juan Peralta, and Koblar Jackson trace errors in reaction barriers. Their 2026 preprint extends work on self-interaction corrections. Density functional theory is the workhorse of computational chemistry. Its barrier heights for reactions can err in known ways.

Adding Perdew-Zunger self-interaction corrections improves those heights much. The team gives a detailed orbital-by-orbital account of the fix. They test three semi-local functional approximations in the study. Those sit on the three lowest rungs of Jacob's Ladder. That ladder ranks functionals by the data they use. The title notes stretched bond errors that rise and fall. Orbital views show which states drive the correction's gains.
arxiv-2601-11554:
Triloki Nath, Manohar Choudhary, and Ram Pandey solve a generalized waist problem. Their 2026 preprint gives an optimality condition and an algorithm. The root puzzle came from John Tyrell at King's College London. He challenged his PhD students with it years ago.

The puzzle posits three given lines in space. They are pairwise disjoint and not all parallel. A triangle must place exactly one vertex on one line. Each vertex sits on a distinct one of the lines. The claim is that a unique least-perimeter triangle exists. The generalized waist form widens that classic setup. Conditions tell when a candidate triangle is optimal. An algorithm then computes the winner in practice.
arxiv-2601-11654:
Kaustubh Shejole and Gaurav Mishra speed up interactive image segmentation. Their 2026 preprint gives an index named PSSI-MaxST. Graph-based methods split an image into foreground and background. User inputs guide where that split should fall.

Existing methods often carry high computational costs in use. They can also react too sharply to user inputs. When foreground and background share like colors, quality drops. The team's index scores pixel-segment similarity for the task. Intensity and smoothness features feed that similarity score. A maximum spanning tree then drives the segmentation. A faster index could make interactive editing feel instant.
arxiv-2601-13154:
Krystof Chrappova, Jeremiah P. Tidey, Christopher Bell, and Simon R. Hall solve the crystal plan of a wet rubidium ruthenium oxide. They also probe its magnetism. The oxide holds water in its plan, which makes it a rich case for study.

They read the plan from three dim electron diffraction, taken from lone grains of a powder made in the lab. The plan sits in a named symmetry class, with cell edges they report. Such care with tiny grains shows how far electron tools can go when X-ray routes fail. For chemists, the plan is the base for all talk of how this oxide acts.
arxiv-2601-13454:
Qingyang Zhang grows distance correlation to data in named groups, for use in big feature hunts. Distance correlation is a score for how two sets of marks lean on each other, in any form. In its stock form it needs number marks. Group marks, such as kind tags, need a code first.

Zhang lets the code be broad. One hot codes fit plain kinds. A semicircle code fits ranked kinds. The code keeps the span facts among kinds, which past tools threw out. That keep lifts the score's skill. In high dim hunts, the score can screen which traits matter for an out come. Such a screen cuts junk traits early.
arxiv-2601-13554:
Kazuki Yokomizo, Aashish A. Clerk, and Yuto Ashida set the base caps of continuous Gaussian quantum metrology. Metrology is the science of fine marks. In continuous form, a sensor reads a stream of light that a system sheds to its world. That stream can carry facts bit by bit as it leaves.

For bosonic systems, those with light like bits, no full account of the best mark grade was known. The team gives that account. Their caps state how fine a mark can be at best, what eva the tool. Such caps tell sensor teams when to stop tune and when a new form is need to gain more.
arxiv-2601-12554:
Iman Peivaste and a large team review how artificial intelligence is reshaping materials science and engineering. AI tools now help researchers handle complexity, speed up discovery, and design better materials. Faster algorithms and growing stores of data drive this shift. The team say AI skill is fast becoming essential for materials researchers.

Their review maps the current landscape of the field first. It then names the key challenges that still block wider use. Data quality, trust in models, and links with physics all loom large in such reviews. Last, they chart future paths for the field. A survey of this breadth serves newcomers and veterans alike. It shows where AI already pays off and where care is still needed.
arxiv-2601-13654:
Shashank Kumar Ojha, Jyotirmay Maity, and Srimanta Middey study how electrons meet domain walls in strontium titanate in 2026. That crystal is a famed test bed for solid-state physics, studied for over seventy-five years. Its traits link structure, charge flow, and response to electric fields in rich ways. Domain walls are thin borders where the crystal's inner pattern shifts.

The team asks what happens when electrons cross or gather at these walls. Walls can act as paths or traps for charge in oxide devices. That makes them of worth for new kinds of electronics. The work adds to the long study of a crystal that keeps teaching new lessons.
arxiv-2601-13854:
Leyang Xue and co-authors explain how abrupt phase transitions can start and grow in 2026. A phase transition is a sudden shift of a system to a new state. Abrupt ones jump, rather than glide, between states. The micro steps that drive such jumps are not fully understood.

The team sets out a theory based on internal node dependencies in a lattice. Branching-driven nucleation is their name for the growth process. Small seeds branch outward through dependent nodes, tipping the whole system. The frame could apply to magnets, networks, and social cascades alike.
arxiv-2601-13954:
Adrien Meyer, Didier Mutter, and Nicolas Padoy cut the labeling cost for finding landmarks in medical images in 2026. Object detection models need costly bounding box annotations to learn. That cost limits how far such models can scale in medicine. Weakly semi-supervised detection uses a single point per instance instead of a box.

Point annotations take far less time yet keep a localization signal. Their system, DExTeR, uses class and instance experts for this weak setup. Detecting anatomical landmarks aids diagnosis and guides interventions. Cheaper training could bring these tools to more hospitals.
arxiv-2601-14254:
James G. Rogers, James E. Owen, Ethan Schreyer, and James Kirk study small planets in this 2026 paper. Their targets are sub-Neptunes, worlds between Earth and Neptune in size. What these planets are made of inside is still an open question in exoplanet science. The team looks at gas leaking away from them.

Their method uses sightings of hydrogen or helium escaping from a planet's outer layers. From those rates, they set bounds on the mean molecular weight of the planet's envelope. The logic is a simple timescale argument. A planet needs a big enough store of light gas to keep losing it at the rate seen today.
arxiv-2601-14354:
Yongchao Huang reworks a learning design in this 2026 paper. The design is the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, or JEPA. It learns by predicting latent representations, inner codes of data, rather than rebuilding raw inputs. That makes it a scalable path for self-supervised learning. It also sidesteps high-entropy observations, inputs packed with hard-to-predict detail.

Past JEPA versions use deterministic regression objectives, fixed targets with no room for chance. Huang argues that this hides probabilistic meaning and limits use in stochastic control, where outcomes vary. His version, VJEPA, is variational. The title calls such models probabilistic world models, built to carry uncertainty about what comes next.
arxiv-2601-14554:
Zhiyuan Guo, C. W. Walter, Eli S. Rykoff, and the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration present a galaxy selection method in this 2026 paper. Luminous Red Galaxies are prized tracers for cosmology surveys. The team introduces IRMaGiC, an algorithm built on RedMaGiC. It is designed to enhance the selection of such galaxies across the redshift range one to two.

That range pushes past where optical selection alone works well. IRMaGiC extends selection into the infrared by joining data from two surveys. They are LSST and the Roman High Latitude Imaging Survey. Readers get a method to pick a clean, uniform galaxy sample at distances where the old tool thinned out.
arxiv-2601-14754:
Guolin Nan, Zhijian Li, Feng Mei, and Zhihao Xu study localization in a non-Hermitian quasicrystal in this 2026 paper. The system is a one-dimensional generalized Aubry-André-Harper chain. It has asymmetric nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. Those hoppings are generated by a Bernoulli imaginary gauge field. A quasiperiodic onsite potential completes the setup.

The team studies anomalous localization in this chain. Localization means states stay trapped in small regions instead of spreading. Mobility edges are the energy borders between trapped and spreading states. Non-Hermitian systems can break the usual rules for both. Readers get a study of where those borders sit when the gauge field itself is disordered.
arxiv-2601-15554:
T. Hanaguri probes two intertwined orders in a layered superconductor in a 2026 arXiv paper. The material is 2H-NbSe2, a well-studied layered compound. Inside it, a charge density wave coexists with superconductivity. How the two affect each other is the paper's question. Hanaguri studies the cleaved surface of the material. The tool is scanning tunneling microscopy at ultralow temperature.

Spectroscopic imaging maps the superconducting gap across that surface. The gap spectrum shows intricate structures, he reports. Those structures reflect anisotropic gaps that open on multiple Fermi surfaces. Surface charge order can reshape the gap in subtle ways. Mapping that interplay helps physicists model layered superconductors. Such materials are testbeds for how competing orders share one crystal.
arxiv-2601-15654:
Arman and Prasanta K. Panigrahi study states of light with very fine structure in a 2026 arXiv paper. Phase space is the map where a light state's traits are drawn. Some states hold structures smaller than the Planck scale. Those tiny features can boost sensitivity in measurement. The authors use non-Gaussian operations to enlarge such states. Bigger fine structure, in the right form, can mean a stronger metrological edge.

Part of the work tests photon-added cat and kitten states. Adding photons broadens these states in phase space. The authors observe a sensitivity gain from that broadening, at higher energy cost. They also build states with weak squeezing and displacement. These are resources labs can actually reach. The balance of gain against cost is the practical thread.
arxiv-2601-15354:
Peng Chen and Jun Jing find how precise a quantum measurement can be when a helper qubit joins in. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with quantum metrology, the science of measuring with quantum probes. Their probe is a spin ensemble, a crowd of spins acting as one sensor.

The ensemble is coupled to a single ancillary qubit, a two-level helper. The coupling follows a Heisenberg XXZ interaction, a standard form for spin systems. The protocol is measurement-based: the qubit is read to learn about the ensemble. The authors derive the precision limit of that weak-coupling setup.
arxiv-2601-16154:
Sam Slezak and coauthors bound how fast open quantum systems reach rest. Their 2026 preprint deals with Lindblad maths for a system tied to a bath. Weak ties to a bath stand for heat flow and rest in many cases. They also stand for Gibbs draws used in quantum code. The speed to rest sets run times for both acts.

The team shows that speed can stay in a set time bound. That bound is of the poly type, not a fast growth type. Firm time bounds help teams trust Gibbs draw code. They also set true heat time scales for open systems. The work links heat maths to code run times.
arxiv-2601-16454:
Wonjun Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon and Gil Young Cho use join links to glue chance in quantum states. Their 2026 preprint deals with how to make full chance states fast. Such states serve many tasks in quantum work and tests. Local chance steps alone make full chance at high cost. Join links, called entanglement, may be the key stock for the task.

The team shows links let local steps build world chance. They bound the cost with the second Rényi entropy, a link size. Tight bounds tell how much link stock a build must spend. That spend sets the true price of chance states. The work names links as the core stock for chance.
arxiv-2601-16554:
Čekanavičius and Jokubauskienė sum near forms for sums of same spread steps. Their 2026 preprint deals with sums of free steps on a grid. Each step has the same law and a flip fair form. The sum law is near a compound Poisson law in such cases. That near law is the mate law that tracks the sum.

The team adds a next term signed law of Hipp type. Next terms cut the flaw of the first near law much. Bergström type growth gives the flaw size in firm terms. Sharp near laws serve chance sums in risk and queue work. The work is a pure chance maths study.
arxiv-2601-16854:
Irfan Mahmood, Adeena Iqbal, and Sohail Mumtaz study a lone wave in a noisy, damped world. The wave obeys a fifth-order KdV rule. Loss drains the wave as it runs. Chance kicks shake it as well. Their 2026 preprint works out how the wave's push spreads in chance terms.

They find a clear form for that spread, tied to a chance clock. The form then trims down to a famed Painlevé rule. Such trims link big wave rules to small, known ones. That link can aid work on fluids, light, and plasma waves. It shows deep ties among rules once seen as far apart.
arxiv-2601-16954:
Ba-Thinh Lam and a team of eight co-authors sort scans where labels are scarce and sources mix. Scan tools must tag each point in a health image. Tags take costly work by scarce pros. Scans also come from many sites and gear types. Those mixes shift how scans look in hard ways. Their 2026 preprint trains tools that shrug off those shifts.

Their tool learns from part-tagged scans across mixed sources. A cluster-based align step joins the sources' traits. No source tags are known in the mix. Sound tags from mixed sources aid small clinics most. Such tools could spread pro-grade reads more wide.
arxiv-2601-17154:
Shivanshu Tripathi, Hossein Mohsenzadeh Yazdi, Maziar Raissi, and Hamed Mohsenian-Rad model fast grid waves with physics-coded nets. New grid gear, like solar and wind links, acts fast in faults. Old gauges are too slow and coarse to catch those acts. Wave gauges now give fine, synced raw wave marks. Their 2026 preprint learns from those marks with less data.

Physics rules built in the net cut its data needs. The net tracks wave forms through fault spans. True tracks help guards act in time. They also help plan grids with more green gear. Data-lean tools suit grids where marks are dear.
arxiv-2601-17454:
Muhammad Ahmed Atif and three co-authors test a common belief in multi-agent learning. The belief says central value learning improves teamwork and stability. The team tests it in a fully tabular predator-prey gridworld. They compare independent and centralized Q-learning head to head. Embodiment limits shape the test. Agent speed and stamina are set as hard constraints.

Such tight control shows when central learning truly helps. It also shows regimes where bodies, not brains, drive outcomes. They call those regimes embodiment-induced coordination regimes. The lesson is broad for robot teams. Design the body and the learner together. A gridworld proof can steer real multi-robot work.
arxiv-2601-17554:
The CMS Collaboration presents a machine learning upgrade to particle-flow reconstruction. Particle flow builds a full list of particles from each collision at the CMS detector. It is central to how CMS reads events at the CERN LHC. The current code rests on physics-based heuristics. Learned models can replace some of those hand rules. The paper gives a full event interpretation with the new method.

Learned flow could sharpen measures of jets and missing energy. It could also speed event reads at huge data rates. CMS handles some of the largest data flows in science. Gains there ripple to all its physics results. The work tests learning inside a flagship detector.
arxiv-2601-17654:
Ruofan Wu, Jae-Won Chung, and Mosharaf Chowdhury present Kareus for energy use in large model training. AI compute demand grows at an unprecedented rate. Energy supply does not keep pace. Energy is now an expensive, contended resource. Recent work cut training time and cost in many ways. Kareus targets dynamic and static energy jointly.

Joint cuts matter because idle draw is a large share of bills. A scheduler that trims both can save at data center scale. Lower energy per model eases grid strain too. The work comes from the University of Michigan team. It treats energy as a first-class design goal. That stance fits an era of power caps.
arxiv-2601-17854: Yuto Nakajima and Hiroki Takahasi prove a result about Hurwitz continued fractions, a way of expanding complex numbers in steps. Their 2026 preprint looks at numbers whose partial quotients contain scaled copies of any finite grid pattern. The quotients are read as points on an integer grid, and the copies appear again and again. They show that the set of such irrational numbers has Hausdorff dimension one.
arxiv-2601-18954:
J. Sebastian Monzon, Frank C. van den Bosch, and Martin P. Rey predict the faint star halos around galaxies like our own. In the standard picture, these halos grow as small galaxies fall in and get torn apart. The team adds new semi-analytic tools to a framework called SatGen to track those stolen stars.

They run the tools across large sets of merger trees, the family trees of growing galaxies. That spread lets them study how much luck shapes each halo's final form. Two twin galaxies can end with quite unlike halos, and their stats show how wide that spread should be.
arxiv-2601-19254:
J. C. F. Balzan and three co-authors read the fine grain inside fast radio bursts. These bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space whose inner structure may reveal what makes them. Their framework, FIRES, models the burst's dynamic spectrum as a pile of tiny Gaussian shots with polarized light.

They apply it to two bursts caught by the CRAFT survey. The model reproduces key patterns: scattering smooths the angle swings on the trailing edge, while the leading edge keeps more of its inborn structure. Reading the grain this way turns each burst into a probe of its source and its path.
arxiv-2601-19154:
Shun Takagi and Seng Pei Liew sharpen the math of shuffled privacy. In distributed data analysis, each user's data is first scrambled locally, then shuffled among users to hide who sent what. Shuffling boosts privacy a lot, a fact past work proved using only the local privacy level as the knob.

Those old bounds can be loose and can miss how the guarantee behaves as settings change. The pair analyze the shuffle past the pure local case. Tighter bounds mean data curators can promise stronger privacy, or collect finer data under the same promise.
arxiv-2601-19454:
Chayan Majumdar, Utkarsh Patel, Supriya Senapati, and Sudhanwa Patra work on two open puzzles in particle physics. Neutrinos have tiny masses that the Standard Model does not explain. Dark matter, the unseen mass in galaxies, also sits outside that model. The authors study one extension that tries to address both at once.

Their model adds a new symmetry, based on the difference between baryon and lepton number. In this setup, neutrino masses are not put in by hand. They arise through a loop process, where new particles run in a circle and generate the mass indirectly. Such masses are called radiative. The same added particles can also offer a dark matter candidate. The paper maps out how this shared framework could work.
arxiv-2601-19554:
Jérôme Touguet and six colleagues work on shaping intense laser beams. A quasi-Bessel beam keeps its narrow core over a long distance, unlike a normal focused beam. Such beams are made with a device called an axiparabola. They are prized in high-intensity laser work, where a long, even focal line is useful.

In practice the brightness along that line wobbles up and down. Those unwanted oscillations limit what the beams can do. The team traces the physical cause of the distortions. They then build a general strategy to control the brightness along the axis of the beam. A smoother focal line should make these lasers better tools for research and industry. The work joins optical design with hard experimental needs.
arxiv-2601-19654:
Paolo Matteo Simonetti and six colleagues speed up the computer models used to study how planets form. Planet formation is tracked with n-body codes, which follow many objects pulling on each other by gravity. Fully interacting simulations are the next frontier, but they are brutally expensive to run. The team presents Mercury-Opal, a version of a known code rebuilt for graphics processors.

Graphics processors run many simple calculations at once, which suits gravity between many bodies. Moving the code to them should let researchers follow larger systems for longer times. Mercury-Arches, the parent code, is a standard tool in the field. A faster version opens studies that were out of reach. The paper describes the port and what it enables.
arxiv-2601-19754:
Élie Casbi works in representation theory on categorifying cluster algebras of finite type. Cluster algebras are algebraic structures built from patterns of exchange. Categorification lifts them into richer worlds of categories, where numbers become objects. Earlier categorifications used abelian categories; this paper proposes a triangulated monoidal version.

Given a Dynkin quiver, Casbi builds a bounded homotopy category from a symmetric monoidal category defined through Auslander-Reiten theory. That classical theory describes how representations of a quiver fit together. The framework aims to capture finite-type behaviour in this new setting. This new frame could unify several known constructions. The work is a foundational proposal for others to develop. The plan is bold but clear. It builds step by step from a known base. Each step can be checked by hand. That care is the point of the work. The frame is meant for wide use.
arxiv-2601-19954:
Alistair Shilton generalises a classical identity for Hermite polynomials. These polynomials appear across physics and probability, from quantum oscillators to Gaussian analysis. For one variable, the multiplication theorem describes how the polynomial behaves when its argument is scaled. Shilton extends the result to Hermite polynomials in several variables.

A general multiplication theorem for the multivariate case was missing. Such identities let practitioners rescale arguments instead of recomputing from scratch. They also reveal structure shared across dimensions. Multivariate Hermite polynomials underlie modern methods in statistics and signal processing. Completing the basic identity toolkit supports those applications. The paper is a compact contribution to a classical theory. The new rule works in two or more dims. The old one worked in just one. That jump is the whole point here. The old one-var rule is a school room staple. The jump to more vars is not a small step.
arxiv-2601-20254:
Hengrui Luo develops wavelet tree ensembles for regression when data live on a triangulable manifold, a curved surface that can be cut into triangles. The learners are unbalanced Haar wavelet trees. Their atoms sit on geodesic triangles, the shortest-path triangles on the surface, and they form an orthonormal system under the empirical measure of the sample.

Stacking these trees into additive ensembles gives a flexible regression method that respects the geometry of the data. Many real datasets, from brain surfaces to climate fields, live on curved spaces rather than flat ones. Methods built for the surface itself can capture patterns that flat methods distort.
arxiv-2601-20554:
Yaacov Pariente and Vadim Indelman study risk-averse planning for robots that must act under partial observability. Such planning is modeled with POMDPs, where the agent cannot see the full state. The authors use the iterated conditional value-at-risk, a dynamic risk measure that guards against bad outcomes rather than optimizing the average.

They develop a policy evaluation algorithm for this risk measure with finite-time performance guarantees. Those guarantees do not depend on how many actions the agent has. Risk-sensitive planning matters wherever an average-good plan can still end in disaster, from driving to medical dosing.
arxiv-2601-20654:
Qian Gao and Ruikang Zhong use reinforcement learning to optimize beamforming for three-dimensional pinching antenna systems that both sense and communicate. They propose a three-dimensional deployment scheme for the pinching antenna array, aiming to improve integrated sensing and communication performance. Realizing that potential takes joint design.

Antenna positions, time allocation, and transmit power must be optimized together, to maximize the total communication rate under target sensing rates and an energy budget. Pinching antennas, which can be placed along a waveguide where needed, offer a flexible new hardware base for such joint designs.
arxiv-2601-18454:
Gabriel Barrenechea, Cristian Cárcamo, and Abner Poza build a math tool to grade a kind of heart and blood scan. The scan tracks flow in time as well as in space, so staff can watch blood move through the heart. A good grade needs a check: how far is the flow in the scan from a flow that obeys the laws of fluids?

The team split the flow in the scan into the part they take as truth and a gap part. They then solve for the gap with a firm form of the flow laws, built to stay calm in hard cases. Tests of the tool show how the grade shifts with scan flaws. A firm grade could help staff trust a scan or ask for a new one. It could also guide firms that build the scan kit.
arxiv-2601-18554:
Alberto Purpura and four colleagues built a new test for how well language models obey asks. A model may do a task well yet miss a set rule in the ask. Past tests blur those two things: a fail could mean weak skill or weak rule care. The team want a test that grades rule care on its own.

Their test, named MOSAIC, builds fresh tasks on the fly with up to a score of set rules in each ask. Rules can cover length, form, tone, and what must or must not show up. Each rule is graded on its own, so staff can see which kinds of rule a model drops. A fine test like this could help firms pick models for work where rules are law. It could also show where models need more training.
arxiv-2601-18654:
Juan Wu, Zhe Zhang, and Amit Mehra study when a maker should tag their work as made by AI. Smart tools have cut the cost of text, shots, and clips, so feeds fill with work of mixed worth. Sites now ask makers to tag AI work. Tags are backed by checks that can miss, and by fines for those who skip the tag. Makers must weigh the gain of a hid tag next to the risk of a fine.

The team model that choice and ask what rules make self-tags work. If the fine is too light, few will tag. If the check is too weak, tags lose their worth. Their work maps the mix of check and fine that makes tags a fair sign. Sites could use that map to set rules that keep trust in feeds.
arxiv-2601-18754:
Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Abderrahmane Lakas, and Merouane Debbah build a test suite for drone agents run by language models on next-gen nets. Such drones fly in tasks where a fault can do real harm. They must act well while foes try to fool or break them. Past test suites grade how well drones think, fly, and use the net. They say far less on how the drones stand up to attack.

The new suite grades three traits at once: how safe the agent is, how well it holds up when hit, and how far it can be trusted. It sets those grades in the world of fast new nets, where links are swift but threats are swift too. A full suite could help teams ship drone agents with proof of their strength. It fills a clear gap in the field.
arxiv-2601-18854:
Chandana Pati and S. M. Mallikarjunaiah teach a smart net to learn the stretch laws of stuff that can't stretch past a cap. Such stuff is found in rubbers, in flesh, and in soft man-made solids. As the pull grows, the stretch nears its cap and the stuff grows stiff in slope. Old maths laws state that cap in a plain way. But their sharp bend makes them hard to fit from test data.

The pair build the cap into a net whose form staff can read. The net learns the law from data while the cap holds by build. A law that can be read, and that can't break its cap, is fit for design work. It could guide parts made of flesh-like stuff, from seals to soft robots. The work joins strict maths with learn tools in a clean way.
arxiv-2601-21254:
Daniel Eyles, Emmanuel Lassalle, Adam Stokes, Ramón Paniagua-Domínguez, and Ahsan Nazir study superradiance, where many quantum emitters act together. When emitters share coherence, they release light that is stronger and more directed than usual. A key tool for describing the emitted light tracks how photon counts relate across two times.

For large groups of emitters, exact tracking of that relation is too costly to compute. The authors present sampling methods that make the job practical. Their approach lets researchers describe big ensembles without tracking every emitter in full detail. That opens studies of light sources and sensors built on collective emission.
arxiv-2601-21354:
T. Fujii and co-authors probe a superconductor that is also a Weyl semimetal, using nuclear resonance and magnetic tests under pressure. The material, a layered molybdenum telluride, hosts unusual electronic states. Pressure squeezes the lattice and shifts how it behaves.

The team tracks the superconducting transition and the field needed to kill it as pressure rises. Resonance data add a microscopic view of the electrons at work. Together the measures show how pressure tunes the superconducting state. Such maps help physicists link the material's odd topology to its ability to carry current with no resistance.
arxiv-2601-21554:
V. Carruba, R. Sfair, and O. C. Winter report a newly found asteroid that shares Venus's orbit and may one day threaten Earth. About twenty such Venus co-orbital asteroids are known. Several could drift into hazardous paths over thousands of years.

The team identifies the new object, named 2025 TV10, and charts its motion for the first time. They then assess whether its path could bring it close to Earth. Early tracking of such objects is vital, since small nudges grow over millennia. The work adds one more body to the watch list for planetary defense.
arxiv-2601-21654:
Hao Shen, Hang Yang, and Zhouhong Gu build a stable benchmark for deep research systems that search academic literature. Such systems plan queries, call tools, and synthesize answers over many steps. Testing them against live search services is a reproducibility trap.

Live backends drift over time, hit rate limits, and return different results per run. That variance makes fair comparison between systems almost impossible. ScholarGym fixes the environment so runs can be repeated and compared honestly. A stable gym lets the field measure real progress in automated literature research instead of noise from the tools.
arxiv-2601-21754:
Haoyu Wang and nine co-authors argue that language-based trial and error falls behind learning from experience. Language models excel at tasks framed in words. On unseen tasks that are symbolic or spatial rather than verbal, they lag badly.

Earlier work blamed the mismatch between training text and the test setting. The authors press further, contrasting verbal feedback loops with learning from lived experience in the environment. Their claim favors agents that improve by acting and observing, not by reading critiques alone. The distinction shapes how the next generation of agents should be built and trained.
arxiv-2601-22254:
I. Lamperti and a large team report fast gas flows from a nearby galaxy with two bright cores. Their 2026 preprint uses new data from a tool on the Very Large Telescope in Chile. The galaxy, MCG-03-34-64, may host two active black holes close to each other.

The team map gas that streams out at high speed yet holds very little dust. They trace the flows in the glow of hot gas near the cores. Such outflows can shape how a galaxy grows and forms stars. Close pairs like this one are rare test beds. They show two cores at work at once.
arxiv-2601-22454:
Yijun Ma, Zehong Wang, Weixiang Sun, and Yanfang Ye built a learner that reads the deep patterns of graphs that change over time. Temporal graphs track ties that form, fade, and shift. Their 2026 preprint notes that most tools are built for one task and lean on narrow claims, like short memory or fixed neighborhoods.

Their Temporal Graph Pattern Machine aims to learn the change patterns themselves. A pattern-first tool could serve fraud hunts, network watch, and spread forecasts at once. It could also move across fields with less rework. The work seeks a general engine for change.
arxiv-2601-22654:
Michael Urs Lars Kastor, Jan Rottmayer, Anna Hundertmark, and Nicolas Ralph Gauger built a U-Net surrogate that predicts cancer-cell dynamics under set parameters. Their 2026 preprint pairs a careful solver, written in C++, with a data-driven model. The target system mixes diffusion, flow, and reaction on a flat domain of cell types.

The solver gives trusted runs; the surrogate gives fast ones, tuned by the parameters. Fast, faithful forecasts let teams scan many drug or growth cases. The model keeps its logic open to inspection. The work serves the math side of cancer research.
arxiv-2601-22754:
Guillermo Gil de Avalle, Laura Maruster, and Christos Emmanouilidis pull machine-readable steps from factory troubleshooting guides with vision-language models. These guides pack diagnosis into flowchart-like diagrams, where layout and technical words jointly carry the sense. Their 2026 preprint seeks to extract that know-how in structured form.

Structured steps can feed operator support tools on the shop floor. Workers could then get the right fix path at the right moment. The hard part is reading diagrams as a human would. The work tests how far current models get. It serves a very practical need.
arxiv-2601-22354:
Jinyong Hahn, Zhipeng Liao, Konrad Menzel, and Quang Vuong extend a classic model-choice test to panel data. Panel data track the same units over time, a staple of economics. Their 2026 preprint generalizes the Vuong test, which picks between rival models by fit, using modified profile likelihoods.

Fixed group effects break the plain likelihood's nice traits, so a fix is needed. The team ground the test in an information yardstick. Sound choice tests keep policy math honest. The work is technical econometrics with wide use. It repairs a tool many rely on.
arxiv-2601-22054:
Baorui Ma, Jiahui Yang, Donglin Di, and Xuancheng Zhang scale up training for metric depth estimation, teaching machines to judge real distances from images. Scaling has powered vision foundation models, but depth is harder. Training data come from mixed sensors with different noise, camera-dependent biases, and ambiguous scales.

Their 2026 preprint introduces a pretraining approach designed to learn from exactly such noisy, heterogeneous sources rather than waiting for clean data. More usable depth data means models that measure the world more accurately. Metric depth feeds robot navigation, augmented reality, and driver assistance, where knowing something is near is not enough and the actual distance decides the action.
arxiv-2601-20854:
Aníbal Silva and three co-authors test where transformers belong inside a classic generative model. Their 2026 paper concerns tabular data generation. Tables are a hard domain for generative models. The standard variational autoencoder, or VAE, is built from multilayer perceptrons. It struggles to model links between features. Mixed data types, such as numbers beside categories, make the task worse.

Transformers offer a contrast. Their attention mechanism is well suited to complex feature interactions. The authors explore transformer placement within the VAE design. Placement matters: the encoder, the decoder, or both could host attention. The study weighs which spot gives the best tables. Its results guide builders of synthetic data tools for business and science.
arxiv-2601-21054:
Rami Atar, Leonid Mytnik, and Gershon Wolansky study a swarm of particles that branch, wander, and thin out. Their 2026 paper concerns trimmed branching random walks. Particles perform random walks on a fine grid. When one particle branches, another is removed from the most populated site. This density-dependent selection keeps the swarm in check. The rule couples every particle's fate to the crowd.

The authors connect this process to a free obstacle problem. Free boundary problems ask where a region ends when the edge itself is unknown. That link lets tools from partial differential equations describe the swarm's spread. The result is a cleaner picture of the swarm's long-run shape. Such models echo population growth with local competition. The paper is probability theory with a geometric payoff.
arxiv-2512-01354:
Zhongjie Jiang argues that flaw-free fake data can harm AI models. Fake data is often made smooth and clean. Human text is not. It holds odd tails, quirks, and bounds from how minds work. Training on smooth data alone strips those traits out.

Over time that loss can speed model collapse. The model starts to copy its own bland output. Jiang shows that mimicking human bounds can reverse that slide. Keeping some imperfection in training data may help models stay sharp, varied, and closer to real human text. The claim reframes fake data quality: fluency and smoothness alone are poor guides if the end goal is a model that keeps learning.
arxiv-2512-01654:
Aaron Beyen, Faezeh Khodabandehlou, and Christian Maes study slow changes to steady nonequilibrium processes. A steady process still flows, with heat or current at play. Slow cyclic changes add excess to key traits. Those traits include activity and entropy flux.

The excess takes a geometric form, a Berry phase. Its potential and curvature encode the response. The team evaluates those terms for slow drives. Geometric response laws help design small engines and sensors that work far from equilibrium. Berry terms are geometric, so they depend on the path of the drive, not its speed, which gives them a robustness experiments can exploit.
arxiv-2512-00754:
Asim Ghosh and Bikas Chakrabarti compare three ways to measure inequality in a 2025 paper. The Gini index dates to 1912, the Pietra index to 1915, and the Kolkata index to 2014. All three grow out of the Lorenz curve from 1905, which plots how income or wealth is shared across a population.

Each index sums up the curve's message in a different single number. Ghosh and Chakrabarti work out the exact relations among the three. They then test those relations on real data. Knowing how the measures connect helps economists translate between studies that picked different indexes.
arxiv-2512-00854:
Nguyen Thi Nguyet Nga, Nguyen Huy Thao, and Phung Van Dong propose a particle that does double duty in a 2025 physics paper. Their candidate is a neutral, vectorlike fermion, a particle much like known matter particles but with mirrored partners. Unified theories suggest such fermions might exist.

A slight break in a lepton-like symmetry can make these fermions nearly paired, forming quasi-Dirac states at the tera-electron-volt scale. The authors show such states can generate neutrino masses through a radiative process, where mass arises from loop effects. The same setup can keep dark matter stable. One particle type explaining two mysteries is an attractive economy.
arxiv-2601-22954:
Yuezhou Hu and nine co-authors improve diffusion language models, which write text by refining many tokens at once. Unlike standard models, they can decode tokens in parallel. But common block-wise versions keep only the most confident tokens and throw the rest away, wasting compute.

Their residual context approach keeps more of that work instead of discarding it each round. Reusing context should make parallel writing faster and less wasteful. Efficient diffusion models could rival standard models for chat and drafting at lower cost. Residual context is the core idea: information the old remasking step discarded is carried forward instead of recomputed.
arxiv-2601-23254:
Baoyi Wang and eight co-authors study grep-like retrieval for repository-level code completion. Completing code across a whole project needs cross-file context, but context windows are limited. Retrieval frameworks fetch the right snippets, using semantic indexing or graph analysis of the code structure.

Their empirical study tests simple grep-style retrieval, based on literal text search, against fancier methods. They also optimize the simple approach for this task. A strong showing by plain search would simplify tooling for coding assistants everywhere. Limited context windows force the retrieval question: cross-file dependencies cannot all be pasted into the prompt.
arxiv-2512-00054:
G. K. Skinner and J. F. Krizmanic comment on claims for a large, thin lens proposed for color astrophotography. The lens is a polymer flat, diffractive design, optimized at several wavelengths over a set bandwidth. Its advocates promote it as a cheap route to large-aperture astronomy.

The comment argues that an earlier paper from the same group overstated the lens efficiency. Correcting the record matters because telescope makers may invest based on published numbers. The exchange is a normal, healthy part of optics research. Optimized at a number of wavelengths over a prescribed bandwidth is the design claim the comment examines and qualifies.
arxiv-2512-03154:
Some early galaxies seem too bright for their age. Jacqueline Antwi-Danso and a large team study one such galaxy in this 2025 work. The Webb telescope found many bright galaxies in the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

Such galaxies may be seen during bursts, when star formation spikes for a short time. The team presents a galaxy they describe as a descendant of those first systems. Its traits can test ideas about quenching, when star birth shuts down. The work helps trace how the first galaxies grew and then settled. Its life story links the bright youth of galaxies to their quieter later years.
arxiv-2512-03254:
A treatment may help some patients and not others. Philippe Boileau and co-authors study how to detect such differences in this 2025 work. The usual test assumes all patients gain the same benefit, which is often false.

To find real differences, the traits that modify the effect must be measured well at the start. The authors offer a differential variance method that leans on few assumptions. Sound detection of varied effects helps doctors target treatments. It also stops trials from missing benefits in subgroups. Variance-based tests ask whether effects spread out, a clue that subgroups truly differ.
arxiv-2512-03354:
Judging a new ad policy offline could save firms real money. Hongseon Yeom and co-authors study off-policy evaluation for ad auctions in this 2025 work. Online A/B tests, the gold standard, use much engineering time and risk revenue from weak variants.

Off-policy methods reuse logged data instead, but ad auctions are harder than recommender systems. Policies there are often deterministic, always picking the same action. The authors add stochastic modeling to make evaluation reliable. Better offline tests let ad platforms improve without costly live trials. Stochastic policies match how ad auctions really randomize, which sharpens offline estimates.
arxiv-2512-02054:
The vacuum of space may act like a material when fields grow strong. Some theories let it break CP symmetry, the mirror rule that links matter and antimatter. Three authors, Ospedal, Turcati, and Duarte, study this kind of electrodynamics in 2025, one where the field equations are not linear.

First they work out the field equations and how waves move through a magnetic background. They find the CP-breaking term makes the vacuum respond in unlike ways along unlike axes. Then they compute small shifts to the heat laws of blackbody radiation. The work tests how strange vacuum behavior would show up in light and heat.
arxiv-2512-02254:
How can you tell whether a real network plausibly came from a given random model? Narayan Sabhahit and a large team address in 2025 the construction of typical networks from a model, deterministically, so that a dataset can be compared against what the model usually produces.

Network scientists constantly judge whether a model explains an observed network, from friendships to protein interactions. A deterministic way to build the typical case gives that judgment a concrete reference point. The work strengthens the basic statistics of networks, where randomness is both the model and the obstacle to testing it.
arxiv-2512-02354:
Aadityan Ganesh, Clayton Thomas, and S. Matthew Weinberg study the rules that set fees on blockchains. When users pay to get a transaction included, the fee rule shapes what miners and users do. A good rule should be simple to follow on chain, with no gain from gaming the system.

Their 2025 study adds a stricter test: a miner should gain nothing from a side auction held off chain. The authors characterize fee rules that pass this off chain influence proof test. The results help designers build fee markets that stay fair even when side deals are possible. Fee rules shape trust, and trust is what lets a chain gain and keep its users.
arxiv-2512-02554:
Changxiao Ma and eight co-authors generate fake pedestrian images to train person recognition systems. Person re-identification matches the same person across cameras, but large labeled datasets are hard to build. Privacy limits and labeling costs keep real data scarce.

Synthetic people could fill the gap, yet past generators often lose the person's identity or give users little control. OmniPerson is a unified generator built to preserve identity while staying controllable. Better synthetic data could improve recognition training without filming more real people, a gain for both accuracy and privacy. Fake crowds can be made in bulk, while real crowds take time, cost, and care to film on the street.
arxiv-2512-02654:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches and six co-authors report a banner year for their security AI in hacking contests. Capture the Flag events test teams on real style security puzzles under time pressure. The authors ask whether such competitions are becoming obsolete as AI agents improve.

Their system, Cybersecurity AI, is described as topping multiple major events in 2025. The authors report it outranked thousands of human teams again and again. Whether or not contests fade, results like these force a rethink of training, defense, and how security skill is measured. Scores like these will push schools and firms to train staff in new ways for a new kind of foe.
arxiv-2512-02954:
Jared Siegel and eight co-authors measure how strongly exploding stars and black holes push gas around inside cosmic structures. Baryon feedback redistributes gas away from the dark matter layout and suppresses the matter power spectrum on small scales. The size and scale pattern of that suppression are uncertain.

The team reads feedback strength from X-ray gas mass fractions, kSZ effect profiles, and galaxy galaxy lensing together. Three probes agreeing point to strong feedback, per the title. Pinning feedback down is essential before weak lensing surveys can turn galaxy shapes into tight cosmology. Three eyes that agree beat one eye that shouts, and that is the strength of the case this team puts in print here.
arxiv-2512-03054:
Ciro Benito Raggio and eight co-authors make federated medical learning cheaper so poorer hospitals can join. Federated learning lets institutions train shared deep learning models without pooling their data. Heavy resource demands, though, exclude centers with limited computing, widening healthcare disparities.

Their green AI approach freezes parts of the encoder adaptively during training. The test task converts MRI scans to CT like images across sites. Lower cost training invites more diverse hospitals in, which improves the shared model and spreads its benefits more fairly. Low cost is not a side gain here; it is the point. A tool priced out of poor wards helps just the wards that need it the least in all the world.
plos-pone-0010154:
Caitlin McCabe, Sue Goldie, and David Fisman weighed a treatment plan for pregnant women with HIV in 2010. Suppressing the virus in late pregnancy prevents transmission to the baby. Directly observed therapy, where staff watch each dose, improves that suppression. Their PLOS ONE study projected both effectiveness and cost for the third trimester.

Cost-effectiveness analysis asks whether the health gained is worth the money spent. Watched therapy costs more to deliver than handing over pills. If it prevents enough infant infections, it may be the better buy. Their model was built to make that judgment for health systems.
plos-pone-0010254:
The authors were Catarina Hioe, Terri Wrin, Michael Seaman, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested antibodies against a loop on the HIV surface. The V3 loop on the virus envelope protein gp120 was once called HIV's main neutralizing domain. It was later dismissed as too variable between strains to serve as a useful antibody target for vaccines.

New structural and chemical data suggested V3 still holds conserved features. The team showed monoclonal antibodies against V3 neutralized many HIV-1 subtypes broadly. A variable target that still yields broad protection could change vaccine design assumptions.
plos-pone-0010354:
Michael Waterston and Christopher Pack asked whether magnetic brain stimulation sharpens vision, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The method, called rTMS, pulses magnetic fields through the skull. At some settings it was thought to dull the stimulated brain area briefly. Researchers often treated it as a reversible, virtual lesion for experiments. Waterston and Pack tested that assumption on visual tasks.

After stimulation, subjects actually got better at telling visual stimuli apart. That result cuts against the simple dulling story. If pulses can improve performance, many past experiments need a second look. The finding also hints at uses for boosting perception. Either way, the study warns against easy labels for a complex tool. What rTMS does may depend on task and timing.
plos-pone-0009754:
Honey bees face many stresses, and chemicals inside their own hives are one of them. Christopher Mullin and colleagues measured pesticide levels in North American apiaries. Their survey appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Apiaries are places where beekeepers keep colonies of honey bees. The team found high levels of miticides, chemicals used against hive mites, plus other farm chemicals. Residues build up in wax and pollen that bees live on. Beekeepers themselves apply some of these chemicals to save their colonies. The findings raised hard questions about what chronic exposure does to bee health.
plos-pone-0009854:
Prostate cancer often spreads to bone and changes how bone grows. Murali Ravoori and colleagues measured that bone response in mice without cutting the tissue. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bone response is a key sign of how the disease advances.

The team combined in vivo micro-CT scans of living mice with ex vivo scans and DXA after death. Micro-CT builds detailed three-dimensional images from X-rays. Together the methods quantified how much mineralized bone the cancer produced. Noninvasive measures let researchers follow the same animal over time.
plos-pone-0009954:
Alcohol makes fruit flies hyperactive, and two neurons may drive much of that buzz. Eric Kong and colleagues traced the circuit behind the response. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fruit flies are a standard model for alcohol research.

A pair of dopamine neurons targets the D1-like receptor DopR in the central complex. Dopamine is the brain's reward and movement signal. Activating that path promotes ethanol-stimulated locomotion in Drosophila. A two-neuron circuit is a clean model for how alcohol moves behavior. The central complex is a brain hub for movement control.
